Social media platforms have become an integral part of daily life for most of the world's population. The vast amounts of data residing in these platforms have become an invaluable resource for understanding various aspects of human behavior, including consumer behavior. This is because social media posts can reveal extensive information about one's behavior, preferences, and personality traits. For instance, one can indirectly determine questions such as "What is the user's likely daily agenda?" and "What are the users' interests?" through analyzing their timeline. A useful and direct application of social media data is in consumer service. Specifically, it can be used to predict how extensively users consume certain goods and services in the offline world. One such interesting domain is the restaurant industry. Understanding how much individuals consume at restaurants can have various implications, such as informing marketing strategies, improving customer service, and even facilitating trend analysis. While directly asking individuals about their consumption habits may provide precise answers, this method is both labor-intensive and prone to self-reporting biases. Hence, leveraging publicly available social media data offers a more accessible and potentially more accurate alternative. Our work builds on the premise that user online behavior might reveal aspects of their offline consumption habits. The central inquiry in this paper is whether and to what extent one can predict a consumer's restaurant consumption level using their social media behavior. To address this question, we exploit the wealth of data available on the Chinese social media platform Sina Weibo and the local restaurant review system Dianping. Specifically, we construct a substantial dataset of 8,844 users who have registered on both platforms using their Sina Weibo account (social login). This dataset allows us to link an individual's online social media activity to their restaurant consumption level as reported by Dianping (analogous to Yelp in the English-speaking world). We define consumption level as the self-reported spending habits that users volunteer on the Dianping platform when they review restaurants. The central contribution of our work is the design and implementation of a systematic method to leverage this user-linked dataset for predicting restaurant consumption level using a variety of machine learning models. The base for our predictive models is a rich set of features derived from both raw online behavior (e.g., user timelines, posts and comments, followed accounts) and latent features (e.g., topics of interest inferred from latent Dirichlet allocation, clusters of followed celebrities).

Latent Variable Models of Concept-Attribute Attachment LEXICOGRAPHIC ontologies have enjoyed significant successful applications; these are realized as Knowledge Bases (KB) which are widely used in NLP tasks. An example of such an ontology is WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), which, though successful, suffers from several questions such as the domain coverage and the accuracy and completeness of the attributes and relations (Mihalcea and Hruschka, 2004;Evang et al., 2009;Mihalcea and Wacholder, 2010;Lindberg et al., 2012). In reality, a rich set of attributes and attributes’ values for verbal and nominal concepts are absent or only partially provided in WordNet. One typical example is Sports, where relationships among semantic concepts (i.e., Sports, Event, Player, Venue, etc.) and their properties (i.e., Gender of participants, Type of game, Amount of money involved, etc.) are important, yet sometimes not well captured. While manual extension of such a KB is an obvious solution, the manual annotation process is expensive, time consuming and error-prone. A more attractive or even indispensable solution is to automate the ontological extension process. One way to automate concept-attribute attachment is to leverage different modalities of the knowledge, most importantly linguistic data (i.e., the textual corpus). Latent Variable Models (LVMs) are popular within natural language, speech, and image processing research communities. They can be used to model probabilistic distributions over the features extracted from text, which could be significantly useful for summarizing the information in text in forms that are relevant for ontology extension. For instance, in the case of automatically assigning attributes and their values to a concept, the latent representation learned from a large corpus of text mentioning Sports and the properties that they might satisfy, can be effectively used to identify new attributes, and if one’s model can capture the different characteristics (e.g., measured variables vs. property words) of attributes, then the matched attributes can be assigned to the suitable concepts. If we think of concepts and attributes as nodes and relations in a graph, LVMs can be used to infer concepts and attributes not yet present in WordNet, and build connections between them. In this paper, we use Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003) as a representative LVM to model the concept-attribute space of such an ontology. LDA allows us to infer the underlying distribution over latent attributes based on the textual co-occurrence patterns of concepts observed in a corpus. We evaluate our approach on concept-attribute attachment.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models on morphologically rich languages like Arabic presents an inherent problem. Words in these languages can have an infinite set of possible surface forms which complicates the availability of parallel data (Graff, 2003). Phrase-based translation methods handle this issue by tokenising the source and target languages separately (Koehn, 2009). This approach leads to an easier and more principled handling of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words and compounds, but suffers from data sparsity. Table 1 (Koehn and Schroeder, 2006) shows how a morphologically complex language like Arabic encounters severe word order and word split mismatch in SMT compared to a simpler language such as English. As a result, training a NMT model on such a source and target language pair faces significant challenges due to the radical difference in the tokenisation and segmentation strategies. On the other hand, well-documented solutions for morphologically rich languages include inter-layer alignment and soft word boundary handling (Galilei, 2013). Another approach is to pretrain a word-level language model (LMs) on the target language corpus. The LM's weights are then incorporated at both the training and inference phases (Sennrich and Haddow, 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019). However, such techniques don't address the problem of segmentation and its inverse, desegmentation (or synthesis). Desegmentation is particularly challenging because the system must piece back the correct form from the space of all possible segmented outputs, without knowing the correct segmentation a priori. For example, if the system is trained to translate "فهم" (verb "to understand", present tense, singular) from Arabic to English, it might generate a number of valid "segmented outputs" which would need to be desegmented to produce the single most probable English translation "understand". The standard phrase-based NMT decoder doesn’t directly address the issue of segmentation or desegmentation. The standard NMT decoder works over a fixed segment size and outputs a fully segmented sentence which might miss the long-range and compositional dependencies typical of morphologically rich languages. Consequently, integrating a segmentation stage into the NMT decoding process is appealing, though comes with complexities. A key decision would be deciding when to segment during decoding and how to handle dependencies across segmented words. Moreover, such an approach would require reranking or adjusting outputs to consider not only segment choices but also the desegmented form. Our contribution in this work is to present a novel method of integrating morphological desegmentation into phrase-based NMT decoders.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is one of the key applications in natural language processing. AES systems today still largely rely on carefully designed features to evaluate and score essays. These features include features related to length, vocabulary, grammatical correctness, and more. However, the ideal set of features is not only difficult to design, but also may vary depending on questions or topics asked. Furthermore, the accuracy and robustness of these systems are highly dependent on the complexity and quality of these features, and the pre-defined set of rules can sometimes be restrictive and may not cover all variations of good essays. In this context, we explore a neural approach to automate essay scoring. Unlike traditional systems that rely on feature engineering, a neural approach can automatically learn to evaluate essays directly from the text, without having to define features. Specifically, we propose to use neural networks to learn the relationship between an essay and its assigned score based on sample essays and their scores. We consider various neural network architectures that might be suitable for this task. Some of the models we tested include multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, which are known for their ability to handle varying length sequences. For each model, we develop a specific model architecture that takes a written essay as input and predict its score based on the training data. The learning process is typically framed as a prediction problem where the neural network learns the mapping between the input essay (as a sequence of words or variables encoding certain characteristics of the text) and the expected score (usually a numeric value or grade). We performed an extensive experimentation using a large-scale dataset of essays and human-annotated scores to validate the performance of the different neural models. For this purpose, we defined evaluation metrics commonly used in the AES community, including quadratic weighted Kappa (QWK) for measuring agreement between machine and human scores and the root mean squared error (RMSE) for assessing the absolute difference. The results show that our best model, based on LSTM networks, significantly outperforms a matched baseline by a margin of 5.6% in terms of QWK. This suggests that deep neural networks are capable of capturing complex and nuanced patterns in essays that previous feature-based systems may miss or underperform on. In addition to the comparison with a baseline model, we also conduct analysis to better understand what our neural models learn and how they make decisions.

Introduction Learning to extract temporal information from text has become increasingly important for various NLP applications. For instance, in question-answering (QA) systems, temporal information is often critical for questions such as "When was the last time a certain event happened?" and "When was the company founded?" (Strube and Mary 2008, Schreiber et al. 2014). Extracting temporal information can also provide context to document segmentation (Chen and Ji 2011) and help to better understand long textual dialogues (König et al. 2012). Research on temporal information extraction has been done in two major directions: (a) to directly model relationships among semantic entities (i.e., events, objects, or persons) or (b) to extract temporal relations through syntactic cues (Marcotte et al. 2000, Strube and Mary 2008, Kilgarriff 2009). In the first direction, hierarchical or top-down models have been commonly used. In early work, Kilgarriff (2009) presents a temporal decision model with symbols for semantic units (such as “person,” “event,” and “location”). The model assumed that the temporal relationship between two events can be written as: \begin{equation } \text{sense}_1 \otimes \text{sense}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{operator}} \text{Relation} \end{equation } where \text{sense}_1 and \text{sense}_2 represent the event arguments and the operator captures the temporal relationship. However, such approaches need large amounts of manually annotated data for each semantic unit and the operator set is inconsistent across different input sentences due to the complexity of textual expressions (Nischen, 2014). The second direction focuses on the syntactic cues for temporal relation recognition. The simplest, yet popular, approach leverages the dependency-based relationship between entities to infer temporal relations. For example, verbs acting as predicates are often temporally linked to their subject or object arguments (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002; Strube and Mary, 2008) and some linguistic features (durative/punctual verbs and temporal triggers) can also serve as hints (blunsom et al., 2005; Giezeman et al., 2010). In this paper, we focus on the latter approach and introduce a set of Lightweight Temporal Relation LSTMs (LTR-LSTMs), which comprise simple yet uniform in architecture. The LTR-LSTMs are designed to capture different temporal relationships by modeling: 1. Intra-sentence temporal relations (e.g., "I hiked and then went home."), 2. Cross-sentence temporal relations (e.g., "The event that took place yesterday."), and 3. Document creation time relations (e.g., "Posting made at 2018-04-05").

Thus, we aim here to improve the existing transliteration mining techniques by using a generative graph reinforcement model. Our technique begins with an initial set of transliteration mappings acquired via automatic alignment of transliteration pairs at the character sequence level. This procedure can be done by tokenizing the source and target into their respective scripts, aligning those tokens using a dependence-based, edit-distance matched approach (like the Sequence Matching Language Modeling (SMLM) framework Cooke et al., 2007), and then extracting the best possible mappings from the alignment. The mappings are then modeled on a bipartite graph, where one set of nodes represents the source character sequence, and the other set represents the target character sequence. Edges between these nodes correspond to initial estimated mappings. The graph reinforcement algorithm iteratively explored the graph space seeking to - learn more mappings by connecting unconnected nodes - reassess and reweight existing edges based on the inferred worthiness of these mappings given - bidirectional information: inherently learning that certain source/target mappings are more or less probable or more or less coherent compositionally - continuous

Training natural language processing (NLP) or computer vision (CV) models often requires large-scale datasets. In particular, datasets that provide an association between text and images are increasingly important for developing image captioning systems (Krishnamurthy and Kollar et al., 2013; Venugopalan et al., 2015), questions answering systems (Bordes et al., 2015), and conversational systems (Weston et al., 2015) where users can ask questions about images or objects depicted in images. While traditional approaches for creating these datasets require considerable human effort (Chen and Hovy, 2015) to either manually annotate the texts or create images, recent advances in crowdsourcing have allowed gathering vast amounts of crowdsourced image-caption pairs (Kazakova and Fetterolf, 2014; Karpathy and Fei-Fei, 2015; Agirre et al., 2013), often with relatively low costs compared to traditional human annotation. However, creative and varied text descriptions, which are central to many advanced NLP and CV applications such as paraphrasing or multi-label image captioning, are often sacrificed or rarer in these crowdsourced datasets. The lack of diversity in provided captions might arise for several different reasons. One plausible reason is cognitive bias: when multiple people describe the same image, they tend to provide similar descriptions, often sacrificing vividness or creativity, resulting in caption sparsity. This stems from human nature; when facing repetitive tasks (e.g., describing multiple images of a similar theme, like "dog in the park"), humans tend to fall into repetitive descriptions based on key visual elements (e.g., "a dog is in a park"). Despite efforts to mitigate such biases (e.g., by providing contextual information about the task in [Kazakova and Fetterolf, 2014]), or by intentionally countering the bias (e.g., the MoreDataMoreProblems crowdsourcing [Li, 2017] encouraging more creative responses), it is inherently challenging to systematically generate highly diverse and creative captions while keeping the response within human and machine readability limits. While some previous work (Nenkova and Lapata, 2010; Li et al., 2015) has explored generating paraphrases of previously annotated text, or using datasets with abundant repetition (e.g., user-generated questions on image information like in Yahoo! Answers [Bordes et al., 2010]), those datasets often lack the explicit association of captions to images and the volume compared to datasets manually designed with complete and varied captions. This paper proposes a new approach to tackle the caption sparsity issue in existing datasets and to produce datasets that contain expressively varied text descriptions while still maintaining the image-text association often demanded by both NLP and CV tasks.

Automatic extraction of causal relations from text is essential for various NLP tasks such as information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. Existing methods either rely on explicit markers such as "because," "since," and "as" to identify causal relations. However, causality is also understood implicitly through the context and the meaning of the words and clauses – a far more difficult task given the open class nature of possible causal phrasing and the need for world knowledge and inference. While some work has been done on identifying causality, it suffers from several limitations. Table 1 (adapted from Plank and Scheffler, 2011) shows most commonly used causal knowledge bases and their word sets, which are typically small. 3 These word lists are often incomplete and can result in a very high number of false positives when used to extract causality. While methods like Plank et al. (2005), Zhang et al. (2011), and Mitamura et al. (2005) have made significant progress, identifying all possible variations of causal phrasing – known and unknown – in a given language remains difficult. For example, Spanish verbs such as "conducir a," "ser el resultado de," and "ocasionar" intuitively convey a cause and effect relationship, but are quite different from English causal markers like "lead to," "result in," or "cause." Modifying existing methods for each language and providing evidence for the entire set of possible variations is challenging. Another approach, based on patterns of words and phrases surrounding the explicit markers, has been explored by (Scarton et al., 2011, 2014). However, these approaches either need hand-engineered patterns or domain-specific training data and are not fully generic. To tackle these limitations, we explore the opportunity of leveraging parallel Wikipedias. Parallel corpora allow us to exploit different surface forms of the same textual concept across languages. This approach has been successfully applied to tasks like transfer learning (Conneau and Schwenk, 2017, 2018), cross-lingual word embedding (Conneau et al., 2018), and name transliteration (Saha et al., 2018). We apply this idea to causal relations by taking advantage of the fact that concepts of causality are – more or less – the same across languages, despite having different linguistic forms. Our approach can potentially identify a much wider range of causal phrases than relying solely on English explicit markers. The key to our approach is distant supervision: given parallel sentences (or sentences and their translations), we can induce new causal markers and their patterns by highlighting parallel mentions of these markers.

Training high-quality classifiers often requires large amounts of annotated training data. However, acquiring such data can be expensive and time-consuming. This challenge is particularly significant in situations where data is scarce or when the data acquisition process itself is costly, for instance in many human annotation tasks involved in natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision. Two potential strategies to reduce the annotation cost are active learning (AL) (Cohn et al., 1994; Tong and Koller, 2002; Haupt and Haupt, 2003; Settles, 2009) and crowdsourcing (Howe, 2006; Malhotra et al., 2010; Kittur et al., 2008). Active learning, despite being an established field of research, has not been commonly applied to crowdsourcing platforms. This paper presents a novel application of active learning in the context of Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), a popular crowdsourcing platform used extensively in many human computation tasks, including language-related annotation tasks (John et al., 2012; Callison-Burch et al., 2007; Halevy et al., 2009). AMT provides a platform where workers accept simple tasks for small payments. By issuing specific and well-regulated tasks, it is possible to harness the collective intelligence of the platform for annotating data (Mendes et al., 2012). In this paper, we investigate the feasibility and utility of combining active learning with crowdsourcing by using AMT for two specific language understanding tasks: named entity recognition (NER) and sentiment detection. Specifically, we evaluate the utility of active learning strategies in the context of a noisy crowdsourcing scenario by comparing the learning outcomes of active learning with and without crowdsourced annotations. We apply a suite of AL algorithms, including the well-known uncertainty sampling (Thrun, 1996), to identify the most informative examples based on the model's confidence or expected informativeness. The measured variables for evaluation are both the accuracy of the final trained model and the cost efficiency in terms of the number of annotation requests needed to reach a certain level of accuracy. Relevance of Active Learning in Crowdsourcing Active learning is particularly appealing when applying it to noisy crowdsourcing platforms like AMT for several reasons. First, it minimizes the number of annotations needed to train a model of high accuracy. This is crucial given the cost and potential noise inherent in crowdsourced data. For instance, AMT has an inherent noise component as most workers are not experts in linguistics or machine learning and may misunderstand or inaccurately perform the task. Prior research has investigated various techniques for identifying and dealing with inherently noisy crowdsourced data (Kittur et al., 2010; Offner et al., 2010; Setlur et al., 2011).

Linguistic Steganography Using Automatically Generated Paraphrases Introduction Linguistic Steganography is a form of covert communication that hides secret messages within normally acceptable language. It exploits linguistic properties of natural language to encode information into a message that is protected from unauthorized access. A particular challenge in this area, as with many steganography questions, is the choice of cover medium and the transformations that make steganographic communication effective while retaining "normal" appearance. This makes text (which is language of course, as fractals of language) an attractive but very difficult medium for steganography. As pointed out by Foers (2003), knowledge of language rules and usage, along with a rich mental model of the world, limits the extent to which steganographic encodings can go unnoticed by an observer. While steganographic methods exist that achieve reasonable imperceptibility in images and speech (e.g. audio), linguistic steganography appears to have been less successful partly because of the intrinsic semantic and structural regularity of language (Bergmair, 2007; Foers, 2003). Given the success of distributional semantic models such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) in capturing cognitive linguistic phenomena such as semantic similarity and word concreteness (Baroni et al., 2014), we hypothesized that distributional models might be used to generate high-quality paraphrases (transformations of a sentence without changing its meaning), which in turn can be used to conceal a text in another: the text is encoded in a stego text through transformation and a message is retrieved by applying "backward" transformations. Previous work in generating paraphrases, while not explicitly for steganography, has shown promising results; for instance, Pimentel et al. (2015) and Johnson and Heppin (2017) both demonstrated improvements in paraphrasing quality over base models. However, since their focus is mainly on paraphrasing for translation and summarization, the generated paraphrases may still be discernible as artificial when used for changing the meaning of a text. Our interest here is in automatically generating paraphrases such that the transformed sentences are not only meaning-preserving but also of comparable fluency and acceptability compared to original sentences, thus making them suitable for steganographic purposes. For this work, we build on recent advances in machine learning, and intend to explore the potential of automatically generated paraphrases in linguistic steganography. Proposing Clearly Defined Goals and Deliverables: Our main task in this work is two-fold. First, we wish to evaluate current paraphrasing technology and assess whether it can generate paraphrases that are often indistinguishable from original sentences while maintaining the semantic equivalence required for any steganographic transformation.

Training neural event schema induction models involves learning to optimize a generative model to capture the latent structure of events. Many successful methods for event schema induction rely upon n-gram models or word representations alone, using only head entities and their frequencies to characterize event participants. However, entities within sentences are often complex and contain rich, descriptive information, frequently beyond their head words. In clinical events, for instance, "heart failure" versus "heart and lung failure" paints very different pictures, with the addition of organs and conditions revealing more about the etiology, severity, or outcome of the event. Similarly, "Professor Smith", "John Smith", and "The Smith Firm" refer to distinct entities with different roles and properties, but all may represent the entity "Smith" in an event schema. Moreover, beyond just entity features, event schemas are also sensitive to correlations and interactions between entity roles. For example, "X was in the room when Y happened" can carry implications about causality or context that might not be purely captured by associating certain entities with certain roles, but also requires understanding their relationships and the semantics of their interplay. The key intuition underlying the proposed approach is that by representing entities as potential topics in a probabilistic topic model – specifically, a sparse, hierarchical Dirichlet process topic model – we can account for this richer, descriptive information about entities. Each substring within an event mention could potentially represent a topic, capturing contextual information that extends beyond the head word of an entity. This is in contrast to existing models that typically represent entities as fixed, one-word placeholders. The proposed method, termed "Generative Event Schema Induction with Entity Disambiguation" (GESID), aims to leverage this additional information during the schema learning process. The key ideas of the proposal are as follows: 1. Entity Representation through Probabilistic Topic Distributions: Instead of representing entities as fixed word representations, the proposed approach uses probabilistic topic distributions to represent entities. Each part of an entity mention (such as "heart and lung" or "The Smith Firm") can potentially contribute to different topics, capturing the various aspects of the entity. For example, "heart and lung" might contribute to both "organs" and "diseases" topics, and "The Smith Firm" might contribute to "organizations" and "legal entities" topics. 2. Learning with Sparse Hierarchical Dirichlet Process: To model these topics, we employ a sparse, hierarchical Dirichlet process (S-HDP), which can capture complex, hierarchical structures within the topic distributions.

Tree-kernel (TK) methods represent a powerful class of algorithms achieving state-of-the-art performance in various domains such as natural language processing, bioinformatics and web search (Mirkin, 2012; Lee and Sung, 2009; Song et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2003). At the heart of these algorithms is the embedding of data into a high-dimensional feature space defined over tree-like structures (Stratos and Likas, 2003). The geometric properties of this space, encoded by tree-kernels, enable efficient and expressive learning tasks. However, the resulting feature landscapes pose significant knowledge extraction challenges, primarily due to the intricate and complex structures of the tree operations. This complexity renders the feature set opaque to domain experts, thereby limiting our understanding of the correlations and patterns derived by TK methods. Unpacking the feature space of a tree-kernel involves two main challenges: (1) importance estimation and (2) featurespace interpretability. The first challenge, known as feature selection or weighting, is crucial because it reduces dimensionality while retaining the most relevant aspects of the original data. However, traditional feature selection methods often fail when applied to tree-kernel spaces, as these methods are designed for flat feature representations and do not account for the tree-like structure and the underlying notions of geometric similarity that tree-kernels are based on. The second challenge lies in the explicit interpretation of the selected features. Without interpretability, identifying the features that contribute most to the performance of the model and the underlying patterns learned become nearly impossible. This lack of interpretability can hinder model deployment, model debugging, and, more importantly, model understanding and trust in high-stakes applications such as health care or legal decision-making. Addressing these challenges requires a novel approach that can (1) effectively estimate the importance of each feature within the context of the tree-kernel space, and (2) map this estimation to an interpretable feature representation of the input data. To the best of our knowledge, the literature lacks methods that are specifically designed to tackle both challenges of tree-kernel feature space reverse engineering in a unified way. Therefore, this paper presents a novel framework for reverse engineering the feature space of tree-kernel methods to extract informative features. Our framework distinguishes itself from conventional feature selection methods and tree-based methods in two key ways. First, it leverages the internal decision-making processes of standard tree-kernel based machine learning models, particularly Support Vector Machines (SVM), to estimate the importance of each feature within the tree-kernel feature space.

Aspect-level sentiment classification is a fine-grained task in sentiment analysis. Traditional overall sentiment classification typically considers the polarity of an entire sentence; however, it lacks precision since it aggregates sentiments from different aspects together. To tackle this issue, many researchers proposed various methods to handle aspect-level sentiment analysis in recent years. A particular effective approach is to rely on aspect categories – which are questions or subtopics about the product or service that users may discuss and express their opinions about – to guide the sentiment analysis tasks. For instance, when commenting on a restaurant, the users may talk about service (e.g., "The service is friendly and keeps coming to get our feedback.") or food (e.g., "The pasta is oily and the portion is too small."). By analyzing the sentiment of these different aspects, we can obtain a more complete and detailed view of user opinions. Many existing methods for aspect-level sentiment analysis can be grouped into two main categories: rule-based and machine learning based approaches. Some rule-based methods build sets of hand-crafted rules to identify sentiment expressions related to specific aspects, for example, Janyce Wiebe and Martha Palmer (2002) proposed a set of potential useful features for determining whether an adverb phrase is related to a specific or a general aspect. While rule-based methods can be effective, they are often brittle and may not generalize well to unseen data or to the myriad of possible aspects that may arise in user comments. On the other hand, machine learning-based approaches learn models that can automatically extract sentiment-related information based on the training data. However, these methods must typically decide for themselves which linguistic features to use from the input text to predict the sentiment for each aspect. Without a principled way to decide which features are important, they may not always focus correctly on the relevant sections of the text that highlight sentiment about the aspect in question. For example, if a comment about a "quick service" contains both positive and negative aspects ("delicious food" and "slow service"), conventional machine learning methods may incorrectly or less robustly predict the sentiment for "service". To address this problem, we propose a novel approach that employs a hierarchical structure for aspect-level sentiment analysis. Our method is inspired by the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in various machine learning tasks, including machine translation and image recognition. These mechanisms help focus on particular parts of the input or on particular aspects of a model’s internal representation.

Coreference resolution, the process of identifying all expressions in a text that refer to the same entity or concept, is a fundamental task in natural language understanding. While this problem is well-studied and much progress has been made, its medical domain counterparts, medical concept coreference resolution and medical entity normalization (also known as concept normalization, concept linking, or instance identification questions), present unique challenges and have garnered significant recent attention due to their potential applications in clinical decision making, automated report generation, and the curation and indexing of medical records and literature. One of the primary difficulties in medical coreference resolution is the scarcity of annotated data due to the laborious and time-consuming process of annotation. To circumvent this, researchers have explored semi-supervised learning techniques to augment the training data, which often involve leveraging available unlabeled data. Two such techniques that have shown promise are co-training and multi-view learning with posterior regularization (APPES - "Two-View Training with Posterior Regularization"). Co-training is a semi-supervised learning method that involves training two or more classifiers on different, yet complementary, views of the training data. In the case of medical concept coreference, this might involve using two or more distinct sets of features (such as semantic features capturing the meaning of concepts and temporal features capturing temporal relationships and changes). The classifiers trained on these distinct views predict labels (in this case, positive or negative coreference judgements) for the same unlabeled data points. The predictions are then combined and used to train the core model on a small set of labeled data, or they can be used to predict labels for the unlabeled data itself. Posterior regularization, on the other hand, is a technique that can be applied to multi-view learning by adding constraints to the model parameters. These constraints "regularize" the model to learn a representation that is robust across different views or data features. For example, in the context of finding the most generalizable understanding of medical concepts across different viewpoints (semantic features and temporal features), the model is trained to learn parameters that are likely to produce consistent predictions across all views. The "posterior" in the name refers to the probabilistic outputs of each view, which are used to compute the regularization term to minimize the divergence between the view-specific outputs and the model's predictions. Our work explores these semi-supervised methods for the task of medical concept coreference resolution in clinical text.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, training data can be cost prohibitive or nonexistent for under-resourced languages. To alleviate this issue, one may use cross-lingual embeddings to exploit high-quality annotated data available in a resourced language. Cross-lingual embeddings involve a mapping from a source language onto target language word embeddings (e.g., via parallel corpora). A recent study (Vinyals and Le, 2015) of cross-lingual language modelling shows word embeddings learned on monolingual corpora extracted from an even larger multilingual corpus align better than embeddings learned from translatable word pairs, suggesting that a rich source of examples is key to creating such mappings. Moreover, recent work (Artetxe et al., 2017; Larochelle and Kwiatkowski, 2017) shows that even without explicit supervision, cross-lingual mappings can be learned from monolingual data alone, which is the setting amenable to many applications with missing parallel data. However, applying cross-lingual embeddings to parsing poses several challenges. Typically, we expect useful general-purpose embeddings to share structure across different language-specific parsing contexts or even languages. For instance, a parser may want to fetch sense symbols provided for both monolingual and cross-lingual training. Or, a parser may need to align the distributed representation learnt in one language to a downstream syntactic dependency parse tree, which is to be aligned cross-lingually. Issues can arise if embeddings lack distinctness or equidistance for target task specific prompts: sparsity, learned idiosyncrasies can prevent reliable mapping, while for instance semantic proximity between words of different words and their contexts may help retrieval and mapping over the embeddings. These challenges come in varying degrees depending on the specific parser the embeddings are to be applied to and the target NLP task. This means design or selection of embeddings for a particular application needs to be measured against specific requirements. Our research focuses on the application of cross-lingual embeddings to NLP parsing specifically dependency parsing. We will explore various factors that affect the usefulness of cross-lingual embeddings in this context, including source language, monolingual training data quality and quantity, target language, parser design, and target task – and we will quantify these with experiments across these parameters. We broadly divide our investigation into two parts. In the first part, we evaluate zero-shot performance of dependency parsing across languages by leveraging monolingual BERT embeddings (Devlin et al., 2019). In the second part, we train specialized cross-lingual embeddings tailored towards dependency parsing using a task-specific translation system (Koehn, 2005) and execute a more focused evaluation.

Training neural networks with all the fine-grained details and variance seen in natural language corpora can present significant challenges. Many successful applications of neural networks to language tasks learn to utilize such information through feature engineering, using both sparse and dense features extracted from various linguistic resources. Part-of-speech tagging (POS) is one such task where this diversity is particularly evident, as questions such as "What is the part of speech (e.g., noun, verb, adjective) of a given word in a sentence?" require a model to capture a wide range of linguistic subtleties. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), especially long short-term memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), have been particularly successful at such sequence-labeling tasks due to their ability to model complex dependencies over sequences of inputs (Sundermeyer et al., 2012). LSTM RNNs can capture information over long ranges, making them capable of capturing intricate dependencies and trends in language, which is crucial for language understanding and generation tasks. However, handling dense, continuous features, such as word embeddings, can be challenging within traditional deep learning architectures. Word embeddings are high-dimensional dense vectors that aim to capture semantic and syntactic properties of words within a given context. These embeddings, learned from large unannotated corpora, have proven highly effective across multiple NLP tasks (Mikolov et al., 2013). For a POS tagging model, leveraging word embeddings effectively can significantly improve performance, as they encode rich linguistic information that might not be easily captured through discrete features alone. The complexity introduced by combining discrete features (e.g., character-level N-grams, part-of-speech frequencies, and lexical contexts) with dense continuous features like word embeddings necessitates innovative approaches. Traditional neural network architectures may not be optimized for the interaction between these different types of features. Therefore, to effectively combine these features, design choices must be made regarding the network architecture. This includes the type of layers used, the method of feature combination, and the learning strategy. For instance, since word embeddings are typically dense and high-dimensional, storing and processing them can be computationally expensive. Furthermore, combining continuous and discrete features without a careful design can lead to suboptimal model performance due to issues such as feature redundancy, inadequate feature interaction, and inability to learn from complex non-linear relationships. In this work, we propose an approach to leverage corpus-wide information for POS tagging by designing a neural network architecture that seamlessly integrates discrete and continuous features.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Pattern Dictionary of English Prepositions: The Role of Prepositions in English; A Survey of Research and Resources Prepositions are omnipresent in every natural language; however, their usage and various senses they can exhibit can range from seemingly indispensable to almost arbitrary. In spite of this, research has shown that preposition questions are some of the most frequently asked of language teachers and learners (Aarts, 2011) and annotated resources for preposition usage are surprisingly scarce. In this paper, we present a novel resource, the Pattern Dictionary of English Prepositions (PDEP), alongside a set of over 81,000 sentences, which constitute the corpus of The Preposition Project (TPP). This resource is built on Hanks' theory of norms and exploitations (Hanks, 2013) - the idea that in language, meaning and use varies from the "norm" of well-documented senses to less common or less expected "exploitations." This project moves beyond previous preposition dictionaries that relied on curated, yet limited, attested examples of each preposition and instead seeks to compile a broad and useful corpus of actual use, encompassing both common norms and varied exploitations. Prepositions pose several challenges that have historically hindered uniform treatment. One is the variety of functions they perform, such as indicating location (in, on, at), time (before, while, until), direction (towards, along), medium (by, with), cause, purpose, manner, and more (Vandevoort, 2004). Another challenge is the high degree of polysemy, where one word can have different meanings in different contexts, such as with 'before' in "She read the novel before going to bed" (pre-event) vs. "Before doesn't come before beginning" (time). Then there's the issue of different prepositions being used for similar meanings (alternation, such as "dependent on" vs. "dependent upon"), or the lack of any preposition altogether (zero preposition, as in "I agree you"). Several resources have attempted to address these challenges. For example, The Preposition Project's ancestor, the LDC's PPL Corpus (Striegnitz, 2000), compiled a large number of preposition occurrences. Another advanced tool was LexiquePro’s Preposition Dictionary (TLG, 2001), which provided structure but limited depth. However, these tools often lacked the ability to capture the broad range of senses and the transitional relationships between them. The Pattern Dictionary of English Prepositions (PDEP), however, breaks new ground. As detailed in subsequent sections: 1.   Resource Structure:   Our dictionary is conceptually divided into senses. Each sense represents a particular use or pattern of a preposition.

Training natural language understanding (NLU) algorithms reliably on existing datasets is inherently challenging without an understanding of how these datasets are constructed; these are often manually curated and biased towards a specific domain or problem type. Moreover, determining the relative difficulty of various problems, and inspecting how the algorithm fairs on the particular subsets, is also often relegated to manual analysis of problem questions or answers. Another concern is reproducibility across different datasets and baselines. While some works may report generalization to held-out datasets, their respective minimal and maximal generalization performance remains opaque without further benchmarking. To facilitate such secondary analyses, MAWPS (MathWordProblemSearch) provides fine-grained filtering capabilities allowing users to fine-tune word overlap, solution ambiguity, and other lexical characteristics of the problem corpora. The first half of our work is dedicating to discussing the design and features of MAWPS, as well as its online API, sample usage and a glossary of filtering parameters. We sketch how these features enable researchers and educators to construct custom test sets which closely mimic known problem distributions or biases inherent in popular benchmark sets such as Aristo Math (Weld et al., 2018). By leveraging this framework, we aim to reduce the variability in problem composition within or across experiments. In the second main part of the paper, we present an initial use case of how MAWPS can significantly aid secondary analysis. We employ MAWPS to re-examine the classification performance of several previously trained models on the Aristo dataset (Weld et al., 2018), as well as evaluate them on subsets of MAWPS which we construct to approximate the structure, difficulty, and lexical composition of Aristo. For example, by filtering problems based on grammaticality, lexical overlap with contexts, and problem-solving confidence scores culled from analysis of likely rationales provided in educational resources (e.g., user-submitted answers from forums), we can create synthetic datasets to highlight potential overfit to specific word patterns or token configurations. Our findings illustrate three key points: firstly, a dependence of model performance on the characteristics of the dataset used for training — problematic examples may systematically confount models trained or tested on balanced datasets versus skewed ones, or insomuch as systematic deviations from the entire problem space. Secondly, MAWPS' filtering allows recreation of subsets of problems that are more representative of some but not all of these biases. For example, a set biased towards word structure over content (blindly trained on word frequency or co-occurrence counts) may perform poorly on sets constructed to emphasize problem-solving difficulty derived from overlapping lexical templates and almost-solutions.

Learning Translations via Matrix Completion As the need for achieving multilingual understanding grows larger, so does the scarcity of bilingual training data. This gap exists not just between specific languages, but also in comprehensive resources for many languages. Most translation models are developed using large parallel corpora, which is not only difficult to obtain, but also may not be representative of all aspects of a language. Bilingual Lexicon Induction, the task of learning word translations without a bilingual parallel corpus, is then a useful and necessary endeavor. We present a novel framework for this task based on the matrix completion problem. Our framework keeps in mind the fact that there are many sources of information that could be used to infer word translations. These sources can be diverse and may be noisy or incomplete, such as dictionaries, monolingual corpora, publicly available translation tables, or derived translations from relationships among semantic senses. The framework we propose uses matrix completion to integrate such diverse information sources into an improved estimation of the bilingual matrix of word translations. The exploration of such a problem setting has several benefits. First, as mentioned, it reduces the reliance on parallel corpora, which might be difficult to obtain or may not be useful for certain tasks. Secondly, by leveraging various linguistic data sources or even other modalities such as visual information, our model can potentially capture more subtle aspects of language use and translation equivalence that may not be captured by shallow statistical models trained on limited data. Thirdly, it benefits from the inherent robustness of matrix completion algorithms against noise and missing data, which aligns well with the typical nature of data available for low-resource languages or underresourced translation scenarios. A key aspect of our proposal is its extension possibilities: new data sources or more advanced algorithms for matrix completion can be easily integrated, making the framework future-proof and adaptable to varying contexts. We apply our proposed framework to several datasets and compare the results with the state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that, across high and low resource language pairs, the performance significantly improves when using our method to integrate multiple sources of information. Our method also demonstrates the ability to perform particularly well for low-resource languages where data is scarce, showing the value of leveraging diverse but incomplete or noisy information sources. This paper contributes to the understanding of how diverse and noisy monolingual and bilingual information can be effectively integrated to improve the estimation of word translations, paving the way for more efficient and effective translation models.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on "A Multi-answer Multi-task Framework for Real-world Machine Reading Comprehension". Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) is a key challenge in the natural language processing (NLP) community, where the goal is to answer questions based on given context text, typically a piece of news or questions found in web content. The task has traditionally been approached by asking and answering single-factual questions, but the situation has changed now. Real-world users often produce longer, more complex queries that require answering sets (multi-answer) or entail procedures that require more than one step (multi-task). Consequently, the complexity of the problem has increased, and new approaches are needed. Previous research has concentrated on formulating these tasks independently, despite the fact that in practical scenarios, they often co-occur. For instance, semantic reasoning (i.e., understanding a procedure or an explanation) often requires identifying multiple relevant pieces of information from a document and joining them together to form an answer. Thus, a more holistic approach that acknowledges the inter-relatedness of these conditions seems appropriate. Our proposed solution is a Multi-answer Multi-task (MAM) framework, designed specifically to address the simultaneous challenges of multiple answers and multiple implicit tasks that arise from a given question. One key innovation in our approach is the use of multiple different training objectives for each answer. Unlike traditional MRC methods, which typically treat all answer candidates equally, in the real world different types of answers might require different types of treatments. This multi-task aspect stems from the nature of the question – one might require inference (a task requiring reasoning), another might require recall (a task requiring memory of details). Another challenge with real-world MRC is the problem of answer occurrences. An answer may appear multiple times in the document leading to potential confusion for a model. To deal with this, we use a Minimum Risk Training (MRT) mechanism proposed by Wachsmuth and Wray (2000) . This method assigns different training objectives to multiple answer candidates based on the likelihood of each answer candidate. The more likely answer gets a higher weight in determining the loss function. A further complication comes from the long and varied web content provided as context. Since dealing with the full byte-pair encoded (BPE) version of a document may overwhelm a model, we introduce a simple heuristic strategy for extracting/picking relevant passages from a given document.

Abstractive text summarization has gained much attention in recent years. Traditional methods often produce extractive summaries that fail to capture the essence of an article and may miss supportive details. Recent studies have shown deep neural network approaches to promise better performance. Most existing neural network models focus on generating summaries for articles. However, opinionated text, such as those found in reviews or questions-and-answers forums, presents unique challenges and potential opportunities. Opinionated text often contains diverse viewpoints, detailed descriptions, and structural elements, like opinion markers or evidence. Summarizing this type of text requires capturing not only the extracted points but also the flow and strength of opinions, as well as knowledge about common opinions and argument structures. This is not an easy task, as it requires the system to understand and generate logically cohesive and syntactically fluent text. Furthermore, online reviews and forum questions often contain semantic ambiguities, colloquial language, and varied language structures that are challenging even for humans, let alone machine learning models. In this paper, we propose an attention-based neural network model with a hierarchical structure designed to handle the complexity of opinionated text. Our model builds upon recent advances in neural sequence models (Seq2seq) and incorporates mechanisms to explicitly guide the attention mechanism or selectively focus on salient aspects of the input text. The model is trained on two domains: movie reviews and argumentative texts from Opensubtitle and Debatewise, respectively. We design an importance-based text sampling method that allows the model to selectively focus on parts of the input that carry more information regarding an opinion or argument. First, we perform studies on MT (Machine Translation) as an analogy, summarization is akin to text in one language being "translated" to a much shorter representation in the same language. Then, we adapt existing NMT (Neural Machine Translation) and summarization techniques, and compare the performance with the proposed approach. We manually and automatically assess the generated summaries on measures such as informativeness, grammaticality, and general quality against the measured evaluation methods: ROUGE (R, F, L), METEOR, and BLEU, while also incorporating human evaluations. Our results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art abstractive and extractive summarizing systems across different domains. We further investigate the model’s capability to appropriately summarize arguments, a challenging task that requires not only capturing main opinions but also supporting evidence and logical structure. Our proposed model demonstrates the potential of neural networks in abstracting information from opinionated text and suggests that future work should focus on developing and strengthening the model’s ability to generate more coherent and convincing summaries, especially in the argumentative domain

Training natural language processing (NLP) models on large datasets has proven to be an effective way to improve their performance. However, these models often rely heavily on the frequency of words they've been trained on. This creates the problem of vanishing or rare words - words that either appear infrequently or not at all in the training data. This problem is particularly pronounced in machine translation (MT) where words or even whole sentences may appear in the target language but not at all or rarely in the source language (Choudhary and Hovy, 2008). In such cases, the rarity of these words keeps the model from capturing their representation accurately, thus leading to suboptimal translation quality. At first glance, MT seems like a natural fit for vocabulary-based learning frameworks since words are often used as the primary units in language. This word-based approach has been the standard in MT for several decades. However, the reliance on words creates a bottleneck - the need to handle rare and unknown words properly. Word-based models face certain drawbacks, such as the need to build complex dictionaries with subword units and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) processing mechanisms, which can lead to increased training and model complexity. Moreover, these approaches fail to account for linguistic phenomena like varying word boundaries or phenomena across different languages that can be better captured on a character level (Schwenk, 2007). A potential solution to this issue is to depart from the word-centric approach and instead consider entire sequences of characters - strings rather than words - as the basic units of analysis. This idea forms the basis of our proposed work, which attempts to tackle MT as a problem of transforming one string into another rather than one word into another. The idea of doing MT without words is not novel. It has a history going back to early forms of rule-based MT systems (Brown et al., 1990). However, the introduction of deep learning techniques, especially sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014; Kiros et al., 2015), has given a new lease on life to this line of thinking. These models inherently operate on character sequences, which they transform into another sequence and then projected to a vocabulary space to make use of word embeddings. We aim to take this one step further by avoiding the projection to a vocabulary space altogether, treating the problem in a character-to-character fashion.

Rapid Development of a Corpus with Discourse Annotations using Two-stage Crowdsourcing We present a novel approach for rapidly developing a corpus with discourse annotations using crowdsourcing. Although discourse annotations typically require much time and cost owing to their complex nature, we realize discourse annotations in an extremely short time while retaining good quality of the annotations by crowdsourcing two annotation subtasks. In fact, our experiment to create a corpus comprising 30,000 Japanese sentences took less than eight hours to run. Based on this corpus, we also develop a supervised discourse parser and evaluate its performance to verify the usefulness of the acquired corpus. 1. Introduction Discourse annotation is essential for improving various natural language processing tasks. However, it requires considerable human resource because the annotation task requires a deep understanding of language in order to capture the complexities and nuances of discourse relations. Collecting high-quality discourse annotated corpora thus typically takes a lot of time and money. On the other hand, crowdsourcing is a practical approach for quickly collecting large amounts of data at a relatively low cost. However, applying crowdsourcing to complex tasks such as discourse annotation is challenging, as the annotators may not have the necessary knowledge or experience to perform their tasks accurately and consistently. Furthermore, checking the quality of the annotations may require a significant amount of time. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach for rapidly developing a discourse-annotated corpus using two-stage crowdsourcing. In this approach, we first divide the discourse annotation task into two simpler subtasks. This allows less-experienced annotators to work on the first subtask without compromising the overall quality of the annotations. Meanwhile, more experienced annotators can work on the second subtask, which is more complex, and ensure the consistency and accuracy of the annotations through a two-stage approach. To verify the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to annotate a corpus of 30,000 Japanese sentences in just under eight hours. We then developed a supervised discourse parser based on this corpus and evaluated its performance, demonstrating that the corpus developed using the two-stage crowdsourcing approach is useful for learning discourse representations. Our work has potential for accelerating the development of discourse annotated corpora, which in turn could facilitate the development of more advanced natural language processing applications. 2. Two-stage Crowdsourcing for Discourse Annotation The crux of our approach is the division of the discourse annotation task into two subtasks.

无论是对于复杂的英语语言抽取任务还是对于中文，事件抽取都面临着严峻挑战。过往的方法主要依赖于人工设计的先验知识，通过大量的统计分析和抽象模型来指导抽取工作，这往往需要巨大投入的时间和人力。因此，探索更加有效的、能够自动学习特征的自动化方法是事件抽取领域研究的重要方向。 在文本挖掘和自然语言处理领域，广泛引入机器学习和深度学习方法以期打破传统方法的局限。特别地，卷积神经网络（CNN）因其在图像识别领域的显著成功（Krizhevsky et al., 2012）而被引入文本处理中，以其独特的层次化特征提取能力（LeCun et al., 1998），为自动提取文本的语义信息提供了可能。然而，直接将这类模型应用于事件抽取却并不直接，因为文本中的事件通常是分布在全句上，而不仅仅是局部的。此外，事件抽取要求不仅能够识别事件，还要正确填充事件的参数（如动作执行者、受动者等）。这意味着模型需要知道如何根据句子的全局信息以及上下文来预测这些参数。 针对这些挑战，结合深度学习技术进行事件抽取的工作开始增加。其中关键步骤包括特征表示（features representation）、模型结构设计以及如何将二者有机结合。以中文为例，语言学上具有多样性，如动词的形式变化、名词的复数形式等，这些对于自动抽取事件同样具有挑战性。另外，中文事件抽取缺乏像英文那样丰富的资源库和训练模型，因此研究如何有效利用中文语言学特征，并构建能够处理这些特征的模型，是至关重要的。 针对这些问题，一个可能的解决思路是采用联合建模（joint modeling）的方法。联合建模试图将不同的任务（在事件抽取场景中，可能是事件触发词、事件类型、事件参数的识别等）同时或联合学习，而非通过封闭的流水线（pipeline）方式逐步处理。选择联合建模策略的好处在于，能够减少错误的累积和传播，比如在识别事件触发词时，模型能够从整个句子的上下文中获取信息，从而更准确地预测事件参数。通过这种方式，模型在训练过程中能够自动学习到不同任务间的关联和依赖，从而在一定程度上缓解特征工程的负担。

Training active learning (AL) systems to request specific user input (e.g. labels or feature-level annotations) instead of entire instances (e.g. text snippets or documents) has the potential to usefully accelerate machine learning while reducing the need for human annotation. For instance, in machine translation, the most effective queries are likely to involve a small number of phrase questions or manual edits (Ravi and Knight, 2011). A recent study (Mehdad and Hahn, 2013) of feature-level annotation for part-of-speech tagging combined Active Learning for Feature Selection (ALFS) (Chen and Lin, 2006) with error-driven feature selection, showing comparable to slightly improved performance over feature selection using all training data. Other examples include work on active features for image classification 1 (Keller and Homan, 2010; Turlach et al., 2006; Turek, 2007), active attribute subset selection (Agrawal, 2000) and active graph-based learning (Guo et al., 2011). We refer to such applications of AL as "Active Learning by Labeling Features" (ALF). The problem of deciding which features to request from a human annotator on a specific instance arises from both theoretical foundations of active learning as well as practical considerations. A traditional active learning algorithm, while deciding whether to query an instance, might ask: "Which instance will give me the most information about model parameters?". A feature-level active learning system might similarly ask: "Which specific features for this specific instance will give me the most information about model parameters?" or "Which feature should be labeled for each instance?" Deciding which features to label directly determines what query is being "proposed" by the AL system. Our study begins with the supposition that annotating the most discriminative features for a given instance could provide the same benefit as querying the most informative instances in traditional AL algorithms. On this basis, the ALF methods in this study use feature level selection. We focus on applications of ALF to sequence labeling. These tasks, such as POS tagging and Named Entity Recognition (NER), confront several of the challenges posed to AL techniques: a very large feature set where individual features are informative and diverse; a considerable proportion of features that are informative but infrequent; some but not all features are correlated. For these and other reasons, traditional AL methods have seen success with such tasks (e.g.Rahman and Ng, 2012; Alm et al., 2013; Chahuneau and Ballesteros, 2013). In this paper we evaluate a range of ALF strategies for sequence labeling.

Training neural models with large amounts of labeled data has clearly seen successful applications in many NLP tasks. However, many successful applications of these models have involved scarcity of labeled data. In this paper, we use this latter example and explore techniques to adapt neural models to work well with limited labeled data for tasks like grammatical error correction (GEC). We exploit strategies from low-resource machine translation (MT) research because these methods deal with similar issues as those encountered in GEC. These include handling low-resource settings and minimal language models. In particular, we show that by adding noise to source data for GEC, applying domain adaptation techniques, constructing a new GEC-specific objective function, using training data to pre-train language models, and employing model ensembling, we can significantly improve the performance of neural GEC models. Specifically, our methods result in neural GEC systems that outperform previous state-of-the-art neural systems by a margin greater than 10% M 2 on the CoNLL-2014 evaluation set, and by 5.9% on a different test set called JFLEG. These improvements also surpass the previous SOTA performance in GEC on both evaluations. We also provide guidelines and propose techniques that can be used or adapted for other low-resource NLP tasks. Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is the task of automatically detecting and correcting grammatical errors in written text. It is an indispensable tool for providing automated feedback in learning settings, as well as a crucial component in the improvement of human-written text such as blog posts or documents. One of the main challenges in GEC is its reliance on high-quality labeled datasets. These datasets are often in low supply, because hand annotation is time-consuming and costly. Although much focus has been placed on developing "universal" error analysis models that doesn't require much domain-specific knowledge (e.g., the use of deep language models), such models often need to be fine-tuned on specific datasets or languages to perform the task accurately. This side of GEC draws together multiple NLP subfields, as the task requires not only understanding the correct grammar but also detecting when it is incorrect, and proposing corrections. A wide array of approaches have been explored and applied to GEC, including rule-based methods, statistical approaches like n-grams and Hidden Markov Models, and more recently, advanced machine learning techniques that often build off of pre-trained language models.

Training neural networks with jointly optimized objective functions can optimize both consistency between distant pieces of information and prediction accuracy. In particular, the task of jointly extracting entities and relations (i.e. named entities and their type of relationship to the other entities) shows many potential advantages of this approach, including better training stability and improving the generalization capability of the model (Ling and Weld, 2012). Specifically, one can optimize a loss function that simultaneously trades off between the generalization error (sentence prediction) and the inter-consistency error (entity/relation prediction across the entire sentence set for a given data point). As pointed out by Huang et. al (2015), this inter-consistency constraint helps improve the accuracy of the model by jointly training the different components, and can also be seen as a form of model regularization to encourage structured predictions. However, among the various methods proposed, weighted classification, dependency regularization (He et. al, 2015) and even CRF-based approaches (Lin and Roth, 2006) are more appealing because of their modular structure which allows flexible component extensions, and possibly better interpretability. Offsetting potential model interpretability advantages, minimum risk training (MRT, Taskar et. al, 2004) presents a common interface and principled way for learning jointly from distinct prediction models. MRT pushes the objective to a form of global minimum while the system attempts to explore labelings in a way that minimizes the risk (i.e., the expected loss under an expectation over a distribution over some or all inference variables (e.g., features, model parameters, etc., as in, Vapnik (1998)). For example, for each training sample (document, sentence, and all contexts within), we can define a loss function that takes into account the entity predictions and the relation predictions. The joint optimization can be formulated as finding the minimum global error while trading off between these two, allowing both component models to adapt together. Our work generalizes MRT to the joint training of entity and relation models, benefiting from MRT’s foundations in structured prediction and hierarchical risk minimization. MRT explicitly encodes the objective into a structured form by considering all possible globally consistent prediction sets for each training sample, and hence can incorporate any dependency structure between different prediction variables.
