Training embeddings with large amounts of data is essential for most state of the art neural models. However, these models can still struggle with performance when they encounter out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. Modern approaches attempt to address this by using pre-trained embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe and FastText) which utilize a large corpus of text to predict word representations. These methods are prevalent and often used as a baselayer for many distributed representation learning tasks, such as Word Similarity and NER tasks. While DSMs are powerful, they still struggle in certain scenarios. For example, how can we get a good representation for words in languages for which training data is scarce, or new words introduced in our domain of interest? These words often have no examples and therefore are out-of-vocabulary. Sentiment analysis, online reviews, medical documents etc., can have many such words in domain specific domains. The task of making the existing well-trained models capable of capturing the meaning of a word from limited context is an exciting problem that arises from this limitation. The challenging version of this task is often defined as the Few Shot Word Representation Learning problem. It asks for general word representations learned on large amounts of data to accommodate any novel or rarer words. Current ForWord representation learning techniques include Schematically and # symbols (Yang et al., 2015), Fast Text (Bojanowski et al., 2016) and the learning of Exemplar words (Gan et al., 2017). However, these methods still rely heavily on large datasets and the need for manual annotation. A more promising direction, especially for words that have a few in-domain instances, is to leverage semantic memory (human general world knowledge and experience) and query retrieval from existing knowledge bases (wordNet, Wikipedia, Frames). But it proves difficult to frame the problem such that distributional contextual models and memory systems work hand in hand, allowing them to learn representations without falling prey to overfitting or the lack of generalizability. So, what if we could teach a DSM to use its own pre-trained embedding to allocate another embedding to a novel or rare word? This is the core idea of Mem2Vec, which utilizes a memory to guide changing the embedding of a word given very limited context. Mem2Vec assumes that a word that has some but limited context in a new domain or is rare in the general language can still take advantage of the knowledge of similar(ly used) words in its semantic network.

Training neural models with all the fine-grained syntactic information in context might offer performance benefits without an increased risk of overfitting. The major bottleneck for designing such systems is finding ways to efficiently represent the deep syntactic structures that must be evaluated and built on many times. In this work, we describe a new representation that captures the full grammatical structure of a sentence – both phrase syntax and discontinuous constituents – and combine this with a deep recurrent neural network and principled losses. We examine three types of losses that guide the representation and decoding, of which the first maintains a local equality between predicted (and gold) hypotheses for subtrees of increasing size backwards from the leaf. The second loss ensures subtrees match across word boundaries, enforcing a nesting relationship between predicted and gold rooted at the span of these words. The third loss encourages the alignment of deeper syntactic structure by biasing the derived representation towards compatible among semantic roles. The second weighted loss places constraints on the intermediate derivations that we hypothesize are particularly relevant to discovering properly nested structures. Our preliminary evaluation of the system suggests the effectiveness of such configurations compared with previous systems and demonstrates the value of proper representation in syntactic parsing. In traditional dependency parsing approaches, we usually model this information implicitly. For instance, sequential decoding schemes relying on differentiable oracles (Andor et al., 2016) and tree-based systems (Dozat and Manning, 2017) rely on sequential prediction of assumed syntactic features for each word. While syntactic features in these settings often make substantial use of several word representations, core syntactic patterns like variables, recursive patterns, or discontinuous structures must often be inferred from the features and shape (but not always the structure, see summarization (Ahram and Domingos, 2006; Young and Hockenmaier, 2010)) through a model's training. The ideal window into a contextualized representation is the structure that identifies which parts of the sentence are part of the same syntactic unit. We can view these units as the structured entities that parse into the measured variables in a sequential model. We also note that the matched local parts are not uniquely identifiable since their hierarchical role may vary. However, we can define a complementary structured summary by considering all possible globally and locally consistent parse trees. Because a word changing position generally modifies dependency structure, our new model must view these tree choices as potentially conditionally related on the current subset of observed words in the input.

Automatically identifying the polarity of words is a crucial task in many applications of Natural Language Processing (NLP), such as text classification, sentiment analysis, opinion mining and text summarization (Pang and Lee, 2005;Kim and Hovy, 2004;Nenkova and Passonneau, 2004). A wide range of approaches have been proposed and used for sentiment analysis and polarity identification. One simple but effective approach to classify sentences as either positive or negative is to determine the sign of a bag-of-words (BOW) representation of the sentence extracted from an annotated corpus (Chen, 2004;Pang and Lee, 2004). Slightly more sophisticated methods include the use of machine learning algorithms to classify features such as word trends (Pak and Paroubek, 2010), positivity/negativity of a word following specific words (Hu and Liu, 2004) and even parts of speech (Gatti et al., 2005). However, such approaches suffer from several limitations. First, they require large amounts of annotated data for training and validation. Second, they do not generally provide a clear understanding of what or how much makes a word positive or negative. Third, it is challenging to handle ambiguous words or new words not present in training data. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes the use of random walks on large scale word relatedness graphs for the task of sentiment analysis, or more specifically, for identifying the polarity of individual words. Firstly, the method leverages the power of automatic construction of massive word relatedness graphs using large text corpora. For example, WordNet is a popular word ontology that captures a wide range of relationships and "synonymy-like" relations between words (Fellbaum, 1998). Distributional semantic models such as Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) provide measured variables for word cooccurrence and word context information (Deerwester et al., 1990;Blei et al., 2003). Secondly and most importantly, we use concepts from Markov chains and random walks to capture the long term dynamics of words in the relatedness graph. Each word in the graph is viewed as a state, and transitions between words capture a rough measure of word relatedness. As we will later discuss, the zero-order Markov chain of the random walk allows estimating the polarity of words by associating the expected return of a word to its closest neighbors in the relatedness graph. Thirdly, the proposed method can be used both in a semi-supervised setting, where a small set of annotated positive and negative words are used as seeds to start random walks that propagate to other words in the graph, thus providing polarity probabilities.

Vector space models (VSMs) of semantics are fundamental to many contemporary NLP systems. The classic bag-of-words model (Borodovsky and Ohlander, 1993;Rosenfeld et al., 1994) represents documents and sentences as high-dimensional vectors that are the sum of word vectors, one for each word in the sentence or document. The distributional hypothesis (Harris, 1954) underlies the idea that meaning can be captured by exploiting language contexts. More recent work such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) learns word embeddings – dense, low-dimensional vectors that capture relationships between words – that have been shown in various tasks to outperform traditional bag-of-words methods. The bag-of-words model ignores syntax, and recent work shows that incorporating even basic syntactic features can improve performance on many tasks (Baroni et al., 2014;Chrupała et al., 2015;Johansson and Sahlgren, 2008;Mitamura and Toutanova, 2014;Socher et al., 2013). However, it is unclear whether symbols provided by generative syntax such as those in Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG, Steedman, 2000) can be used to enrich VSMs to provide plausible treatments of compositional meaning. Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG, Steedman, 2000, 2012) can in principle be used to generate sets of syntactically coherent parses and lexical contexts for a sentence and proposes that these contexts can be used to rationalize semantic composition (Baldridge, 2002;Baldridge and Steedman, 2011;Baldridge et al., 2014). More specifically, in CCG a sentence is decomposed into a set of base typed categorial elements (including words and symbols), combined by various combinators. The idea is that these base typed elements and combinators can be treated as concepts in distributional semantic space and that the combinators can be used to modify or combine concepts to form a new concept that corresponds to the meaning of the complex expression. For example, a conjunction like "John and Mary" could be represented by combining the concepts for "John" and "Mary" with a conjunction combinator. This theoretical intuition suggests the use of CCG to guide the embedding of words within sentences. However, most contemporary work in VSMs and NLP does not inherently incorporate a grammar (contra examples such as Deeplex (Harris and Clark, 2007) or models using word lattices (Lin and Pantel, 2002)) and most work that does use a syntax is not purely distributional: for example, parser-based models (De Marneffe and Manning, 2008) or logical encoders (Mitchell and Lapata, 2010). In this work, we explore how Combinatory Categorial Grammar's combinatory symbols can be used to guide the construction of high-dimensional VSM embeddings for sentences, a model we refer to as Combinatory Categorial Autoencoder (CCA).

Training semantic parsing models from denotations (e.g., answers) is a challenging task, where the primary goal is to learn grammars that generate valid programs (in this case, programs that yield the given answer). While the resulting programs are indeed answers, they need to be logically and syntactically correct. This problem is further complicated by the fact that direct supervision questions are not always available and thus the answer itself acts as the indirect and sometimes ambiguous form of supervision. The challenge arises from two main aspects: (1) the need to generate or discover good candidate semantic parses from text; and (2) how to update the model with respect to these candidates. The knowledge of good semantic parses is crucial to provide rich supervision for the model training. Without such knowledge, training could lead to very similar programs from similar input texts, a trend that is detrimental to model generalization. The first challenge is akin to the sample selection problem in statistical learning - which samples to use as training data to properly guide the learning process? However, unlike supervised learning tasks where labeled examples are explicitly given, here the supervision signal comes implicitly via the answer, which needs to be deduced from the text. Off-the-shelf greedy search methods or beam search algorithms can be employed to search for or generate these candidate semantic parses, but without fine-tuning on the specific relevance criteria, these methods may not always return semantically "good" parses that are compatible with the text. The second challenge comes from the fact that different update rules or learning algorithms might lead to distinct learning dynamics, and ultimately different performance. The choice of update rule determines how the model responds to the candidates (supervision), as well as how it explores the space of possible models. For example, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) updates focus on making the model outputting the "most probable" model given the data, while Reinforcement Learning updates (e.g., policy gradient methods) focus more on adjusting the model parameters to increase the expected reward (e.g., accuracy in this case). A learning algorithm that leans towards making the most probable model might get stuck in local optima, whereas one that explores more might wander around losing track of the optimal model space. There's also the problem of computational complexity and convergence speed of different methods, which can significantly impact practical model training. In this paper, we address these two challenges by proposing policy shaping and generalized update equations.

Sentence simplification, which aims to make complex sentences easier to comprehend while maintaining their original meaning, is an important task in natural language processing (NLP). While several models for automated sentence simplification have been developed, current approaches mostly rely on machine translation (MT) technology, where the complex sentences are translated into simpler forms, and this simplification is essentially learned from instance paraphrases in normal-simple sentence pairs. The potential problem with this method is that the MT models may miss out on explicit simplification rules which could significantly improve the simplification accuracy, as the MT models are not trained specifically for simplification. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to integrate a range of explicit rule knowledge into a state-of-the-art Sentence Simplification Model (SSM). This is particularly driven by the recent success of transformer-based architectures in NLP tasks, specifically those related to sequence-to-sequence problems. The proposed model uses a multi-layer and multi-head attention architecture to process input sentences. Unlike traditional MT models which operate purely on the source-target semantic space, our model also incorporates a dedicated rule selector module, which utilizes knowledge from the Simple PPDB (a paraphrase database for sentence simplification). The Simple PPDB contains a wide range of explicitly defined simplification rules or transformations, covering phenomena such as rephrasing, clause-level rewriting, word substitution, and others. The approach we take for integrating the Simple PPDB into our SSM model can be broadly outlined as follows: 1.   Rule Retrieval and Ranking  : Once the sentence to be simplified is processed by our transformer model, the rule selector module retrieves rules from the Simple PPDB that are applicable, based on features extracted from the input sentence and the rules themselves. To rank these rules, we use a combination of rule features (such as confidence scores originating from the rule extraction process, frequency of use in real-world simplification tasks, and the syntactic category of the rule) and sentence features (such as context and sentence structure). 2.   Integration Pipeline  : The selected rules are then integrated into the output generation pipeline of our SSM, alongside the semantic information learned from the transformer architecture. This means that while the transformer model tries to generate a simplified sentence purely based on learned similarities between complex and simple sentence pairs, the rule selector module offers a set of explicit instructions on how to transform specific parts of the complex sentence into simpler forms.

Training LSTM networks can be a very challenging and time-consuming task. Each training run can yield different results depending on the initialization of the model weights and biases, the choice of the optimizer, the learning rate scheme, and the number and initialization of the dropout layers. There are quite a few approaches to tackle the issue, such as early-stopping (Bengio et al., 1995; Widrow and Lehr, 1989), weight decay (Wei Chen and LeCun, 1999), and various strategies for adjusting the learning rate (e.g., (Keskar et al., 2016; Smith, 2015)). However, the optimization of these hyperparameters is typically performed in a trial and error manner, with very little theoretical guidance available. This is partly due to the fact that standard benchmarks for comparing performance of different systems are based on a single value such as the F 1 -score. As a result, it is common to optimize the system for the best single performance value observed across different runs. However, such single-value evaluations often mask the underlying uncertainty of the reported results resulting in various issues such as: - The statistical significance of reported gains is often misjudged. A reported gain that seems large can be due to random fluctuations or due to a non-uniformly distributed performance measure (e.g., most positive examples have very high F 1 -scores while negatives are in a more uniform range). - The comparison between different algorithmic choices can often become misleading due to the high variability in results for a given seed value. - It is often unclear how much generalization has been achieved by an algorithm: does the best configuration on a development set generalize to another development set? To address all these issues, we propose to reveal the underlying score distribution for different runs and learn from that distribution. This requires redesigning the evaluation phase of machine learning: instead of tracking a single performance score over all iterations of one or multiple training runs, one should report and compare the measured score distribution together with additional diagnostics to account for statistical fluctuations. The base idea is to generate N independent runs, each with a different initialization and following by its own independent optimization run. We then aggregate and report the score distribution over these N runs for a set of shared hyperparameters (e.g., dropout layers, choices of optimizer) and report on the variability for these parameters. Our hypothesis for this paper is that a better understanding of score distributions over multiple training runs can provide insights on: - How robust a system is to small adjustments in hyperparameters leading to different and potentially contradictory suggestions for tuning.

Training natural language processing (NLP) systems reliably on one domain of text (such as news or medical literature) and then using these systems to process text from another domain (such as conversational social media or literature), the so-called open-domain learning setting. In this work, we study domain adaptation for NLP, the process of adapting a system trained on one domain to perform effectively on another. This is a challenging problem because even if the two domains have access to the same set of tasks and potentially share some minimal language of discourse, they still exhibit significant differences in domain-specific structure and lexicon. Traditionally, domain adaptation is often tackled with representation learning techniques (Ruder et al., 2017), which learn task-invariant features from both source and target domains. These features are designed to capture meaningful semantic trends that are common to both domains, even if surface forms differ. The most obvious but inefficient way to perform domain adaptation would be to collect and label data from the target domain. However, collecting such data is often prohibitively expensive or impractical. Thus, the most common approach is to train the model using available labeled data from the source domain and unlabeled or limited labels from the target domain. One challenge is that existing or even future labeled data in the target domain can be insufficient to prevent the model from overfitting to the source domain. This is because even shallow text models tend to overfit quickly while the 'diversity' of the entire open domain often leads to a large increase in the plausible model complexity. To mitigate this issue, semi-supervised learning (SSL), which incorporates both labeled and unlabeled data, can be particularly effective for large open domains. SSL methods can leverage the large amount of unlabeled data in the target domain, which is often easily and cheaply obtainable, to learn more robust representation that is less biased towards the source domain. However, most existing work on semi-supervised NLP focus on one or two aspects of the problem, such as side information via auxiliary tasks or exploiting additional labeled data in the target domain. The base model used in these approaches is typically a standard deep learning model, such as a word embedding or deep neural network, which may still fail to capture domain-specific concepts or distributional differences across different domains. Furthermore, these methods can be less effective when there is sparse labeled data from both the source and target domains for the main task of interest.

Semantic parsing, which maps natural language (NL) sentences to formal meaning representations (MR's), plays a central role in enabling computers to understand and execute NL instructions and queries. Modern semantic parsers use graph-structured MR's, where nodes represent concepts (e.g., entities, attributes) and edges represent semantic relations, as this representation exhibits a tight coupling with knowledge bases (KBs), and can be handled by combinatorial logic and KB reasoning (Buisson and Gardent, 2016; Wang and Xing, 2017). Two recent influential directions in semantic parsing are: (1) to represent semantic graphs alongside with NL sentences (e.g., knowledge graph embeddings) (Socher et al., 2013) and (2) to use neural networks for end-to-end semantic parsing (e.g., structured prediction) (Dong et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017). The knowledge graph embedding-based methods have demonstrated impressive performances on some datasets (e.g., Knowledge Graph Construction (KGC) and NLVR) (Hill et al., 2016; Marino et al., 2017). However, they typically require a fixed or a pre-processed KG that tightly matches the given context, which is hard to obtain for domains without existing KGs. These methods also mostly use a fixed vocabulary of potential entity/relation types, and their performance can degrade in settings where the diversity and interpretability of MR's is critical (e.g., dialogue systems and question answering). On the other hand, while the neural structured prediction (NSP) methods show promising results in semantic parsing (e.g., interpreting simple queries), they typically represent MR's as sequential structures, and focus on generating query results from "keyword" nodes in the graph. However, real-world query interpretations (e.g., "show me all professors from CS department who work at Harvard") require understanding and generating complex graphs with structured information (e.g., entities and attributes). The lack of methods that combine both a graph structure, and the ability to efficiently represent it with neural NSP models, limits the performance of existing approaches. A structured summary of existing methods in semantic parsing is given in Section 2. Our work takes inspiration from both directions and proposes an end-to-end method Sequence-to-Action (StA) for semantic parsing. Our method models semantic parsing as an end-to-end graph generation process, where the goal is to generate semantic graphs for given NL queries using the action of an RNN network (as shown in Figure 1). The RNN takes an input sentence and predicts the sequence of graph actions (e.g., add-edge, add-node, or delete-node) that construct the MR. StA is an extension of graph-generating neural network models (e.g., neural machine translation (NMT)) where the "words" are graph actions instead of word tokens.

Social Q&A platforms have become increasingly popular sources of information over the past decade (Liu et al., 2015;Shao et al., 2016). Unlike traditional factoid-oriented Q&A systems, these community-based Q&A (cQA) services handle various types of questions and answers (QA pairs), including open-ended questions questions without concrete answers (Rashkin & Chaturvedi, 2019). These platforms often adopt moderation mechanisms to pre-filter posted content, but the volume of untrusted content can still be very large. The challenges of extracted context keeps changing as new information is generated dynamically over time. Unlike knowledge bases or traditional text, those new information may not be retrieved simply with keyword searches or synonyms, due to its short-length features. Therefore, early question detection is critical for efficient question retrieval and understanding among semantic search. These needs have motivated numerous recent efforts to develop advanced question answer pair detection and retrieval techniques for cQA forum questions (Zhou et al., 2018;Rashkin & Chaturvedi, 2019). Yet, similar to traditional question detection and retrieval in information retrieval or multi-label text categorization, existing approaches mainly rely on pre-processed features For instance, Vikram et al. (2019) use features such as question length, the frequency of query keywords in the question body, the presence of special characters. Others use the count of 5W1H words (what, why, when, where, who, how) or questionmarks for question detection (Graw et al., 2019, 2015). However, these approaches often struggle for detecting question sentences in informal online content, and they might achieve only modest performance. While efforts have been devoted to develop better features (e.g., Graw et al., 2019;Vikram et al., 2019), it has not been explicitly studied how different question contexts, domains, or patterns might affect these methods, and whether question characteristics in cQA forums differ fundamentally from traditional informal text or other question datasets. For example, do questions from cQA forums and web forums differ from each other in language usage patterns? In this paper, we address these questions by analyzing large-scale cQA corpora from various domains. We aim to identify salient linguistic patterns and structural features that can effectively detect question sentences in informal online content. We propose a novel question detection approach based on such patterns. Our approach goes beyond simple keyword matching or the use of basic features like question length and word counts. It focuses on patterns observed in cQA question sentences. We formally define and identify these patterns.

Training embeddings directly from unlabelled text has proven to be an effective means of capturing lexical-level semantic information (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014). Most existing work on embeddings focuses on alphabetic languages. A particular challenge in the case of Chinese is that – unlike alphabetic characters which are orthographically equivalent to the phonemes of the language and hence lend themselves naturally to "word" embeddings – Chinese characters (which often incorporate phonetic, morphological, and etymological information (Kane, 2009)) keeps meaning tightly encapsulated alongside form. Consequently most Chinese NLP systems rely either on word segmentations or on a hybrid of character and word embeddings (Wu et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015). 1 In what follows, we explore whether weighted sums of character embeddings can provide better "Chinese word" embeddings than traditional character-based or CRF-segmented word-based approaches, either in isolation or as a supplement for higher order NLP tasks. Distributional character embeddings have been explored previously (Kobayashi and Sugiura, 2016; Wang and Smith, 2018) For a given Chinese word, it is represented as a sum (or average) of the embeddings of the constituent characters. A key advantage of this approach is the simplicity and scalability. However in practice this naive approach has its limitations. Chinese characters, being composed of multiple components (radicals), can share similar form or meaning while being semantically related. A previous work (Kobayashi and Sugiura, 2016) demonstrated that by incorporating auxiliary components from the character, the learned embeddings are more informative. 1 We also consider analysis leading to sub-character units (e.g., the left and right sides of a given character), but focus primarily on complete characters and bigram representations due to simplicity and scalability. We extend this line of work, presenting: (1) a novel, sparse character-level embedding base model that can be learned efficiently from large-scale text corpora, and (2) complementary bigram models for cases where disambiguation across similar character arrangements is necessary. This is where shared components within characters can be leveraged to capture subtle semantic differences. We use a simplified implementation of the FastText framework (Bojanowski et al., 2016) combined with component-based aggregation, specifically zero-order Gaussian mixture components (Z-Score) over the components of each character. We demonstrate the utility of these approaches on word similarity and text classification tasks. We first train the base embedding model and then, on a held-out dataset, show that augmenting the character-level embeddings with bigram component information yields improvement in performance.

Multiword expressions (MWEs), such as "break a leg" or "by and large", have been widely recognized as a major bottleneck for statistical language processing. They are frequent in natural language, but cannot be easily predicted from their individual words (Jackendoff, 2003; Apresjan, 1974). Over the years, researchers have proposed various approaches to handle MWEs (Ehret and Lezi, 2010; Barzilay and Lee, 2003; Tsujii, 2005; Saji and Isozaki, 2007; Sylven et al., 2008, 2010; Gao and Xue, 2009; Piao et al., 2010; Koo et al., 2010; Narain et al., 2010; Ng et al., 2010; Ritter et al., 2011; Si and Guo, 2010; Henderson, 2010; Henderson, 2010; Offord and Gries, 2010), with their own strengths and weaknesses. However, the development of MWE recognizers has been largely isolated from that of dependency parsers, even if different projects have the same corpus. This paper reports on an early attempt to explore the benefits of integrating MWE recognition with parsing at the point of parsing. Our study compares two different approaches: the use of a pre-built MWE recognizer followed by a state-of-the-art English parser, as advocated, for example, by Ritter et al. (2011), and an integrated approach where the parser captures all contexts relevant for recognizing and parsing MWEs. First, we describe how we learn a MWE recognizer from annotated data inconsistent in size, kind and quality; and how we extend the parser to capture MWE information. We then compare the performance of these two approaches on measured evaluation metrics: unlabeled attachment score (Piao et al., 2010) and F-score (Nakov et al., 2007). We also confront the MWE recognition accuracy and its impact on parsing. The MWE recognizer we build uses a regression model over a large set of features – part-of-speech tags, dependency relations, syntactic labels, lemma and headword, punctuation, co-occurrence with stop words, semantic role markers, and other light syntactic and semantic features. However, as most features and even the predictive log-likelihood are almost entirely based on co-occurrence patterns and shallow relations, we do not expect complete freedom from errors. We therefore aim to characterize the quality of the MWE recognizer rather than to optimize its performance, hypothesizing that even if the MWE recognizer is not perfect, there is still room for improving overall parsing performance with a tuned interaction between MWE recognition and parsing. We then evaluate the two integration strategies – pregrounding and postgrounding – and explore the effect of MWE recognition quality on parsing.

Grammatical error correction (GEC) is a fundamental task of natural language processing (NLP) that aims to automatically detect and correct errors in text to improve readability. The errors being corrected include misspelled words, wrong tense or number forms, and incorrect word orders, among others. Recent GEC systems have predominantly been based on a statistical machine learning approach, relying on large annotated datasets and statistical patterns between surface errors and corrected forms (Zhang and Lapata, 2017). However, as neural language models have grown in popularity and sophistication, there has been a significant shift towards using these models for more complex tasks, including GEC. Neural models for GEC usually follow a sequence to sequence (Seq2Seq) framework where an input sequence of words (with some errors) is fed into an encoder that produces a latent representation, which then serves as the input to a decoder generating the corrected sequence (Sennrich et al., 2016; Krishnan et al., 2017). The encoder-decoder architecture with attention mechanisms has shown strong potential for GEC, particularly in capturing the importance of different words or sub-sequences in the input when generating output (Luong et al., 2015; Keskar et al., 2016; Sennrich et al., 2016; Wang and Cho, 2016). Despite their success, current neural GEC models often struggle with local errors that involve small edits, such as correcting the orthography (e.g., 'eat' to 'ate') without modifying the surrounding context. This highlights a limitation in the current model designs in effectively combining word-level contexts with character-level information, which is crucial for accurately correcting such local errors. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid model for GEC that augments the standard neural encoder-decoder setup with nested attention mechanisms. The idea is to use two attention layers: one for word-level features and a second for character-level features, allowing for a hierarchical analysis of input sequences. This nested attention framework is designed to capture dependencies at both the word and character levels, explicitly addressing the issue of local errors while still being able to handle and correct larger-scale structural errors.
