For instance, in Japanese, the word 家内 (meaning "house" or "family") is often mis-segmented as 家 (house) and 内 (inside) due to its structure, leading to morphological analysis tools incorrectly splitting the word into distinct morphemes based on the segmentation. To address this problem, we propose a novel approach that uses a recurrent neural network language model (RNNLM) to perform morphological analysis directly on unsegmented text. The key idea behind our proposed model is that, due to the structured nature of language, a semantically generalized language model, unlike conventional language models, can provide probabilistic estimates of morpheme boundaries. Several NLP tasks benefit from morphological analysis, but this task can be particularly challenging in languages where segmentation is inscrutable, such as Japanese, which is known for its complex dependency structure and numerous agglutinative words. A detailed examination of previous research reveals that some approaches to tackle unsegmented languages have proposed either rule-based systems that rely on predefined dictionaries (Tiedemann, 2012;Juhonen and 2015) or unsupervised learning methods that attempt to learn segmentation and morphological analysis simultaneously (Tsujii and Hashimoto, 2015). However, these methods are either overly restrictive or fail to account for the fine-grained semantics of word sequences, which are crucial for accurate morphological analysis. Our proposed model addresses this limitation by leveraging a RNNLM, a type of language model capable of capturing complex sequential dependencies in text, including those that are indicative of word boundaries and morpheme internal positions.

Hierarchical segmentation of documents into fine-grained thematic segments is essential for many applications such as information extraction, summarization, and question answering systems. Existing methods either do not utilize clearly identifiable topical shifts in documents, or fail to distinguish between main topics and subtopics. In this paper we describe a hierarchical segmentation method that can identify both, using a bottom-up instance-based clustering algorithm Affinity Propagation. This algorithm has shown good results on numerical data, but its applicability to text data and its ability to handle hierarchical structural needs to be investigated. We extend Affinity Propagation to deal with hierarchically structured data. The extracted segments keeps changing as new information is incorporated in its model. We apply this method to a large-scale corpus to examine how well our method can identify subject shifts and sub-topics and evaluate its efficiency. We compare our method with other state-of-the-art text segmentation methods. We find that our proposed method can derive a comprehensive and hierarchical topical segmentation of the corpus without the need for prior knowledge on the number of segments expected out of the document. We also show that its performance compares favourably against the existing methods both in terms of recall and precision and that it is capable of extracting subtopics within main topics, which is often ignored by existing hierarchical methods or even ignored by flat segmentations. We discuss the impact on and improvements for systems that use document segmentation as their starting point. Our method introduces a new instance-based, density-centred approach to text segmentation. This sets it apart from existing methods that primarily rely on algorithmic rules derived from statistical language models. Our method carefully builds a topical tree starting from the document structure without any previous knowledge of the expected number of topics or segments. The method in itself remains fairly modular and can be easily adapted to different applications, and the segment centres help to identify "keyword" sentences or phrases that likely carry the most information relevant to a segment. We believe that such a kind of contextualisation and segmentation can be very beneficial for all systems requiring fine-grained analysis of documents. The rest of this paper proceeds as follows: in Section 2 we present the Affinity Propagation algorithm. In Section 3 we describe the topological extension of this algorithm to derive a hierarchical segmentation. In Section 4 we describe and report results for experiments with a subset of a manually annotated corpus and a large set of Wikipedia articles.

Anaphoric shell nouns (ASNs) such as “the issue” and “the fact” play significant roles in nearly every substantive natural language text (Abbott, 1984;Rice, 1994). These ASNs can range from clarifying to confusing depending on their context (Harnish, 1994), which underlines the importance of understanding and correctly interpreting them. However, the interpretation of ASNs can often be challenging due to the variety and ambiguity of their potential antecedents (Hacquard, 2010;Lee et al., 2015). Despite their importance in NLP, training data to predict the antecedents of ASNs is scarce – unlike many other linguistic phenomena that have been tackled with more available resources (Hupkes et al., 2018). Collecting human annotators’ precise identification of antecedents for every ASN in a large corpus would demand an enormous amount of effort. This presents a practical challenge for researchers, especially those working on large-scale corpus studies. Cataphoric shell nouns (CSNs) are related linguistic constructs similar to ASNs but have a different syntactic structure. They typically point forward in their context (Wechsler, 2000), often following a clause or phrase they refer to (e.g., "the fact that is the key."). Unlike ASNs, CSNs typically provide explicit information about what they are in reference to, often through the clause that precedes the noun (e.g., “the extent to which the technology is effective” implies a specific scale or degree). Due to their construction, antecedents of CSNs can be identified in most cases more easily by automatic methods, compared to the often ambiguous and varied contexts surrounding ASNs. This paper introduces a novel approach to interpreting ASNs by leveraging antecedents of CSNs as the primary training input. The fundamental idea is that understanding the antecedents of one type of shell noun (CSNs) could provide insights into the contexts surrounding the other (ASNs), since both types of nouns function to abstract or point to elements in their context. If we can develop models to accurately predict antecedents for CSNs, we can potentially adapt or generalize these models to ASNs. The proposed method involves several steps: 1.   Identification and Extraction of Anaphoric Shell Nouns (ASNs):   We first identify ASNs in our corpus. Due to the challenges mentioned above, we deliberately choose public, large-scale corpora to maximize the number of potential ASNs encountered, without focusing on one domain. These include news articles, academic papers, and general-interest websites. 2.   Automatic Identification and Extraction of Antecedents of Cataphoric Shell Nouns (CSNs):   We design our model to recognize CSNs and extract their canonical antecedent clauses or phrases.

This is evidenced by various benchmarks and extensive research conducted in this area. A particular claim, which this paper aims to scrutinize, is that NMT has achieved "human parity" in certain domains. This narrative has been gaining traction, with notable reports suggesting that NMT systems can now match, if not exceed, the quality of human translators (e.g., Sutskever et al., 2014; Vinyals and Le, 2015; Bahdanau et al., 2015). This excitement is understandable given the potential implications for language translation. Sentence-level neural machine translation has demonstrated remarkable capabilities, excelling beyond traditional rule-based and statistical methods in specific language pairs (e.g., Lample et al., 2018). However, claims of human parity are typically based on evaluations limited to the sentence level, which may not accurately reflect the complexity of the task in real-world scenarios. In particular, document-level translation introduces a plethora of additional challenges not addressed at the sentence level. A document is often a cohesive unit of content, where the context extends beyond a single sentence, includes nuanced relationships among the sentences, and may involve specific stylistic, genre-centric, or technical requirements. These aspects are crucial for translating documents effectively, yet they are not addressed by traditional sentence-level evaluations. This paper addresses the gap in current evaluations of machine translation (MT) systems by proposing, and empirically testing, alternative evaluation protocols in comparison to the traditional sentence-level evaluation paradigms. Specifically, we focus on a document-level evaluation that considers "adequacy" and "fluency" at the document level, as these two dimensions are the cornerstone of human translation quality assessments. The need to rethink traditional evaluation methods has been acknowledged in the community (Koehn and Knowles, 2017; Callison-Burch et al., 2006), and our study specifically responds to this call by conducting a rigorous empirical investigation.   Our Research Question and Hypothesis     Research Question:   Has NMT achieved human parity on document-level translation?   Hypothesis:   Despite current claims of human parity in NMT, particularly at the sentence level, when evaluated at the document level, there remains a discernible difference between human translation outputs and those of current NMT systems. This hypothesis hinges on the notion that while NMT excels in processing isolated sentences with high accuracy and fluency, the nuances of complete documents—the ability to sustain coherence, capture intended sarcasm, adapt to genre-specific conventions, or handle technical terminology correctly across the document—remain challenges that current NMT systems struggle to fully address.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models for low-resource languages has recently garnered significant attention. To translate from a rare language Z to a more common language X, such as translating from Luxembourgish to English, the number of available parallel training examples (source sentences in Z and their translations in X) drastically increases the difficulty of this task. This is because traditional NMT models are data-hungry; they rely on hundreds of thousands or even millions of parallel sentences to produce accurate translations. For rare languages, this amount of training data may not always be available, leading to poor translation performance. A common strategy to mitigate this data scarcity is to utilize pivot translation. Pivot translation involves using a third, more resource-rich language Y (in our example English) to form a triangle (X, Y, Z) in order to generate training data for the Z-X pair. This can be done through back-translation, for instance, by translating X-Y examples to Y-Z and then to X-Z (using a pre-trained Y-Z model). Alternatively, language models (such as multilingual NMT) can be used to implicitly learn mappings between different languages, including the Z-X pair. However, these methods typically do not directly engage with the problem at hand or do not fully leverage the inter-language relationships. One of the pioneering works in this space, Wu et al. (2016), proposed a multi-task learning approach that jointly trains the NMT models for Z-Y and Y-X, with the assumption that training data for the Z-X model can be generated by exploiting the Z-Y model. However, this joint training approach faces limitations as it does not explicitly model the inter-language relationships necessary for the Z-X translation, relying instead on inferred relationships from another parallel data (Y-X). In our work, we explore a novel "Triangular Architecture for NMT" (TA-NMT) designed to bridge this gap. The fundamental idea of our approach is to use Z as an intermediate or "latent" variable in the translation process between X and Y. This allows us to explicitly model the Z-Y relationship and leverage it to improve the Z-X translation, even when standalone parallel data between Z and X is limited or absent. Specifically, instead of directly training a Z-X NMT model, we define X-Z as the indirect translation task where Z is treated as a latent variable that mediates between the source X and target Y in a unified translation model.

Entity linking is an important subtask in various applications such as entity disambiguation, question answering, and information retrieval. The goal of entity linking is to map each mention of an entity in unstructured text (e.g., book, movie, person) to a candidate entity in a knowledge base (KB), and then choose the correct entity from the candidates. In recent years, various approaches have been proposed and used for entity linking, such as those based on part-of-speech (POS) tagging and dependency parsing of local contexts (Ejarque, 2005; Lee et al., 2012; Fan et al., 2014), those using word embeddings (Baroni et al., 2014; Rogers et al., 2013), and those based on matrix factorization to capture both relationships among semantic entities and contexts of the entities (Bizer et al., 2011; Bian et al., 2013). On the other hand, there has been little work on looking for and leveraging the appropriate knowledge in a large-scale KB when linking entities. We believe that such knowledge can indeed aid the task. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to entity linking based on a statistical language model-based information retrieval with query expansion, where we incorporate both local contexts and global world knowledge to expand the initial query. We use a positional language model to weigh the importance of named entities in the local contexts at different distances to the query to reflect their relevance for resolving entity ambiguity. Furthermore, we carefully design how to integrate the global knowledge to the initial local queries to explore the generalization, completeness, and consistency of the representations in the global knowledge. Note that this is different from the conventional approaches to directly use the query expansion from existing KBs (Cafarella et al., 2008). Instead, the proposed approach first constructs the contextual query based on textual local contexts, and then exploits both the structured and textual features of a large-scale KB to further refine this contextual query. Our experiments on the TAC-KBP 2010 data show that incorporating such contextual information indeed aids in disambiguating the named entities and consistently improves the entity linking performance. We also compare our results with the official results from KBP 2010 participants and show that our approach is competitive. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in entity linking and structure-aware query expansion. Section 3 describes our approach to link entities to a KB with query expansion.

With the rapid development of the internet and social media in recent years, Chinese web data has increased exponentially. A significant portion of these data are opinions and evaluations posted by users. Understanding these opinions is crucial for businesses, advertisers, and governments who wish to be responsive to their customers and the public. A particular challenge in this area, however, is that Chinese is a difficult language for natural language processing (NLP) due to its syntactical complexity, lack of word delimiters, and the large number of minimal language units. Previous studies on opinion mining and sentiment analysis have primarily focused on English data and mainly concentrate on aspect-level sentiment analysis. That is, these systems primarily tell you whether a user is expressing a positive or negative sentiment towards a certain subject or attribute. However, they often fall short in analyzing the finer nuances of opinion, such as the reasons why a user feels positively or negatively, whether the user places constraints or exceptions to their overall opinion, and how they compare products or entities with each other. Moreover, the presence of evaluative intentions, such as expressing a preference or recommending, requires a more comprehensive analysis. In this paper, we present the Chinese Evaluative Information Analyzer (CEIA) and propose techniques to improve its performance. We focus specifically on evaluative information, which we define as any information that conveys attitudes, opinions, judgments, sentiments, preferences, or criticisms. Unlike traditional sentiment analysis that often only categorizes opinions as positive, negative, or neutral, evaluative information analysis aims to uncover the richer, more nuanced content of an opinion or opinion-based text. Firstly, CEIA is designed to identify and analyze a significantly more diverse set of evaluative information. This includes: 1) sentiment towards entities (e.g., positive/negative opinions about a product or service), 2) attitudes (e.g., approval or disapproval), 3) comparisons (e.g., which product is preferred and why), 4) opinions with constraints (e.g., "I like A unless B is available"), 5) preferences (e.g., explicitly stating a liking towards a product or service), 6) recommendations (e.g., urging others to use a particular product or avoid one), and 7) reasons or explanations behind opinions (e.g., explaining why X is preferred over Y). To achieve this, we introduce two novel contributions over previous research. Firstly, we construct an original annotated corpus specifically for Chinese evaluative information, which allows us to train CEIA on a diverse set of evaluative language patterns and to identify the types of evaluative information.

Training embeddings with multiple senses can be challenging as it requires estimating many parameters simultaneously without explicit supervision. To address this issue, we propose an end-to-end learnable and denoised skip-gram model. We show the importance of disambiguating individual senses of a word and present our Disambiguated Skip-Gram (DSG) model which is an integrated model that performs both context-based embedding and word sense disambiguation (WSD). The DSG model links a word's representation and its senses, enabling the prediction of a word's word sense (and thus its embedding) given context extracted from an unlabeled corpus alongside a fine-grained WSD prediction from knowledge sources. At a high level, our model learns a set of embeddings for each word, where each embedding corresponds to a possible word sense. This allows us to learn a distribution over possible senses for each word, given the context in which it appears. The key insight of our Disambiguated Skip-Gram model is to connect the notion of word sense with that of embedding representation, as if a word sense can be treated as a separate "aspect" of a word's distribution over potential senses. By doing so, for each word, we gain a differentiable or even fully end-to-end differentiable way to learn this representation. Whereas, previously proposed methods for learning multisense word embeddings often decouple sense representation learning from traditional word embedding learning, while adding an extra layer of label supervision in the form of word sense disambiguation annotations, or rely on an ensemble of individual embeddings or carefully designed inference over a precomputed multiheaded set (as in earlier works), we propose to learn the word senses and embeddings simultaneously as part of a single neural model. Moreover, inspired by successful methods for regularizing and "denoising" word embeddings, such as Word2Vec sub-sampling (Mikolov et al., 2013) and Negative Sampling (Mikolov et al., 2013), we propose an additional layer of regularization to the embeddings of the sense base. Instead of sub-sampling or using negative examples, we explicitly "denoise" the sense embeddings by confronting them with the projected context embeddings. This is done by adding an additive penalty term on the similarity between sense embeddings and context embeddings, which encourages the embedding for each sense to align more closely with context words and less with words that are less relevant in the local context. This added regularization term forces the embeddings of different senses to behave like they belong to the distinct subspaces even if they share much in common based on common lexical aspects.

In Table 1, we summarize how state-of-the-art open-domain conversational systems can be broadly classified into two categories. Rule-based systems (SRI, Apple's ELIZA, etc.) rely heavily on hand-crafted templates and rules to generate responses. While these systems can provide a consistent and structured conversation experience, they are limited by their ability to generalize beyond predefined domains and react to novel or unexpected user inputs. Such a system would predict responses to any user input by analyzing the input and relying on the meanings of words, including syntactic, semantic, and discourse phenomena. However, several key challenges lie in the way of realizing such a system. Second, generating natural-sounding responses that align with contexts and pragmatics while respecting world knowledge is non-trivial. To address these challenges, we redesign and reassess the input analysis and response generation components of an open-domain conversational system. The architecture consists of three interdependent modules: input understanding, context modeling, and response generation. Each of these modules is built on techniques that have shown significant success in various NLP applications (Mikolov et al., 2013; Vaswani et al., 2017; Peters et al., 2018). Moreover, we propose employing external knowledge sources like knowledge graphs to enhance the conversational agent's ability to integrate and reason about the world. We construct an open-domain conversational system based on the proposed architecture and conduct human evaluation experiments to assess its performance.

Disambiguating Dynamic Sentiment Ambiguous Adjectives (DSAAs) is a crucial challenge in sentiment analysis. The challenge is exemplified by adjectives like "large", "small", "high", and "low" that inherently carry positive or negative sentiment depending on the context in which they appear. For instance, "large" is usually associated with positive sentiment when referring to dimensions like "room" or "feast", and negative when referring to quantities like "amount of debt" or "time spent". Similarly, "small" can be positive when associated with qualities like "gift" or "budget", and negative when associated with verbs like "hope" or "expectation". Therefore, understanding the exact sentiment conveyed by such words is critical for precise sentiment analysis. Traditional sentiment analysis methods, such as lexicon-based approaches, have limitations in addressing DSAAs because semantic orientation of such adjectives can be context-dependent. For example, "high" can be associated with positive sentiment when referring to performance ("high score") or economic indicators ("high profits"), but with negative sentiment in terms of risk or cost ("high risk", "high cost"). Similarly, "low" can be viewed as positive in terms of costs or risk ("low cost", "low risk"), but negative in terms of quality ("low standards", "low quality"). Existing methods often lack mechanisms to disambiguate the sentiment of such contextual words based on their context. The proposed method in this paper introduces a knowledge-based approach to disambiguate DSAAs based on the context in which they appear. First, we mine the web to predict the sentiment expectation of target nouns that could be modified by DSAAs. Sentiment expectation in this context refers to whether a noun is generally associated with positive, negative, or neutral sentiment. This forms a reference point for analysis. Given the socio-linguistic complexity of attributing sentiment to the use of DSAAs, we introduce the concept of sentiment expectation. This approach designates the perceived or inferred sentiment of a noun based on the measured sentiment associated with that noun in various contexts, as opposed to a direct semantic orientation. We argue that sentiment expectation can serve as a more nuanced and context-sensitive attribute that better aligns with human perception of sentiment in natural language. To determine sentiment expectations, we extract large-scale lexical and syntactical patterns from the web using advanced pattern recognition techniques. These patterns are designed to capture complex relations between adjectives and nouns in various contexts. The collected data is then used to infer the sentiment expectations of target nouns.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental source of real-time first-hand information about ongoing events. On the other hand, microblogging platforms are rapidly evolving and challenging to harness, due to issues such as low-fidelity information (e.g., briefness, voice ambiguity), lack of contextual and semantic grounding, and potential spread of misinformation. In recent years, microblog processing has involved a plethora of various NLP tasks, including topic modeling (Example, Tolias et al., 2016), text classification (Milic-Frayling et al., 2011), sentiment analysis (Pang and Lee, 2008), and event detection (Sambasivan et al., 2014). However, these tasks often are designed for individual tweets in isolation. Microblogging is not a purposeless collection of semantic entities. Instead, the content of microblogging varies through the life cycle of an event. Some events might have short life cycles while others might span over a long period. Moreover, some events are more appealing and hence attract more users' attention, leading to a higher volume of similar or related information. In fact, the life cycle of microblogging content around an event has varying volume, cluster intuitively For instance, a significant event can lead to an initial burst of high-volume tweets, followed by a longer period with shallowly lower frequency tweets reflecting wider user engagement. To better understand such dynamics, in this paper, we focus on the time-series aspect of microblog data and propose MultiView Diffusion (MVD), a novel multi-view learning framework to tackle the task of event detection in Twitter, especially for short-lived events. MVD provides a more comprehensive understanding by considering multiple key characteristics of the data simultaneously. Specifically, we leverage and integrate three distinct views of microblog data: (i) the content-level view, (ii) the temporal view, and (iii) the social view. First, the content-level view is captured through the embedding of tweet content into a semantic space, where together tweets from a single real-world event are expected to cluster. Second, the temporal view is represented by the time stamps associated with tweets, which can indicate recurring patterns of activity or sudden and continuous increases in tweet volume over a period of time. Third, the social view is represented by user networks, aiming to capture shared understanding of events that often propagate through social communities. The three views are linked and analyzed in parallel by MVD, allowing the system to learn better semantic representations for the data by addressing the informative interplay between them.

Training neural networks directly on unsegmented text has been seen successful in Chinese NER (Zhou et al., 2020). However, when it comes to event detection, the deep neural network approaches (e.g., event detection using neural entity linker (EDNEL) (Robertson et al., 2017)) often suffer from questions such as "What is the correct piece of text for an event trigger?" (the word-trigger mismatch problem (Strube and Mary, 2005)), which remains a primary challenge for event detection (ED) especially for languages without natural word delimiters such as Chinese. In most Chinese NLP tasks including ED, word units are often used for representation. However, unlike many other languages such as English, Chinese words are not well-defined from a syntactical perspective (Hawkins, 1990). The boundaries between Chinese characters can be ambiguous due to the morpheme-discovery problem. As a result, relying solely on words can lead to a mismatch between word-based models and actual event triggers. For instance, event triggers in Chinese can span over multiple words, such as "中美贸易冲突" (US-China trade conflict), which consists of three words. Moreover, Chinese event triggers often contain contextually specific and less common words, which might not be well represented in word-based models. These contextual words may often be composed of multiple characters that carry independent syntactic or semantic information. For example, the word "贸" (trade) is a standalone morpheme, while "美" (beautiful), despite having been borrowed to represent the United States, still retains its original meaning. A more elegant approach to tackle the word-trigger mismatch problem in Chinese ED is to directly leverage and model the compositional structure of character-based triggers. Given that characters, unlike words, are the basic syntactic unit of Chinese and are unambiguous, a character-based understanding could potentially better align with the structure of Chinese event triggers. This paper proposes Nugget Proposal Networks (NPNs), a character-level framework for Chinese event detection that directly addresses the word-trigger mismatch problem. NPNs can identify and propose candidate event triggers in the form of "nuggets" – entire nuggets centered at individual characters. This is done by learning a hybrid representation of characters to capture both structural (morpheme composition) and semantic information. Central to NPNs is the idea that potential event triggers in Chinese might be best explored by examining the informative contexts around characters rather than just words. The model learns predictive representations of characters, which are then used to generate nugget proposals.

Training natural language parsers across multiple languages is a major challenge. A key difficulty is linguistic variability: each language has its own grammar and word order, forcing us to either abandon the assumption of a universal grammar (which has the advantage of enabling various inferences but can still lead to quite different structures for different languages) and settle for separate, language-specific systems – or face questions of how to adapt and generalize our methods and knowledge across languages. In this paper, we propose an approach that aims to strike a balance between these options, using a form of universalistic linguistic knowledge to guide grammar induction and dependency parsing across a range of languages. Our approach is based on the principle that while languages may vary greatly in surface form, they may share underlying syntactic properties. Specifically, we assume that there is a set of linguistic universals - in our case, a matrix representing commonly occurring syntactic relations between pairs of syntactic categories - that can be applied across languages. These relations are not directly tied to any particular language grammar but have been widely observed across natural language typology studies, including language studies on dependency grammars (Hudson, 1990). The central idea of our approach is to integrate these potential universals into the parser's training process in a way that guides but does not rigidly constrain the inferred grammar. We use a probabilistic dependency parser, allowing us to encode our linguistic knowledge as a set of "soft" rules. These rules are assumed to apply across languages, although the evidence they are grounded on is often specific to a particular language or family (e.g., Japanese postpositions deviating from the universal head-initial word order, or the marking of subjects in ergative languages, see Dixon, 1994). However, because these rules are based on cross-linguistic generalisation, they help to 'inform' the learner about probable dependencies likely to occur in most languages. To implement this idea, we use posterior expectation constraints to influence the learning algorithm, imposing a requirement on the proportion of dependencies that are "compatible" with our set of universal rules. An alternative approach would be to treat the universal dependencies as a base model and add language-specific exceptions. Instead, we use them explicitly only to guide inference but do not add new parameters or structure beyond what is already in the probabilistic model. The architecture of our system includes: 1. A pre-training phase where we compile a cross-linguistic set of likely dependencies based on published linguistic corpora and typological datasets.

Training natural language processing (NLP) classifiers with many conjunctive features (combinations of primitive features) can lead to inefficiencies in both time and space. This is especially true when the deep features (which are the combinations of primitive features) are more complex, such as polynomial expressions. For example, in dependency parsing, a feature might be a combination of questions such as "does this word (prime) have a syntactic function and an edge going to a part-of-speech annotated noun?" which might be represented as a polynomial expression of the primitives. While complex features (like polynomial expressions) can often lead to better results due to their ability to capture more nuanced information, they also increase the computational cost, making the optimization and lazy evaluation of these features more complex and computationally expensive. As a result, training such classifiers becomes slow, particularly when dealing with large-scale datasets or when multiple features are combined in complex weighted sums or polynomial expressions. Additionally, the storage required to represent all possible feature combinations grows combinatorially with the number of features and their combinations, causing memory issues especially when looking for the weights of these features during both training and evaluation. To address these issues, several approaches have been proposed in the past. Some of these reduce the feature space by applying techniques such as feature hashing (Weinberger et al., 2009), which maps feature vectors to binary vectors in order to reduce the dimensionality and memory requirement. However, feature hashing can introduce label noise in the classification model and may not be suitable for all types of features, especially those that rely on order or distances among features for their semantic meaning, such as polynomial or weighted sums of primitive features. Another approach is to use a library-based feature representation, such as the one used in (Wallach, 2006), where each feature is represented by a list of sub-feature values that can be efficiently accessed and combined. However, these approaches still require evaluating and tracking the weights of each feature, which can be computationally expensive during training and possibly also during prediction. The naive evaluation of all feature combinations could be too slow for large feature sets or for applications where real-time prediction is required. Therefore, optimizing the evaluation or storing partial results of feature weights for commonly occurring features and their combinations becomes crucial. Our solution to this problem introduces a novel method to reduce the computational complexity of classifiers trained with advanced features – particularly those that are conjunctive or represented as polynomials.

Training natural language processing (NLP) systems at massive scale is of key importance for many applications. To achieve scale today, nearly every system employs some form of distributed and parallelized computation to harness deep computing resources (Dean and Ghemawat, 2008). However, training at scale drastically increases the running time, even with parallelism, and questions remain as to just how large (in terms of data and number of model parameters) systems can grow while maintaining practical training times. Coreference has traditionally been seen as one of the most challenging tasks in NLP, and it is also a key requirement for wide coverage semantic role labeling, named entity extraction, and information extraction systems. To achieve accurate, practical inference for such applications, thousands of hours of training time have historically been considered necessary (Cells, 2008), a trend that is unsustainable as the semantic tasks grow in size and the sample of data grows larger. In this paper, we describe a Coreference framework that addresses the scalability issue of previous approaches by incorporating a novel discriminative hierarchical model, as described in Section 2. While previous approaches to coreference have often relied on iterative approaches such as expectation maximization (Spitkovsky and Collins, 2005;Kumar et al., 2011) on top of symbols斗般的 feature computation between mention pairs (Mintz et al., 2009;Sang and DeRose, 2007;Siu and Dyer, 2012), such techniques can lead to high computational costs for very large numbers of mentions (a task requiring months of compute time, even using current distributed deep learning systems in practice: see Discussion for details). Instead, we’re proposing that a large part of the problem and its solution can be reduced to the effective representation and aggregation of the candidates (mentions and their context), leading to reduced computational costs while maintaining or improving upon previous results on coreference accuracy. The hierarchical model significantly improves speed and generalizability of coreference methods: as we demonstrate later in the paper, the model can be trained in hours on a single machine for datasets with millions of mentions. For example, we are able to train our framework and perform inference for 6 million author mentions in under four hours on a single CPU. Previously, one of the most popular ways to perform coreference for large vocabularies/persons is by using pairwise mention features (Mintz et al., 2009;Sang and DeRose, 2007;Siu and Dyer, 2012). These systems compute features for all pairs of mentions (mention–mention features), treating each mention inherently as a single “entity”.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on topic: A Unified Model of Phrasal and Sentential Evidence for Information Extraction ### Introduction Information Extraction (IE) systems are widely used to automatically extract information from natural language texts. A key task in this area is event extraction, which involves identifying and annotating the entities and relationships relevant to a specific event or status change. Traditional approaches to this task often rely on local evidence such as the words or part-of-speech tags that occur near the phrase being considered, especially the co-occurrence of event word and potential role fillers. However, this methodology has limitations: it can fail when the event word and potential role filler are in separate clauses, and it does not effectively leverage the full context of the sentence to decide if a phrase should be annotated. In many cases, Sentential Context (SC), derived from the relationships among semantic entities beyond adjacency in the local context, provides crucial information for event extraction. For instance, consider the sentence "President Obama visited the city of Lincoln, where the town hall meeting was held." In traditional phrasal context approaches, the local context around the phrase "town hall meeting" is examined for evidence of its potential role in the visit event, but the relationship between "city" and "meeting" that indicates the meeting's location is lost. Here, both SC and Phrasal Context (PC) are relevant. Where the phrasal context might provide evidence that "town hall meeting" is likely relevant to the event, the sentential context (including the relationship between the event word "visited" and the entities "city" and "meeting") provides additional crucial information about how these entities relate to one another and in turn, the role they play in the event. ### Goal of This Work The main goal of this paper is to develop a unified model that efficiently leverages both sentential and phrasal evidence for improving the accuracy of event extraction tasks. Traditional systems, which often rely purely on local or phrasal context, may incorrectly or less robustly identify role fillers in situations where a dependence between the event and the role filler exists but is not locally apparent. By incorporating SC explicitly into the evidence used for role candidate selection, our model aims to address scenarios where role fillers are present but the indication of their roles may come from distant parts of the sentence or may rely on understanding the sentence's semantic structure for correct interpretation.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, Facebook and Instagram, have become key players in the digital world. They enable individuals to share and disseminate information rapidly and are rapidly evolving into a key channel for obtaining news and information. As these platforms grow, they are increasingly used to generate and spread political information. This increases the likelihood of exposure to misinformation – intentional or unintentional falsifications of information (Tsfati, 2013;Effron, 2016;Vosoughi, 2018). The spread of misinformation can have significant social and political consequences (Bennett and Livingston, 2018;Pew Research Center, 2019). Thus, it’s critical to develop methods that can identify and combat misinformation. However, detecting misinformation presents several challenges. First, digital platforms spread misinformation faster than the truth (Vosoughi et al., 2018). Misinformation often spreads via networks of interconnected users, which makes it particularly hard to locate and stem its spread (Rohr et al., 2020). Furthermore, misinformation can be intentionally created or unintentionally spread by well-intentioned individuals (Weakliem, 2008;Pennycook and Rand, 2019). The different modalities of misinformation, including text, images and videos, also complicate the detection process. The problem of identifying and combating misinformation is also intricately connected with the problem of understanding sentiments and opinions expressed over digital platforms (Gloor et al., 2011;Levy & Neal, 2006;Tang, 2013). Sentiment analysis is crucial because sentiment and misinformation can often be inter-linked: a post with negative sentiment could be more likely to spread inconsistent facts (Bessi & Ferrara, 2016). Furthermore, understanding the sentiment around a topic or the sentiment expressed about different facts helps to analyze potential misinformation patterns. Thus, the question arises: how can we develop systematic approaches to understand misinformation on social media? While traditional methods for information verification are feasible in journalism and academic contexts, they are not scalable to the changing online environments where misinformation can spread rapidly (Marshall, 2017). One key solution for tackling the complex challenge of misinformation and sentiment analysis on digital platforms lies in harnessing the power of machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms. ML models can learn patterns from large datasets and NLP techniques can process and understand the structure and meaning of human language. However, we observe a lack of ML and NLP techniques that specifically aim to combine misinformation detection with sentiment analysis. This paper bridges this gap by introducing a novel method that: 1. Captures sentiment information from user posts. 2. Associates sentiment with potential misinformation through ML models trained on data that links sentiment to fact-checking outcomes.

Training neural models across different sources can be challenging when the data sources present strict distribution differences or domain biases. In particular, when the data distributions differ dramatically, the learned models may not generalize well to new domains. This is particularly evident in neural networks that process high-dimensional, dense features such as word embeddings. In spite of this, domain adaptation methods for instance features have only been applied to binary features (Daumé III, 2009;Efron and Hastie, 2016) and not directly to neural networks with dense features. Thus, there is a gap between existing adaptation methods and how they could be applied to neural networks. This paper explores two extensions of traditional domain adaptation techniques to the context of neural networks: one for adapting feature augmentations and another for learning shared domain features. Specifically, we propose two methods to adapt the feature augmentation technique of Daumé III (2009) from binarized feature spaces to neural feature spaces, and also to use the Shared Interest Tracking (SIT) method of Ando and Zhang (2005) in a creative manner for domain adaptation. We provide a thorough evaluation of our methods in various domain adaptation scenarios, and show that they outperform the traditionally used adaptation method of Daumé III (2009) applied to context-agnostic models like Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) as well as competitive results against state-of-the-art methods in the case of neural networks. The paper contributes towards more robust neural domain adaptation and bridges a gap between existing domain adaptation methods and the use of dense, high-dimensional neural features. To establish context, we first discuss the challenges of domain adaptation in neural networks and the limitations in applying existing domain adaptation techniques to neural features. For instance, when learning a model on a large and "rich" dataset, but deploying it in a real-world scenario where it encounters data from "poorer" sources, the performance might be unacceptable. Domains in this context can refer to different sources (e.g., biomedical articles vs. legal documents, or training data from a single source vs. a diverse variety of sources). The domain shift can be due to differences in terminology, formatting, style, or other factors that are implicitly captured in the data features but not easily modeled by distributional assumptions. Traditional domain adaptation methods have often tackled this problem by attempting to align features between source and target domains. For binary/pairwise features, a common approach by Daumé III (2009) is to zero-inflate the source data to capture feature rarity, which may be under-represented in the source.

Latent subjectivity can be broadly interpreted as the topic or entity of which sentiment is being expressed. To estimate latent subjectivity for a given document, one approach is to model it as a latent variable using traditional techniques such as topic models (Blei, 2003) or maximum-likelihood estimation (Lacave, 2013). A topic model would model the latent subjectivity (topic) and the sentiment (polarity) at the same time, but the latent representation has minimal language-specific structure, as it is built independent of linguistic features. Using traditional LSA or PLSA (Landauer & Dumais, 1997; Hofmann, 1999) to predict subjectivity is less likely to be successful, as the subjectivity's distribution is not necessarily connected in a linear way to matrix cosines derived directly from word co-occurrence. These latent variable models do not directly consider the role of discourse structure, which has been shown to play an important role in communicating sentiment and meaning (Moore and Malinowski, 2010). Discourse connectives, such as "however", "but", "then", "therefore", and "meanwhile", explicitly mark the relationships or flow between different parts of the text. They can serve as signals about changes in the underlying subjectivity, transitions in different topics or entities being discussed, and other shifts in assumed world knowledge. The idea here is to incorporate the linguistic knowledge embedded in discourse connectives to improve the algorithm's ability to model and learn latent subjectivity transitions. One approach could involve adding a specific features for each type of discourse connective as predictors, learned using traditional methods such as logistic regression or neural networks. However, this is labor-intensive and requires manual feature engineering. Another approach is to model transitions through a latent variable approach but doesn't learn the explicit role of the connectors themselves. The proposed method, which we call 'Discourse Feature Integration (DFI)', integrates discourse connectives into the latent variable models directly. This is done via introducing transition features that encode a connection between the current and future predicted subjectivity values. We define a window around each discourse connector to explicitly mark segments of text that are connected by these linguistic elements. These transition features aim to capture the relationship between changing latent subjectivities and the identifiable transitions signalled by discourse connectives. A detailed outline of the DFI method includes: 1.   Text Preprocessing and Discourse Connector Detection  : We first process text so that each discourse connector is identified within the context of its surrounding sentences.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, while such data's cost and availability make it unviable for many languages and domains, less clearly illuminated is the insufficiency of using this data for the intended purpose of various NLP applications. For instance, in machine translation, the translation and quality assessment of bilingual sentences is usually assumed to be questions of mapping sentences from one language (domain) to another. This paper examines the extent of transferability between different domains (sentence types) and tasks, using a paired-sample fractal analysis. Two sets of data are used for this study: extracted from an academic conference proceedings and a set of fiction texts. We find that while the word order, word frequency and usage distributions are similar across the two domains, the syntactic structures and argument constructions have significant differences. This implies that models trained to handle one type of text would not necessarily perform well on the other, without additional data or adjustments. Our findings shed light on the importance of domain-specific adaptation and the need for more exploration on domain/language independence in natural language processing. Historically, the field of natural language processing has been driven forward by the steady growth in the quantity and quality of available annotated data. However, the development of next-generation NLP systems, particularly in domains that are less represented in the common available benchmarks, faces a stark challenge: how to build high-performing models without sufficient annotated data. Modality, while another means of addressing the label scarcity in learning-based systems, is its own domain-specific approach, not necessarily generalizable. A more general approach could involve analyzing how language (and linguistic patterns within language) generalize across domains and tasks. To bridge this knowledge gap, this work adopts a novel, domain-agnostic methodology to study generalizability and transferability across language domains and tasks. Fractal analysis, a technique commonly used in image compression and reconstruction, is used to compare the syntactic and semantic structures of sentence pairs across two domains. The principle underlying fractal analysis in natural language is that similar recurring patterns should be measured, visualized and compared across a range of scales. Two matched corpora are used in this study: one from academic conference proceedings and another from fiction texts. These domains are chosen for their differing sentence and linguistic structures but share sufficient English language usage for the purpose of applying fractal analysis.

Automatic text generation from knowledge graph (KG)-structured data has many applications, such as question answering, story generation, and task-oriented dialogue systems (Kumar et al., 2016;Rashkin et al., 2015;Li et al., 2015;Narasimhan et al., 2016). One such structured representation is the Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR, Banarescu et al., 2013), a minimal language-independent representation of text meaning. In AMR, the meaning of a text is represented as a graph, where nodes represent concepts and edges represent semantic roles. An emerging task in the AMR community is to automatically generate text from an AMR graph (Wu et al., 2016;Shao et al., 2016b;Plusch et al., 2016), following recent progress in the natural language generation (NLG) community using sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014). The seq2seq model excels at modeling long-term context dependencies and hierarchical structures. As a major application, the English Abstractive Text Summarization (EAS) task was first formulated this way (Nallapati et al., 2016). However, with shallow structures like sequential data (i.e., the linearized AMR structure), the model may lose important information from the graph structure (Lin et al., 2015b). This may limit the performance of the model to generate text matching the AMR representation. This limitation is particularly serious for large graphs in practice: as shown in Figure 1 , longer sequential representation (right panel) may lose graph-level information that can't be conveyed entirely by the local sequential context (left panel). Motivated by this, we investigate the use of graph structures to encode AMR graphs. We introduce a graph-to-sequence (graph2seq) model for AMR-to-text generation. Specifically, instead of linearizing the AMR graph as a sequence, we use a graph neural network (Wang et al., 2017) to globally and symmetrically capture AMR concepts and edges. This allows the model to take into account both global and local information simultaneously. To model sequential dependencies and generate text, we use a new layered LSTM structure, inspired by the original structure of seq2seq models. The added layered LSTM structure uses outputs from the graph neural network at the previous step, and outputs the next character. Thus, the graph-to-sequence framework combines the strength of graph neural networks and the sequential dependencies modeling. In this paper, we present the details of the graph2seq model and its connections to prior work. Extensive experiments on three publicly available datasets (Wu et al., 2016;Shao et al., 2016b;Plusch et al., 2016) show that the graph2seq model outperforms the state-of-the-art seq2seq-based models by as much as 1.8 BLEU points.

Multi-document summarization (MDS) is a fundamental task of text summarization, where the goal is to create a short summary of a set of related articles about a specific topic. The aim is to provide a coherent and informative summary that captures the main ideas of all the source documents. While the task of MDS has been extensively studied, challenges remain in questions such as how to preserve coherence while simultaneously aiming for informativeness and efficiency. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based approach to MDS, using text links as the primary building blocks for discovering coherent structure and extracting information from multiple documents. We extensively explore ways to construct a representation of the source documents as a network graph, and optimize this graph to produce a highly informative and coherent summary. Textually, coherence can be understood as the connectedness of ideas within a text (Givón, 1991; Sanders et al., 2007). In MDS, this concept is complexified because individual documents within a set of source documents often share similar ideas but also contain distinct, yet sometimes complementary, information. In our work, we treat the task of MDS as a coherent selection and ordering problem. We model the relationship between sentences in the source documents as a network, capturing implicit links that reflect various forms of coherence, such as anaphora, shared discourse entities, and different levels of semantic relatedness. Unlike traditional graph-based summarization methods which may rely solely on syntactic relationships or surface-level patterns, our method explicitly models deeper textual links based on semantic and discourse analysis. The proposed method involves two main stages: Network Construction and Coherent Selection (optimization). 1. Network Construction : We build a graph representation of the source documents by mining various forms of text links, including lexical co-occurrences and discourse relations through a combination of lexical and syntactic analysis techniques. The candidates for the text links are the sentences that make up the source documents. We use NLP techniques to construct these sentences and link them based on the discovered coherence relations. 2. Coherent Selection (Optimization) : Given the network representation of the source documents, our goal is to find a path or sub-network within this graph that forms a coherent summary. We optimize an objective function to minimize the divergence from the whole document set while maximizing informativeness and readability. The objective function is designed to respect coherence by maximizing the density of the summary network in meaningful clusters of related concepts and minimizing unnecessary transits between these clusters.

Training parallel corpora is the core resource of Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) models. We can have more parallel data by using pivoting through more languagepairs and using automated translation from one language to another (Krings, 2000). However, pivoting requires additional training data or other computational resources (e.g., a tree-to-string conversion model), which are not always available (Cohn and Lapata, 2010). Another approach to overcome this issue is to preprocess the language of interest, as fracturing out untranslated words (OOV) for SMT data collection (Koehn, 2005; Nye et al., 2011). However, SMT models without training data at all for the language pairs of interest have only been investigated in early work (Koehn et al., 2003). One recent approach addresses this issue by generating glosses or "superarbitraries" from a pair of related languages and using them to train an SMT model (Koehn and Hoang, 2010). Another line of work uses cross-lingual automatic paraphrase selection from web-based comparable corpus or multi-lingual corpus (Falaschetti et al., 2005; Vilar et al., 2010). However, using different training data for each language is difficult because it often assumed that the model is trained with paired corpora in each language pair. Furthermore, if we also consider cross-lingual lexical resource generation (e.g., using similar (Peña et al., 2011) or parallel corpora (Atanasova and Lamb, 2009)), cross-lingual representation, and multilingual embedding models (Conneau et al., 2017), it is clear that the computational and manual effort needed to exploit different data sources or even different textual representations increases rapidly. This means if one aims to utilize varied resources in addition to parallel corpora, there may be multiple additional stages and methods, each of which comes with a certain learning cost and requires additional expertise. Therefore, in this paper we argue that instead of gathering more parallel data or other external resources, it is more practical to look for monolingual resources that can be exploited for SMT improvement. The core of our idea is to use monolingual paraphrases to enrich the training data and alleviate the OOV bottleneck in low-density language pairs. Paraphrases for untranslated words are potentially informative for SMT models. However, the theoretical rationale of the use of paraphrases in SMT is relatively undeveloped. We use distributional semantic similarity to capture paraphrasing, which has been widely used in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) (Resnik, 1996). But it has not been clearly demonstrated that paraphrases, themselves, can significantly improve SMT models in particular.

Training agents for task-completion dialogue systems is a challenging task. Traditional methods often first predict a dialogue policy from dialogue data and then use this policy to generate dialogue responses and update the policy using reinforcement learning (Riedl and Young, 2004;Young et al., 2010;Li et al., 2016b). A recent alternative is to combine planning and reinforcement learning for dialogue policy learning (Henderson et al., 2014;Cui et al., 2017), which is beneficial for applications such as information seeking or task assistance (Komatani et al., 2001;Pang and Ng, 2001). Plan-based methods generate a dialogue plan from verbal and non-verbal input at training time and then use this plan to drive online interaction to decide action. This semantic representation of planning can be more sample-efficient than directly learning the policy from the policy's parameters. Hence, even though planning is computationally expensive, it is an attractive approach due to its interpretability and sometimes improved convergence. However, current plan-based dialogue policy learning methods often require an automatic planner or trusted data (Liang et al., 2016), which might or might not be available in the application domain of interest. Recently, Deep Dyna-Q (DDQ) (Cui et al., 2017) was proposed, extending the classic Dyna-Q algorithm (Watkins and Dayan, 1992) to incorporate model-based planning for task-completion dialogue policy learning. DDQ represents a policy as a policy network and a model as an RNN summarizer. Instead of acquiring in advance a domain planner for generating plans, DDQ extends the Dyna-Q framework to generate plans from simulation and uses these simulated plans to update the policy network in a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) fashion. By doing so, DDQ effectively allows for learning without relying on automatic planning or trusted planning data. A major drawback of DDQ, however, is that it depends heavily on the quality of the simulated experience. Low-quality simulated experience may lead to poor policy learning or even divergence. For task-completion dialogue systems, the policy should ideally adapt to changing user requirements over a long conversation. Learning from simulated experience may expose the policy to a very limited set of scenarios, potentially leading to overfitting for specific scenarios or limited robustness. For example, a defender policy that is trained against a randomly generated attacker may be vulnerable to zero-day exploits or real-world adversaries that are designed to break the defender's model. To improve the effectiveness and robustness of dialogue policy learning, we propose to extend DDQ by incorporating an additional mechanism to evaluate and control the quality of simulated dialogue.

Training neural event patterns can be challenging due to the variance in triggers of the events and the complexity of their event arguments. These issues have resulted in designing neural networks that utilize weak supervision signals from natural language corpora (Surden, 2019). Weak supervision provides a way to represent complex patterns that are difficult to define, but the accuracy of the paraphrases generated depends on the context in which these patterns appear. This paper proposes a method, called "IDEST" (Iterative Domain-aware Event Synonym Transformers), that addresses these challenges by iteratively presenting and learning paraphrases of extracted event patterns from overlapping event domains, such as news events. Unlike knowledge-based systems, IDEST is data-driven and creates distributed representations of event patterns rooted in the verbal and textual accompaniments of these patterns. An important point of departure for IDEST is its reliance on semantic context beyond simple co-reference resolution but rather on contextual paraphrasization. By leveraging multiple days' worth of news coverage containing the same entity, we aim to project its event patterns into a distributional semantics space, where equivalent patterns converge despite syntactic or lexical variation. This approach can generalize across various date points (and their accompanying events and entities), leading to a more robust representation or paraphrase model. By iterating through this process, IDEST learns and updates its representation, which accommodates rare patterns and can also significantly reduce the bias towards more frequent event patterns, while maintaining generalizability. The learning architecture of IDEST uses a transformer-based model, tailored for paraphrasing at the event level (as opposed to sentence or word level), to generate distributed representations for event patterns. Instead of manually annotating paraphrases, we derive a "pseudo-paraphrase" from the context, which is optimized iteratively. The "weak" supervision signal here is the presence of related entities (e.g., the same "person" or "event location") mentioned in different textual descriptions across days. This approach designates the model to find the common denominators among event pattern descriptions, which together form a paraphrased, generalized event pattern representation. For example, if on a given day, newspaper A reports "CEO XYZ announces company's acquisition of ZYX Corp and expects to save 100 million in costs", and on another day (within the same timeframe or coverage of the event), newspaper B reports "XYZ's takeover of ZYX Corp could yield significant cost savings, confirmed by the company", the IDEST model would identify the event pattern of "acquisition of company X by Y" leading to "cost savings."

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on "Deeper syntax for better semantic parsing": ---------------- The main goal of semantic parsing is to decompose sentences into a well-defined semantic representation, which allows for subsequent reasoning, question answering, or other high-level language understanding tasks. In this paper, we argue that the grammatical structure underlying a sentence – its phrase syntax – plays a crucial role in this process and that using a deeper and more nuanced syntactic representation can significantly improve the quality of the resulting semantic parsing. Our approach is guided by the intuition that different syntactic structures (e.g., passive constructions, coordination, control, and raising) may encode or obscure different semantic information, and that capturing this structure in a more abstract and rich way will lead to a more precise and informative semantic representation. Rather than relying only on surface syntactic features (e.g., part-of-speech tags, dependency parses), we propose the use of a deep syntactic representation that abstracts away from purely syntactic phenomena and closely aligns with the semantic structure of the sentence. Our deep syntactic representation is based on a number of carefully selected abstract constructions and relations which serve as indicators for specific semantic roles and entailments in the sentence. We define these constructions using a combination of linguistics-inspired generalisations or heuristics and statistical patterns that we identify through large-scale corpus analysis and machine learning. Examples of these deep syntactic features include abstract constructions for indicating the initiator of an action (akin to the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs), the possessor and the possessed entity (as distinct from simple grammatical subjects and objects), and the sentiments or intentions expressed by a speaker (e.g., marking ascriptions of emotions or beliefs, distinguishing between direct speech and reported speech in discourse). We present extensive experimental results from applying this approach to French semantic parsing, using a large and varied corpus annotated with semantic frames from the FrameNet paradigm . Our evaluations show that the use of the proposed deep syntactic features leads to significant improvements over a baseline using only traditional, shallow syntactic information. The performance gain occurs in two main realms: the measured accuracy of the semantic parse increases, reflecting more correct determinations of the roles of the sentence elements in relation to the semantic frames; and the resulting semantic structures are more structured and informative for downstream tasks, as judged by systematic manual analysis.
