In this work, we propose a general and effective neural network model for graph-based dependency parsing which overcomes this limitation and provides an elegant way of using phrase-level features, thus potentially exploiting the benefits of large language models. We first show that by using CNNs and secondary pooling layer, we can get an order of magnitude faster inference. We then propose tanhcube, a novel activation function which takes a vector of features and combines them into an effective representation, by exploiting the ordering of features. Specifically, is a matrix representing the derived feature combinations. This function was inspired by the weighted combination of features in recent works such as "Two-Stream Graph Convolutional Networks for Sentence Classification" (Zheng et al., 2018) and "End-to-End Dependency Parsing via Stack LSTM and Input Feed" (Zhou et al., 2017), but allows weights to depend on the ordering or derivation history. For a parser with this function, we show improvements over systems using both fully hand-crafted features and the heuristic shallowly learned ones. Modifying the system for distributed representation benefits gives further accuracy in the downstream syntactic dependency evaluation. Phrase-level features are expensive to use in conventional graph-based parsers because they require a syntactic parse to be available. In previous work (Kumar, 2015), a graph-based parser has used hand-computed phrase-level scores by adding words and features greedily. To incorporate these phrase-level features into the neural network model in a more general and scalable way, we use a max-pooling layer over the phrase level scores computed on all possible spans or paths in the graph. We show that this side-information, which together with the total dependence graph, can further improve accuracy without a significant hit on speed. The proposed model is explicitly designed to accommodate low-cost feature combinations by making no assumptions about the order in which features should be combined or weighted. Consequently, dependency parsers based on this model can automatically extract relevant high-order feature combinations from atomic features. We present experiments demonstrating that our model is readily applied to dependency parsing and obtain state-of-the-art results across different dependency tasks for English data.

Language models are widely used in many natural language processing applications, including speech recognition (Rabiner et al., 1969; Jelinek et al., 1976), machine translation (Brown et al., 1990) and language generation (Black et al., 1998; Cohen et al., 1998). One of the most popular choices is the n-gram language model (Goodman, 1953) which assigns a probability distribution over possible word sequences based on observed counts. The n-gram model is simple and can be extracted from an observed corpus with relative ease. However its simplicity leads to knowledge constraints. For instance, it doesn't capture word order or conditional dependencies beyond the n-gram boundary. Another limitation of the n-gram model is its inability to capture topic information in a given situation. Unsupervised topic models based on LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) (Blei et al., 2003) have emerged as an alternative language model. LDA uses hierarchical Bayesian models to predict topics and words in a document. It excels at identifying abstract topics within a document corpus. However, LDA assumes all the content in a document pertains to a cluster of topics. This is a strong modeling assumption that is often not suitable for domains like news reports where different parts of the document report on different foci. Modifying LDA for this problem led to EM based approaches (Wallach, 2006). These approaches model the document by identifying a dominant topic or carefully analyzing the document to split it into different topic regions (Wallach, 2006). However, the previous model could only marginalize for each ngram independently, which results in a large number of trial parameter changes. While n-gram models doesn't learn abstract concepts like LDA does, and the LDA based model doesn't have the ability to exploit the context on all levels of word order in a document the way n-gram models do, there may be ways to combine these advantages, benefiting from the strengths of both. We explore this idea in this paper. We couple the traditional n-gram model's ability to capture long-range and multi-way dependencies of language with a distributional topic model. Our model learns on a large corpus of documents and simultaneously predicts 1) the topic that best explains the observed n-grams for a multiword context, and 2) the topic probabilities so as to perform better on tasks like information retrieval or question answering where such knowledge would be very useful.

Simplification of complex sentences can significantly alleviate the challenges in Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems. Complex sentences can be rephrased into simpler sentences, and such simplification has the potential to help both processing systems and natural language understanding by humans, especially individuals with reading disabilities. In this paper, we introduce Split and Rephrase (SAR), a novel simplification task which aims to split a complex sentence into a meaning-preserving sequence of shorter sentences. We create and publish a large benchmark dataset containing 1,066,115 sentence pairs, where each pair consists of a complex sentence and its corresponding split and rephrased representation. We then propose and evaluate several models to address this task. These models include both vanilla sequence-to-sequence models and more specialized models that incorporate semantic information. The benchmark dataset is publicly available, and we hope to stimulate further research on semantic simplification beyond current methods based on simple word frequency or part-of-speech ratio. To understand the difficulty and potential of this task, we employ several approaches, including language models and attention-based sequence-to-sequence models. We evaluate both vanilla models and those that incorporate semantic information such as entity recognition and dependency parsing. By comparing model performance between the sequential decoding and simultaneous decoding strategies or even character-level decoding, we demonstrate that the split-and-rephrase problem is indeed challenging and requires a balance between preserving the original meaning and rewriting text into simpler form. The proposed benchmark and models can facilitate the development of more robust and flexible simplification techniques that can benefit a wide range of NLP applications, including but not limited to machine translation (MT), information retrieval (IR), and text summarization. For instance, MT systems often struggle with complex sentences, as they require more computational resources to generate accurate translations, and simplification might achieve better results and efficiency. Similarly, text analysis models such as semantic role labeling (SRL) and dependency parsing can be burdened by long, complex sentences, and preprocessing using SAR could potentially improve their performance. Furthermore, for the reading assistance community, SAR could be used to transform hard-to-read sentences into more accessible forms, aiding readers with learning disabilities or low literacy levels. Our experiments also reveal interesting insights into the nature of sentence simplification. For example, some sentences can easily be split and rephrased by changing only a few words or arranging existing words appropriately. However, a significant number of sentences present challenges due to intricate complex relations of clauses, such as embedded relatives or consecutive conjunctions.

Automatically Solving Number Word Problems by Semantic Parsing and Reasoning The problem of automatically solving number word problems (NWPs) has been approached from various directions in natural language processing (NLP) research. Number word problems, which verbally express arithmetic computations, represent a subset of computational linguistics' interest in language grounding – the conversion of natural language sentences into executable machine-readable code. A complete solution to numerical word problems generally entails: (a) understanding the meaning of the problem, (b) representing the solution step by step, and (c) verifying the correctness of the final solution. Prior works have tackled this problem in several ways. Rule-based systems (Snyder, 1982;Tillman and Melamed, 2014) are one traditional approach that parses Sentences into meaning representations structured to directly translate to arithmetic semantic trees. These methods allow for a comprehensive study of the problem-solving process but require an extensive human effort to handcraft individual components of the system, including morpho-syntactic and semantic rules. A challenging aspect of automatic NWP solving is the inherent uncertainty introduced by natural language sentences. Off-the-shelf general-purpose parsers, for example, may not accommodate the specific or rarer grammatical phenomena encountered in word problems. To address this, and to scale systems more easily, recent work has leveraged machine learning with shallow structures (Dougherty et al., 2005;Zaremba and Sutskever, 2014). These systems can learn to map sentences or their paraphrases to semantic forms, potentially more flexibly accommodating dialectical or stylistic variations in word problem posing. However, these approaches often struggle with more complex syntactico-semantic structures and may have trouble generalizing from limited training data. One key innovation proposed in this paper is a novel meaning representation language (MRL) which serves as an intermediate layer between natural language understanding and the mathematical representations required for solving numeric word problems. The MRL is specifically designed to capture nuances in both arithmetic and linguistic expressions, including the variety of ways numbers can be represented (e.g., words vs. numerals) or mathematical operations can be formulated (e.g., "subtract 5 from 10" vs. "10 minus 5"). To automatically extract structured meaning from NWP input sentences, we introduce a context-free grammar (CFG)-based semantic parser. The challenge here lies in creating a robust grammar that can capture the syntactic variability of word problems without becoming too arbitrary or overwhelmed by exceptions. This requires a delicate balance between specificity and generality in the grammar rules. To tackle this, we use a hybrid approach: while 9,600 semi-automatically derived grammar rules form the core of our parser, we also integrate a machine learning model to adaptively refine or extend these rules based on training data.

Training segmentation models using human-annotated data is clearly prohibitive for many languages without easily accessible or suitable annotated resources. Further, these models are language-sensitive and are not clearly extensible to other languages due to differences in the extent and nature of compounding. In this work, we describe maximum entropy (ME) models as an inductive method for generating segmentation lattices for translation input. We train our ME models on compounding-related and orthography-related features distributed over the input and output sentences. The inference of this model can actually predict many fracturing strategies appropriate for languages with productive compounding. The ME model is trained to predict segmentation lattice paths with respect to its latent structure (prior) but adapts to new data (data-driven). In order to validate our method, we evaluate on three language pairs where compounding in the source language is reasonably common but to different degrees: German-English (GE), Hungarian-English (HU), and Turkish-English (TR). We compare to a state-of-the-art baseline system that generates multiple lattices using different configurations of standard segmentation tools and show significant improvements for two of the three language pairs when using the output of our ME model as potential input segmentation lattices. We also investigate how the features and data distributions used for training the ME models influence the quality of the predicted lattices. Our work is distinct from existing segmentation lattice generators in focusing on the latent structure of lattices for generating potential ways of breaking text in a way that aligns with the source language's compounding rules, rather than solely trying to predict high-quality word boundaries for a particular language. Our ME model is focused on generalizing across languages, using features that reflect the latent structure of compounds as well as surface-level orthography, which aids in learning a model that operates on and generalizes across a broad range of languages without specific training data for each. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background on segmentation lattices and previous work relating to the problem we address. Section 3 introduces the ME model and describes the feature set used to predict segmentation lattices. Section 4 describes the experiments and results on GE, HU, and TR. Section 5 evaluates the discriminative power of the features used in the model on whether we are predicting a good lattice path or not, as well as the influence of different feature groups.

Character-level models, which process text through character sequences instead of word sequences, have achieved state-of-the-art results in a variety of natural language tasks, including language modeling and neural machine translation (Wayne, Bordes, and Weston, 2014;Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016;Gehring et al., 2017;Bojanowski et al., 2016). However, understanding what these models learn at the character level has been minimal, with current techniques lacking the ability to decompose and qualitatively interpret their learned patterns. In this paper, we extend the Contextual Decomposition technique introduced in (Murdoch et al., 2018) to investigate character-level models for word-level prediction tasks, specifically morphological tagging. The primary goal of our work is to explain and understand what linguistic patterns character-level neural networks (i.e., Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks) learn and whether they are amenable to qualitative analysis with respect to linguistic rules such as phonological, morphological, or even syntactic information. Character-level models are inherently useful in language tasks where the relationship between characters is as important as or even more important than the word-level relationship. For this reason, we focus on morphological tagging which requires understanding how characters form words and the resulting morphemes. The task of morphological tagging is prevalent in many languages, in particular those with rich morphology like Arabic, Chinese, German, and Russian. For such languages, morphological analysis is an essential preprocessing step for tasks such as language modeling, machine translation, named entity recognition, summarization, and many others in natural language processing. Assuming that character-level models would be especially well-suited for morphological tagging and that they might discover linguistic patterns implicitly during training, we seek to answer two primary research questions: 1.   Understanding Character Patterns:   What patterns do character-level models learn, and can these patterns be interpreted in the context of linguistic rules? 2.   Relevance to Linguistic Rules:   Do character-level models implicitly validate certain linguistic rules that were applied manually by linguists or explicitly encoded within lexicons? Or are they discovering new, implicit patterns that are systematic but not currently part of human-designed linguistic rules? To address our research questions, we employ the Contextual Decomposition technique which provides insights into what input features each model relies most heavily on at different layers of the network. This technique allows us to probe different layers of the model, see how outputs evolve across layers, and reconstruct the network's internal representations.

Analyzing the semantic orientation of opinions expressed in natural language reviews is an increasingly important task for applications such as sentiment analysis. In the majority of existing work, the semantic orientation is typically predicted at the document-level. While determining the overall sentiment of a document can be useful, finer-grained sentiment analysis can yield additional insights and help the system understand why a user likes or dislikes a particular product or service. This level of analysis corresponds to pinpointing the sentences that contain "gold" opinions - sentences that assertatively and strongly express users' opinions about the entity under review. Thus, presenting such secondary-level insights can potentially provide better results and user experience for certain applications. However, pinpointing fine-grained semantic orientation, especially at the level of individual sentences, is a challenging task for several reasons. First, obtaining annotated training data at this level of granularity is difficult due to the labor-intensive nature of the annotation task. As a result, such datasets either do not exist or are extremely rare. Secondly, properly capturing individual sentences containing important opinions can be difficult because the intentions and emotions expressed within a document are sometimes not well captured by the document-level sentiment indicators. To tackle these challenges, we propose the weakly supervised Multi-Experts Model (MEM). MEM is designed to perform both sentiment polarity and strength prediction at the sentence level given this context. A key feature of MEM is its use of "experts" - heuristic shallow models which are trained on assumed, but possibly noisy, secondary-level label data. In this work, we interpret "experts" broadly, including both specialized models (e.g., carefully engineered models for a particular task, or current state-of-the-art models) and, implicitly, heuristic methods (e.g., feature engineering, regex for sentiment words identification) based on the assumption that they might achieve good performance and "know" something about the sentiment orientation in a sentence. But it is not always feasible to train such experts from manually labeled training data or use them in practice. This leads to one of the primary challenges the MEM model tries to address: how can we effectively combine signals from these multiple, possibly limited, "experts" along with potentially noisy coarse-grained labels when training a more sophisticated and task-specific model? Our model framework and approach to semantic orientation analysis are outlined as follows. Firstly, we gather potential indicators of sentence-level semantic orientation from a variety of sources, which serve as our "experts".

Learning entailment rules is a fundamental problem in semantics that has gained much attention recently due to its applications in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Entailment rules between predicates are represented as transitive graphs (entailment graphs) where each edge corresponds to an entailment relation between predicates. A particular challenge in this area, however, is that learning these questions requires accounting for a large number of involved constraints and hypotheses. This paper addresses the problem of learning entailment graphs and argues that they exhibit a structural property, suggesting a very efficient approximation algorithm. The process of learning entailment graphs can be viewed as an optimization problem due to the constraints induced by the entailment knowledge. One such constraint, for example, is transitivity: if A entails B and B entails C, then A logically entails C. Another constraint is symmetry: if A entails B, then B also entails A. These constraints can be represented as constraints in a mathematical optimization problem. However, the sizes of these constraint sets can grow indefinitely as the number of predicates increases, making exact optimization infeasible with current algorithms and computational resources. We propose an efficient tree-based approximation algorithm for learning entailment graphs. The core idea of this approach is to utilize the tree-like structure of entailment graphs or a related concept called forest-reducible graphs. Forest-reducible graphs are tree-like graphs that can be reduced to simpler structures by repeatedly "pruning" nodes that have no outgoing edges while maintaining the graph's connectivity. By leveraging this structure, our algorithm can reduce the problem of learning the entire graph by iteratively making local decisions, thus significantly reducing the computational overhead compared to current exact approaches. Our tree-based algorithm, named ApproxEntail, can in practice be as efficient as a linear time algorithm, which is in stark contrast to the state-of-the-art exact learning algorithms that often have exponential time complexity in the number of predicates. The algorithm is iterative in nature, with each iteration making decisions based on local graph properties and previously inferred edges or constraints. The decision making in each iteration is surprisingly straightforward, involving only a linear scan over the graph, making the overall process highly efficient. To evaluate the effectiveness of ApproxEntail, we compare its performance against that of a state-of-the-art exact algorithm for learning entailment graphs on a variety of datasets. Our comparative evaluation is carried out on two metrics: (i) the approximation error (the difference between the predicted graph and the true graph) and (ii) the running time.

Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms reliably on large unstructured text corpora typically requires hand-labeled training data. However, these are often scarce and expensive to gather. As a result, deep learning algorithms that can learn from unsupervised or semi-supervised data have become indispensable for improving the performance and breadth of NLP applications (Mikolov et al., 2013;Collobert et al., 2011;Peters et al., 2018). But why unsupervised learning? The reason comes down to the fact that annotated data is relatively rare, and often comes alongside with limited coverage over the immense space of fine-grained semantic class, limiting its ability to represent the nuances of language. For example, the entity recognition task requires to identify mentions of a semantic class (e.g., journalist), but even then, among semantic entities, we can further derive a number of specific semantic types or "subtypes" (e.g., writer, editor, author). Classification of such fine semantic classes are particularly challenging because they often have scarce and noisy labels, yet very large in the number of potential classes. For instance, in the US News corpus (Sudhof et al., 2004), we list as much as 92 fine-grained semantic classes for nouns. The scarcity and noise issues come from the fact that different training data may have different structures and foci, and sometimes, the semantic distinctions between subtypes can be so subtle that they are often overseen even by human annotators (Antoniak and Song, 2000;Song et al., 2013). A more general problem, known as semantic subtypes induction or fine-grained class discovery, deals with automatically predicting which of a set of fine-grained semantic classes should be ascribed to each noun phrase (NP) in unstructured text data. To address the scarcity and inconsistent nature of hand-labeled data, several work has explored the usage of unsupervised and semi-supervised learning algorithms in this area. Early work measured the similarity between noun phrases using distributional, context-based, and knowledge base-based approaches (Sun et al., 2012;Stenetorp et al., 2012;Huang et al., 2014). These methods typically require auxiliary resources (e.g., dictionary, knowledge graph) that are more aggregative than the fine-grained semantic classes we are interested in and may not directly support real-world NLP applications. Since then, semantic subtypes induction has explored supervised learning with a small number of seed examples (Fader et al., 2009;Ritter et al., 2011). However, manually specifying these seed events is time-consuming and inherently limited by human interpretation.

Recognizing Biographical Sections in Wikipedia Wikipedia is one of the largest collections of encyclopedic data ever written. On Wikipedia, every article is structured around headings and subheadings which organize and structure content. In the context of biographies, these sections often carry important information about the subject. A biographical section captures information pertinent to a specific aspect of the person's life, such as their early years, family, education, and career. However, Wikipedia pages describing a person vary greatly in structure and content, and it can be challenging to automatically identify which sections contain biographical information. In this paper, we address the problem of recognizing biographical sections in Wikipedia articles. This problem can be formulated as a sequence labeling task. Given a person's Wikipedia page, the goal is to identify which section headings contain biographical information. Recognizing biographical sections can be useful for several applications including information retrieval, content summarization, and education - for making specialized search interfaces that allow users to easily navigate biographical information. We present a supervised approach to solve this problem. We first address the challenging issue of automatic data labeling. We develop an approach that marks section headings as biographical or not by leveraging Wikipedia's categorization schema. We then evaluate a range of feature sets that capture different aspects of the section titles and section relevance. We show that surprisingly simple features, such as the presence of specific keywords in the section title, the position of the section in the article, and whether the section is explicitly tagged as biography-related, yield excellent results. Our experiments demonstrate an accuracy of 84% (F1 score), which is substantially above a baseline system that simply classifies sections based on a predefined set of keywords. Our approach sets the stage for understanding the structure of biographical information on Wikipedia and provides a foundation for more advanced analysis and extraction of biographical content. 1. Introduction Wikipedia has become a primary resource for large-scale research in historical and cultural studies. This is due to its coverage and availability in a machine-readable format. The task of automatically identifying biographical sections within Wikipedia articles presents several challenges and opportunities. Firstly, sections in Wikipedia vary greatly in terminology and structure. The headers used are user-generated, making it difficult to define systematic rules to identify a biographical section. Secondly, sections themselves might not be labeled appropriately. A section might contain non-biographical content, or biographical content might be scattered across different sections, each potentially labeled in a manner that does not convey the presence of biographical information.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, while such data's cost and availability scale with the number of languages, quantity-sensitive training techniques and increasingly large computational resources enable deep, highly comprehensive models. These models are then evaluated using competition-driven datasets (e.g., for parsing or translation), but the existence, diversity, and size of corpora are limited by practical and cost-related factors. A gap exists between the model's expressive power and the available data, leading to the following questions: (a) can the model still perform well if we reduce the number of nonterminals or features extracted from the training data ("label set coarsening"), and (b) if we do, how should we best coarsen the labels? To address these, we introduce a category-coarsening algorithm for Sentential Transducer (ST) parsers (Junczys-Dowmunt and Van der Goot, 2016), and adapt this technique to Syntax-Augmented Machine Translation (SAMT) (Koehn and Hoang, 2020). The key intuition is that over-segmentation of the sentence structure leads to fewer instances per parser rule for the less frequent constructions, which in turn makes these rules difficult to learn and generalize. By coarsening the tree symbols (nonterminals) to reduce their number while retaining the shallow structures' expressive power, we can improve the system's overall robustness and efficiency in learning. In our approach, we coarsen the label set by identifying semantically similar or frequently co-occurring families of nonterminals and merging them into a more general category, akin to grouping words by suffix or in inherent meaning cluster. Note that this is not a general-purpose, flat clustering or feature reduction technique; rather, it is model-specific and respects the structural hierarchy of the underlying syntax. The algorithm is the following: 1.   Tree Collection and Categorization  : First, we construct a sample or reference set of trees for the target language. These could come from any source, including a treebank, crowd-sourced data, or even synthetic data generated from a model. For each unique structure or family of similar structures identified by hand, we assign an augmented label to include both the previous label and a category index that represents the coarsened class. 2.   Coarsening  : Using the collected trees, we cluster these new labels based on either structural similarity (e.g., same number of daughters, same branching structure) or semantic similarity (e.g., categories that are often used in similar situations and have the same production rules).

Hybrid Grammars for Discontinuous Parsing Introduction Over the past four decades, there has been vigorous progress in the development of formalisms and algorithms for analyzing and generating natural language text. While much of this work has focused on well-behaved phenomena of language (e.g., context-free or relatively regular syntactic structures), a significant number of challenges remain for questions such as how to model and analyze the discontinuous nature of syntactic and narrative structure (e.g., idioms, parentheticals, and centred clausal structures of various types). While a range of techniques and formalisms have been developed for handling these issues (for a general introduction, see Jurafsky (1996) or Osgood and Osgood (1973) for a historical perspective; Birch and Osborne (2015) for a recent survey; and the articles by Fischer (1976), Engelfriet (1984), or Merlo and Stevenson (2006) for detailed treatments), most of the solutions proposed either are language-specific or are limited in their expressiveness or handling of complexity. As a result, the task of accurately and efficiently parsing various kinds of discontinuous structures remains an open research problem. One recent direction that has received some attention is the development of Forth generation of dependency grammar, which is quite amenable to discontinuous structures but is less common than phrase structure grammars. However, traditional dependency grammars still typically assume projective structures. Moreover, they are often more expressive at the syntactic level than is needed, resulting in computational overhead. A more recent line of research builds on the work of Satta (2002) and employs tree-substitution grammars (Ahrens and Dank, 1994) or grammatical inference (Kudo, 1999; Magri and Pratt, 2007). But these approaches have their limitations too, such as reduced expressiveness or computational complexity that inhibits their use on large corpora or complex languages. To the best of our knowledge, the lack of a widely accepted formalism and parsing algorithms for discontinuous structures is partly due to the inherent complexity of such structures: they require either explicitly marking or storing non-projective or poly-synthetic relations in the grammar, which complicates the entire language description. Consequently, dependency parsers (Manning et al., 2014) – which are often chosen for their expressiveness and ease of implementation – either make simplifying assumptions (e.g., so-called head-rule or non-projective head-first dependency schemes) or modify the algorithms to handle non-projectivity. Phrase structure grammars (XTAG; XTAG Research Group, 2001; or dependencies realised as non-projective constituency trees; see, for instance, Phillips (2014)) typically still rely on compositional rules that express their continuous structure in general and often cannot naturally represent discontinuous phenomena.

Training embeddings using all the fine-grained annotation sets clearly leads to achieving strict type consistency, but this requirement comes at a cost; these models have more parameters to train and require large amounts of labeled data which might not always be available. To address this, we need to explore the possibility of training embeddings that are more appropriate for this task, yet do not require corresponding labeled data sets. We propose an embedding adaptation framework where instead of training embeddings on the actual labels, the embeddings are trained based on structural and paradigmatic relationships present in the data. Table 1 (Section 3.3) provides an overview of how we can approach this. We start by exploring simple knowledge constraints based on word order, then build a hybrid model based on paradigmatic relations derived from verbal and nominal paradigms, and finally explore a conditional similarity model that learns to predict missing parts based on existing relationships among semantic features. The main innovation in our proposed framework is the conditionally modeled similarity measure between semantic features. Unlike traditional embeddings that represent words as points in vector space, this model learns to conditionally predict the semantic similarity between any two cells in a paradigm table based on similarities and relationships inferred across the entire paradigm structure. This approach does not require pairing between the cells explicitly, which makes the training much easier. By conditioning the embeddings this way, we train models that learn semantic relationships among features even if different parts of the paradigm are labeled differently across data sets. However, the conditionality here comes from the relationships between cells, not the actual labels, which makes the approach more data efficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a range of linguistic datasets to show how even with limited labeled data, we can still achieve strong performance on paradigmatic cell filling, often even surpassing models trained from the complete, but less representative, fine-grained annotations. The Encoder-Decoder Approach to the Paradigm Cell Filling Problem (ECFP) that we propose offers a novel and data-efficient way to approach the task of completing word inflection tables from partial ones. This method leverages deep learning together with an adaptation of word embeddings that are particularly tailored for the morphology domain. Our approach centers around conditioning embeddings explicitly on the structural and paradigmatic relationships inherent within the paradigm structure and leveraging these to infer missing data.

Training natural language parsers takes thousands of annotated examples, prohibiting many researchers who first move to online processors from using today's state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, rapidly evolving languages require frequent updates, which forces even established methods to start from scratch each time. Incremental parsing methods handle new words or phrases without requiring the entire sentence to be consumed – a step towards practical real-world applications and cross-group evaluation and collaboration. But one challenge remains: how do we choose the best local features that guide the inference, when language of interest or target domains are out of scope? Recurrent neural networks for sequence-to-sequence tasks keeps coming backwards due to this problem. Many works apply simple handcrafted rules, heuristic, or filter-based methods. However, these seem to have reached their ceiling, and recent studies have started to look into more complex models that continuously and dynamically learn to select useful among available features. One successful approach in related domains such as language modeling or machine translation is the well-documented attention mechanism. It has been proven effective to scan through a global context and selectively focus on important sub-areas, such as particular parts of a sentence or even specific words, that are keys in the current prediction. This paper introduces a novel application of the attention mechanism, which we call dynamic feature selection with attention. The goal of this work is to show that this concept can significantly improve the ability of transition-based parsers to use locally available information in predicting future transitions while the rest of the sentence is still in the future. We argue that even within a small, local context, an incremental parser can still benefit from carefully analyzing which features (e.g., features related to specific previous decisions taken or particular tokens) are particularly useful for making a prediction at any time. We specifically propose an attention mechanism which dynamically, and based on the local context and current parser state, selects which part of the local context should be examined to make the next parser decision. Attention mechanism, initially proposed by Bahdanau et al. (2015) for machine translation, is used in various domains where it’s beneficial to focus on particular parts of the input. For example, in NLP, attention can be used to selectively look at certain words or parts of the sentence, or in computer vision, to focus on discriminative regions of the image.

Training embeddings using large unlabelled text corpora has gained much traction recently, and one of the reasons is that unsupervised models trained on such corpora often intuitively capture linguistic relations. One key relationship is the hypernymy relationship (or hyponymy, depending on perspective), where a word can be considered a more specific kind of another word. A concrete example would be "car" and "vehicle", with "car" being a kind of "vehicle". Such a relationship is of particular importance in tasks like lexical entailment, where determining whether one word implies another is a crucial sub-task. The core idea behind this work is to explore and exploit knowledge of lexical entailment, particularly hypernymy relationships, within distributional word embeddings such as Word2Vec and GloVe. Specifically, our aim is to identify and utilize "Hearst patterns" - specific adjacency patterns in texts that are strongly indicative of hyponymy relationships, as identified by Hearst (1992). We want to leverage this knowledge to improve performance in predicting whether a pair of words are likely to be in a lexical entailment relationship. Hearst (1992) proposed that certain patterns between sequential words in a text can be used to approximate implicit semantic relationships, particularly hypernymy. One example identified by Hearst is the pattern "X and other Y's", which is likely to signify that X is a hypernym of Y. Another example is "X but not its Y's", which is plausible to signify that X is not a hypernym of Y or vice versa (depending on context). In both examples, extracting the words "X" and "Y" provides a clear hypernymy relationship clue. To approach the problem, we focus on embedding models and their respective vector spaces. Unlike human language doesn't come in explicit vector format, distributional models inherently learn that certain words appear near others based on textual context. This creates a spatial hierarchy or topology in vector space that reflects some degree of semantic relatedness, which in theory can include hypernymy. We begin by analyzing a prominent model that was originally proposed to measure prototypicality but we argue is actually capturing hypernymy implicitly due to Hearst patterns in its training data. This qualitative analysis is performed by examining large amounts of output examples and identifying how the model's decisions align with expected outcomes from known Hearst patterns. The intuition here is that if a model is consistently picking up patterns indicative of hypernymy, perhaps we can explicitly leverage this ability to improve lexical entailment predictions.

Training reliable named entity recognition (NER) systems has historically required large amounts of manually-labeled data. However, these resources are limited; and additionally, they may not cover less common languages or domain-specific entities which are encountered less frequently but are of significant importance (Triveni et al., 2015;Nothman, 2013; questions@NLTK: https://sourceforge.net/p/nltk/mailman/message/31952066/). Therefore, constructing language models for domain-specific named entity recognition (domain-specific NER) is an important challenge. One strategy to mitigate the need for manual labeling is distant supervision (Huang et al., 2015;Fader et al., 2011). Here, we are given a dictionary from a domain of interest that contains (entity, description) pairs, as well as a large amount of unannotated text from the domain. These unannotated texts are then labeled with individual components of the descriptions provided in the dictionary, resulting in noisy training data with missing or sometimes erroneous labels. While several techniques have attempted to exploit such information, including simple partial match-based SVMs (Fader et al., 2011), and incorporating oracles (Tur et al., 2010) on top of sequence tagging models (Huang et al., 2015), these models often assumed clean labels for training and their assumptions don't scale well with the often substantial noise and ambiguity in the generated labels (Christian et al., 2012;Sethuraman et al., 2007). We show, through empirical testing, that a new model, AutoNER, trained on noisy distant supervision from the dictionary outperforms all existing alternatives. 2 To tackle the noisy label problem from distant supervision, we propose two candidates: the fuzzy conditional random field (fuzzy CRF) and the AutoNER model. First, the fuzzy CRF is a natural extension of the traditional sequence labeling framework of CRFs where each token can be assigned multiple candidate labels. The idea is that it should be possible to learn to allocate uncertainty over possible label candidates given by the distant supervision's noisy labels . While fuzzy CRFs offer improved performance compared to previous methods, the natural architecture of sequence labeling (CRF) still requires a structured label space. Second, we go beyond the traditional sequence labeling framework and propose a novel neural network model called AutoNER. The key idea behind AutoNER is to allow for zero or more possible labels to a token (as opposed to multiple in the fuzzy CRF), and then let the neural network decide based on the input evidence. We use a Tie or Break scheme to evaluate multiple possible labels for a token.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Top-Down Nearly-Context-Sensitive Parsing: The study of syntactic parsing is one of the most fundamental and active areas of natural language processing (NLP). Given the unrealistic assumption that human language parsing can be reduced to simply processing words or phrases without reference to grammatical structure, a compelling – yet far from trivial – task has been to devise computational models that capture the complexity and structure of human language. These models attempt to reconstruct the hierarchical structure of a sentence, decomposing the text into a series of word-dependencies represented in a parse tree. The extracted parse keeps track of which words are related to each other and how. Syntactic parsers are broadly classified into two categories: top-down and bottom-up, depending on the ordering of their analysis from word to Sentence or Sentence down to word, respectively. Unsurprisingly, given the tractability of bigrams and the partial determinism of context-free grammars (CFGs) over the history of the field, the dominant historical approach to parsing has been bottom-up, often formulated within the context of dynamic programming (DP). This approach works by building the parse from the leaves up to the root of the tree. However, the bottom-up approach intuitively seems less aligned with how humans actually comprehend and generate language. Recent work in psycholinguistics has shown that human language understanding appears sequential and often assumed complete while the processing occurs. Early evidence of this nature was the work by Marslen-Wilson, Tyler, Waksler, and Older (1984), later formalized in studies focusing on comprehension as a processual phenomenon, such as Trueswell and Tanenhaus (1994). Thus, understanding the structure of a sentence might not require a complete "parse" of the entire sentence but doesn't come in disembodied chunks either -- instead the structure is built incrementally, or at least understood to be fully available earlier than if one were to wait for the entire sentence. The notion of incrementality in parsing aligns well with the top-down approach, particularly when viewing it as a way to approximate the human cognitive process of sentence understanding. In top-down parsing, one starts with a globally available grammar knowledge and gradually refines a hypothesis for the sentence from abstract structure to concrete words, activating one or more fully connected parse hypotheses over the course of the sentence. Top-down parsing thus provides a computational model that broadly reflects the cognitive evidence, but it has traditionally been at odds with achieving zero-error performance due to the ambiguity of language and the lack of a strong theoretical model that could guide the searching process

Training embeddings directly from unlabelled text has been seen successful in various NLP tasks. However, these embeddings still leave much to be desired. Distributional word embeddings capture semantic meaning using simple co-occurrence statistics and inherently ignore many aspects of language organization. As a result, they often fall short in capturing complex, nuanced representations of text corpora. This paper introduces SCDV (Sparse Composite Document Vector), a novel distributed representation approach that significantly advances our ability to capture and utilize language structure in unsupervised settings. The core idea of SCDV is to form sparse document vectors through a process of soft clustering. Rather than merely grouping similar words together, we cluster word embeddings to capture multiple, often competing semantic contexts in which words occur, thereby enabling the representation of complex, nuanced documents. This clustering process is structured to capture both relationships among semantic entities (i.e., ISA hierarchies following recent work such as "Relation-aware Graph Convolutional Networks" (Zhu et al., 2018)) and relationships between these entities as topics (IS-APART relations). After the initial clustering, we chain these clusters together in various ways to form composite vectors, capturing multi-layered document structure. The novelty of SCDV compared to previous work, such as NTSG (Liu et al., 2015a) lies in the use of soft clustering specifically designed to handle multi-topic documents. This benefits in two key ways: 1.   Flexibility in Multi-Topic Representation  : Many documents inherently cover multiple topics or themes. SCDV handles this multi-topic aspect naturally through its soft clustering framework, allowing it to model more complex text in a unified way. 2.   Efficiency and Scalability  : We achieve significant computational improvements compared to dense vector representations commonly used in unsupervised learning tasks (e.g., distributional paragraph vectors in [Levy & Goldberg, 2014]). The use of sparse vectors not only reduces memory usage but also lessens computational burdens, especially during training and inference stages. While the sparse nature of the vectors might seem counterintuitive compared to the common approach of using dense or very low-rank tensors for document embeddings, our approach is grounded in the observation that language is inherently sparse. Each document only represents a small portion of all possible topics and relationships. SCDV intelligently directs these sparse representations to meaningful clusters of multi-topic and multi-contextual information, thereby preserving and utilizing the most relevant aspects of the input text. We evaluate the efficacy of SCDV through extensive experimentation on a variety of tasks, including but not limited to: - Multi-class classification over extensive datasets such as IMDB and 20 Newsgroups.

Language acquisition is traditionally understood as the process of learning a language. However, if we move beyond this classic definition and instead consider the acquisition of language together with the meaning and understanding of its context, we enter into a broader and more complex realm: grounded language acquisition. Grounded language acquisition refers to the process by which an artificial intelligent agent (like a robot, a digital assistant or a machine learning model) learns to make sense of language, simultaneously while interacting with and understanding the world that the language is referring to. This can be as simple as learning that "tree" refers to a certain kind of physical object that keeps changing its shape and colour with seasons, or as complex as learning that "city" is a concept that creates geographical, social, economic and political boundaries with dynamic relationships and implications. At the heart of grounded language acquisition is the idea that the meaning of language is not semantic entities in isolation, but rather a network of associations with the physical and abstract world. This concept aligns closely with theories of situated cognition (e.g., Clancey, 1997), and enactivism (Varela, 1991). These theories suggest that cognition - and language acquisition - cannot be separated from the environment in which it takes place or from the actions that are performed within that environment. The problem of grounded language acquisition is particularly challenging for machines. Unlike humans, they typically lack the capacity to directly perceive, act on, and interpret the world. This sets up the acquisition process with a number of complex, interrelated challenges: 1.   Perception and Segmentation  : The agent must first learn to segment the continuous perceptual stream into meaningful entities, actions, and events. This can be exceedingly difficult because contexts are often ambiguous (e.g., distinguishing a tree from its surrounding environment and "knowing" it's part of a larger concept of "forest" or "environment" requires sophisticated analysis beyond simple object detection). 2.   Meaning Assignment  : Once segmented, the agent must learn to associate these entities with meanings that are grounded in their physical manifestation and context. For instance, the word "snow" should be associated with thermal sensations (cold), visual patterns (white, fluffy, falling particles), and potentially action cues (glide, build a snowman, ski). 3.   Language and Physical World Interaction  : The agent needs to understand that language describes the world, but also influences perception of it. For example, if we're told a structure is a "blind alley," we might zero in on certain architectural features and ignore others.

Training embeddings directly from the fine-grained character-level information in unsegmented text without an additional dependency tree annotation has been proven useful for various tasks (Kudo and Richardson, 2018;Ran et al., 2019). In this work, we extend this exploration to improving the neural models for Chinese word segmentation (CWS), questions how this kind of cross-modal (character and word) information can be used, and whether a simple approach (which we describe in detail) can give better results than the state-of-the-art neural word segmentation (NS) models for leveraging data extracted from an autosegmentation method. We further explore if simple knowledge transfer measures like word-embedding similarity optimization suffice for this task. Embeddings trained on a character's closest word features (a word-based context) have been shown valuable in improving neural parser accuracy for languages with less annotated training data but without explicit segmentation (Kudo and Richardson, 2018). By aligning character and word embeddings, they reduce the known language inconsistency (in this case, the lack of character order invariance in the word) when directly considering sequence pair sentences in Chinese. In fact, the proposed model benefits from the sequential structure of Chinese at both the word and character levels. For a given character in context, we train an embedding that confers knowledge from its surrounding word as well as the shallowly contextualized word features assumed in the word embedding space. The label of the entire word is available and its embeddings (as the core features of training variables) come from a pre-trained word embedding model (Pei et al., 2015;Huang et al., 2015). For example, for each char c in word w, represented as a sequence w = [c1, c2, ..., cn] (also showing the position 1...n), the character embedding input vector would include the pre-trained word embedding for w and all other word or character embeddings in the same or less general context of c, such as the previous characters [c1...c(t-1)] and the next [c(t+1)...cn], explicitly marking its position within the word's fixed order . Such contextual embedding learning is feasible given sufficient training data and changing the character byte-pair encoding (BPE code vector) or one-hot style features of a character embedding into these more informative ones. Our proposed method uses just the pre-trained word embeddings as the context for each character's zero shot learning, without the need for an external dependency parser (as Biaffine Parser; Chen and Manning, 2014) for the character-based job.

Introduction Information Extraction (IE) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP). It involves automatically identifying and extracting structured information from unstructured sources, such as text documents. Traditionally, this process has been highly unrealistic without human assistance. However, over the past few decades, the development and progress in NLP research have led to improved techniques and tools which are capable of significantly automating and streamlining the IE process. A major breakthrough in this field was the emergence of Open Information Extraction (Open IE), which was first introduced by Banko et al. (2007). Unlike traditional IE, which is usually domain-specific and targeted towards predefined information types, Open IE aims to be domain-agnostic and extract anything of interest from raw text, without prior knowledge of the expected output. This is in contrast with traditional IE, which often relies on hand-crafted patterns and templates, weighted by a comprehensive grammar or ontologies - which we refer to as closed knowledge. Hence, while traditional IE systems can be very accurate within the boundaries of their predetermined scope, they are limited in their ability to adapt to new domains or extract information that was unforeseen by their creators. In contrast, Open IE systems aim for a more flexible and wide-ranging ability to extract whatever might be considered "interesting" from a text, without being provided beforehand with a list of predefined attributes or types of entities and relations. This kind of flexibility makes the Open IE task particularly useful in situations where the expected output cannot be predetermined, such as in the extraction of knowledge from news articles, blog posts or social media platforms for later semantic analysis, or for applications like question answering systems or generating knowledge bases. The Evolution of Open Information Extraction The concept of Open IE was initially introduced around the year 2007 by Banko et al. (2007). They provided a simple, dictionary-based approach that used the output of a named-entity recognizer (NER) and applied regular expressions to extract binary relations (X, Y) or subject-verb-object (SVO) patterns from a sentence. The simplicity of the initial approach, as well as its potential for ease of implementation and flexibility, drew significant interest from the research community. However, the framework and approach proposed by Banko et al. (2007) had several limitations, most notably in its coverage of only binary relations and SVO patterns, which limited its ability to capture richer linguistic structures and relationships in text.

Learning Emotion-enriched Word Representations Introduction Word representations (or word embeddings) have been successful in capturing word meaning and semantic relationships in several Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. These representations are typically learned from various forms of text data, where the underlying assumption is that the distributional hypothesis (Harris, 1954) correctly catches the semantic and context-based meaning and relationships of words (Erk, 2019). However, a limitation of such methods is their inability to explicitly distinguish the emotional connotations of words (Kemp et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2018). The distributional hypothesis, when applied to datasets containing rich emotional contexts, can mislead word embeddings, often placing words with very different emotions in similar spaces (e.g., "happy" and "sad" may appear close in the vector space due to shared co-occurrences in similar context). This limitation becomes particularly problematic in certain affective tasks such as emotion classification and emotion similarity where a word's emotional content is a key component of its meaning. In these tasks, traditional word embeddings fail to differentiate between words that may share semantic or contextual similarity but carry opposite emotional connotations, leading to suboptimal performance (Kashin et al., 2019; Riordan et al., 2020). To address this gap, we propose the use of emotion-enriched word representations that explicitly encode emotional information into the word embeddings, resulting in spaces where words with similar emotional valences or intensities are distinctively closer compared to those with opposite or different emotional connotations. Emotion Classification & Similarity: Task-based Motivations Emotion classification typically involves assigning a document, sentence, or phrase to a predefined emotional category such as "happy", "sad", "angry" etc. (Hoque et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2020). Emotion similarity, on the other hand, assigns measured similarity between two emotional signals or responses (Pang et al., 2008). Both tasks benefit from models that accurately capture the emotional nuances of words. Traditional approaches often treat emotion as another aspect of word meaning to be learned from data (e.g., including affective labels in a semi-supervised or supervised setup). However, such approaches still predominantly rely on the distributional hypothesis and may not sufficiently differentiate emotionally similar words from those with different emotions. A key challenge is addressing the ambiguity and context dependency of emotional terms: words like "happy" can be used to express a range of emotions ("I’m happy to meet you", "I’m happy you passed the exam", "I’m happy to see you happy") each with slightly different emotional nuances.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, such data can be cost prohibitive or nonexistent for many languages and domains. Unsupervised and semi-supervised methods have been developed to learn from unlabeled data but are still imperfect. Semi-supervised methods can drastically improve the performance by utilizing a small set of annotated examples, yet this kind of data may also be difficult or expensive to obtain and obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised sequence labeling model, which learns from fract-supervised word representations (few labeled and many unlabeled data). Our model is inspired by a well-known unsupervised learning approach named Morfessor, and is designed to learn word representations while taking into account both the form and the meaning of words. The Morfessor approach has proven to have strong potential to learn meaningful word segmentations when combined with semi-supervision from morphologically annotated data - though making the method fully unsupervised remains challenging and has yet to outperform supervised approaches. The proposed approach named Morfessor FlatCat builds on the modular structure of previous Morfessor variants, extending them with a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) structure. The HMM enables us to accommodate any existing or new tokenization unit in the flat structure of this variant, allowing for the symbols to be both single words and morphemes. All shallow structures of this kind are assumed flat while the deeper structures can contain label sequences in a more hierarchical fashion. This mixture allows us to align with the training data at whatever extent the current level allows. The HMM structure naturally allows us to capture long-term dependencies as well, unlike traditional word-based unsupervised models. The HMM is specifically designed to deal with the problem of learning a sequence labeling model with the ability to capture morphological structures. The model learns simultaneously a segmentation into subwords and their features, which are then used to predict the sequence of labels for each segment. During the design process, it has been the objective to ensure scalability of the training process together with decent generalization capability. Generalization of the model is achieved by learning a suitable representation of subwords, allowing to couple the information from unlabelled data to the supervised labels in an efficient way. While the previous Morfessor methods can learn from large amounts of unlabeled data, semi-supervised FlatCat does not rely on such amounts of unannotated data.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on PATTY: A Taxonomy of Relational Patterns with Semantic Types. ### Introduction Understanding and reasoning about relationships between entities is a key aspect of natural language processing (NLP) and information extraction (IE). In various tasks such as question answering (QA), entity disambiguation, and knowledge graph construction, identifying the relations between entities described in text and grounding them to semantic types are critical steps. While there have been numerous studies on language pattern extraction, many systems and resources are limited to specific applications and data domains, or do not provide an exhaustive taxonomy of relational patterns. Moreover, while knowledge bases (KBs) and ontologies provide rich structures for representing semantic types and relations, the dynamic, context-dependent, and often imprecisely expressed nature of language presents a challenge to directly translate relationships described textually into structured knowledge. This places a significant need for a comprehensive resource that systematically identifies, categorizes, and semantically types relational patterns found in natural language texts, thereby providing a bridge between free-text data and structured knowledge sources. This paper presents PATTY (a Taxonomy of Relational Patterns with Semantic Types), a novel resource that addresses the above challenges. PATTY consists of a large-scale collection of text patterns that denote binary relations between entities and are organized into a hierarchical taxonomy reflecting their semantic types. The resource is built using algorithms specifically designed for mining frequent patterns from textual data at Web-scale, in combination with the rich semantic types and entity population available in large KBs. PATTY is an open-access resource, allowing for easy integration into a diverse range of NLP and IE tasks. ### Background The extraction of relational patterns in text remains a challenging but crucial task for natural language understanding. Pattern-based approaches have been explored in early forms of IE (Cowie et al., 1991) and have gained renewed interest in recent years due to the availability of large textual corpora and advancements in algorithmic efficiency (Mann and Yarowsky, 2005; Sudo et al., 2009; Surdeanu et al., 2012). However, traditional approaches have often been domain-specific, relied heavily on manually crafted knowledge bases or dictionaries, or focused on a limited set of relation types (Mann and Thompson, 1988; Riloff and Jones, 2000). Recent advances in frequent pattern mining, particularly in the domain of large-scale textual data (Pennacchiotti and others, 2015; Biemann and Gross, 2013), provide an opportunity to approach this task in a more scalable and automated way.

Accurately and efficiently estimating word similarities is essential in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Word Similarity is useful for tasks such as word sense disambiguation, text classification, document clustering, information retrieval, and machine translation (Luong et al., 2015;Kiros, 2015). Over the years, researchers have proposed various approaches to estimate word similarities (Ehret and Holley, 2019;Strube and Ponzetto, 2017). These methods range from word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013a, 2013b) and graph-based word representations (Baroni et al., 2014) to dynamic language models (Logan et al., 2003;Hill et al., 2016;Peters et al., 2018). These approaches are well-documented to be effective and have established a certain gold-standard for word similarity. However, standard techniques for estimating word similarities, particularly those based on word embeddings, have two major drawbacks: computational cost and potential scalability issues. Word embedding methods generally require training on large amounts of text, which makes them computationally intensive and time-consuming. For instance, methods such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013a), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), and FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) typically need to train over a large corpus for weeks or even months to obtain high-quality embeddings. Moreover, large embeddings can be prohibitively expensive to store and process, which poses scalability issues in real-time applications and "big data" scenarios. One effective way to learn word embeddings is the distributional hypothesis (Harris, 1954;Kilgarriff, 2001) which suggests that words that occur in the same context tend to have similar meanings. This observation can be formalized by modeling the co-occurrence relations of words. However, while explicitly counting first-order co-occurrences (e.g., counts of word pairs in a co-occurrence matrix) can yield useful insights into word similarities, this might not be enough to fully capture advanced semantic relationships, especially when such second-order co-occurrences of interest often lie in the tail of the co-occurrence distribution (Baroni et al., 2014). Ideally, one would want to estimate the similarity between words based on all available co-occurrence information, including second-order co-occurrences. Computing these complete co-occurrence information would inherently be computationally expensive (O(|V|² |D|), where |V| is the vocabulary size and |D| is the sum of word occurrences). Therefore, traditional methods for computing word similarities using co-occurrence matrices are generally infeasible for large-scale or streaming NLP applications, where speed and lightness in computational resources are desirable. This paper proposes a new method, Streaming Word Similarity Mining on the Cheap (SWSC), addressing both the computational and scale issues associated with traditional word similarity methods.

Tree-to-String Translation (TST) is a fundamental problem in machine translation (MT) which uses parse trees instead of strings as the basis for language modeling and decoding. The main advantage of TST over traditional statistical MT is that it facilitates translation into more complex languages (e.g., Chinese, Japanese) and supports the construction of more expressive tree grammars for syntax and semantics representation. However, most of the existing tree-to-string and tree-based translation systems (DeNeefe and Knight, 1998; Chiang, 2007; Zhang and Gildea, 2005; Gildea and Osborne, 2009; Nye et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2012; Birch and Osborne, 2012; Zhou et al., 2012) are based on rule-based substitution systems, without tree adjunctions which are essential in realistic linguistic expression. They either use purely substitutional grammar rules or sometimes employ simple concatenation but with limited configurations. Synchronous Tree Adjoining Grammars (TAG) (Stede and Zhang, 1994; Sun and Li, 2001) accommodate a wide range of linguistic phenomena such as discontinuous constituents, head movement, long-distance dependencies, and feature unification which are all significant in different levels of the language structures. Their expressive power comes from the fact that TAGs can generate syntactic structures in a more hierarchical and flexible way than other grammatical frameworks, making them appealing for tree-based MT. Explicit TAG derivation is not practical due to inherent exponential time complexity for parsing and generation (Daniel and Klein, 2013). On the other hand, model-based approachs doesn't learn the explicit TAG derivation but instead extracts "minimal" tree-to-string rules from TAGs that allow for flexible and effective decoding (Li and Gildea, 2012). Electronic medical records (EMRs) contain valuable information for patient care and research, but extracting this information remains challenging. One task of particular interest is question answering (QA) on EMRs, where a user can pose natural language questions to the EMR and receive relevant answers. However, the development and evaluation of QA systems for EMRs face questions such as "What questions should be posed and answered?", "What evidence should be extracted from the EMR to answer these questions?", and “How useful and of high quality are the answers?”. Establishing such a QA system requires a data collection effort to gather questions, alongside with their corresponding evidence in EMRs and gold-standard answers, which is a substantial exercise. In order to facilitate research on this problem, we introduce a corpus for QA in EMRs, emrQA. Our corpus was generated by repurposing existing expert annotations from clinical notes in the community-shared benchmark datasets from the i2b2 Shared Tasks forum. Specifically, we leveraged the existing annotations of named entity recognition, concept extraction, and assertion generation, which were conducted for various NLP tasks such as automatic discharge summaries, patient risk assessment, and clinical text classification. To create the emrQA corpus, we first re-annotated the clinical text and identified symbols that represented units of information such as different symptoms, diagnoses, and treatments. We then generated assumed answer expressions for each unit. For instance, in a clinical note that states "The patient experienced acute chest pain", the assumed answer expression could be "Acute chest pain". By applying this process to the re-annotated text, generating possible questions using templates (e.g., "What symptom did the patient experience?"), and linking these questions to the assumed answer expressions, we were able to create a large number of question-answer pairs. To contextualize and frame the corpus, we define two fundamental tasks relevant for QA in EMRs. First, given a natural language question, we aim to map the question to a logical form (a structured representation, e.g., "s: {?patient:symptom:chest pain}"). Second, given a question in natural language, we aim to find the answer from the collection of assumed answer expressions. We characterize our corpus in terms of size, coverage of medical concepts, types of questions, and linguistic features. Our final corpus contains 1,000,000 question-logical form pairs and 400,000+ question-answer evidence pairs, situated within 100,000 unique clinical notes spanning diverse medical topics and covering the care of over 30,000 patients.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, training data can occasionally contain errors or biases. These issues might lead to suboptimal performance if not properly addressed during the training process. One comprehensive strategy for addressing these issues is to incorporate domain knowledge into the training algorithm to guide the parser towards more accurate and generalizable models. This paper presents an approach to modify the predictions of context-dependent embedding models (e.g., ELMo (Peters et al., 2018)) based on minimal language-specific knowledge, specifically, part-of-speech (POS) and morphological information. Part-of-speech keeps track of word categories, while morphological analysis provides information about word inflection, word formation, and the relationship between root words and their derivatives. This information is particularly useful for languages with rich morphology such as Hindi. Sentences in Hindi, for example, can change their semantic meaning based on the precise aspect of verbs and nouns due to the presence of grammatical case, tense, gender, number, and definiteness. Our approach leverages this knowledge to fine-tune standard embedding models and demonstrates its effectiveness on several Hindi downstream tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition (NER), dependency parsing, and semantic role labeling (SRL). Understanding the role that domain knowledge can play in enhancing the performance of NLP models is particularly timely given the growing interest in adapting English-centric models to other languages and domains while maintaining high accuracy. Embedding models in particular have shown remarkable success across a wide range of tasks; however, their performance can sometimes deviate or be limited in certain domains or languages, especially for those less studied or analyzed as significantly, like Hindi. Evolutionarily, adding in-domain or domain-specific constraints to models is key to generalizing well and improving performance on unseen data and "edge" cases. For models like ELMo or BERT, where contextualized word embeddings are derived from language model pre-training, adding domain-specific understanding could potentially lead to more structured and interpretative representations of words. This structured understanding, in turn, could help downstream tasks better, as demonstrated in this work. The proposed approach consists of two interrelated components: 1.   Part-of-Speech-Guided and Morphologically-Enhanced Embedding Models  : This component modifies conventional embedding models (e.g., ELMo or BERT) to include POS and morphological information before generating embeddings. The intuition here is that adding information about the grammatical category, inflectional changes, or morphological structure of a word can help capture the subtle nuances that are often lost in purely statistical and distributional models.

Training neural networks with large amounts of labeled data is a fundamental approach in contemporary machine learning research. However, collecting such data is often costly and time-consuming. Semi-supervised learning has emerged as a promising alternative that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. In this work, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework, based on recursive autoencoders (RAs), for sentiment analysis tasks and more generally sentence-level prediction tasks. Our model adapts the recursive structure to sentences and learns representation space for multi-word phrases, as fractals or motifs, to better capture nuanced information for sentiment prediction. We extensively evaluate our model on a number of benchmark datasets and compare it with several state-of-the-art approaches. Results show our model consistently outperforms others in predicting sentiment distribution, and we also demonstrate its applicability in a new Sentiment Distributional Learning (SDL) task. Unsupervised and semi-supervised learning have emerged as powerful tools for making the most of available data. An autoencoder (AE), a neural network consisting of an encoder and a decoder, maps input data into a latent representation and converts it back, originally proposed for dimensionality reduction (Hinton & Zemel, 1994). Recent work has explored the power of AE as a building block for various neural network architectures, including deep AEs, variational AEs, and their applications to training generative models (Kingma & Welling, 2013; Goodfellow et al., 2014). Autoencoders are particularly appealing in the context of semi-supervised learning for several reasons. First, the unsupervised training of an autoencoder allows it to model the data distribution in an unsupervised fashion. Second, when combined with the supervised learning of a desired task, the encoder provides useful representations of the input data, which can be leveraged to improve the performance of the supervised classifier. This approach has been shown to be effective in various domains, such as image classification (Kingma & Welling, 2013), speech recognition (Hinton et al., 2012), and natural language processing (Lamb et al., 2016). However, standard AEs are typically designed for static inputs (e.g., images, fixed-length byte-pair encodings). For text analysis, it is often natural to model the nested structure of linguistic objects, for example multiword phrases, sentences, paragraphs, or even documents. Recursive neural networks (RNNs) are designed to handle such arbitrary length inputs and have been applied successfully to tasks including language modeling (Sutskever et al., 2011), machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014), and sentiment analysis (Kumar et al., 2015).
