Our experiments demonstrate that Piggyback can achieve comparable or even better performance than these methods while being more robust and simpler to implement. We also discuss various aspects of Piggyback's performance and potential limitations, as well as avenues for future improvements. Furthermore, we explore the potential of search engines in language processing tasks beyond NER, such as changing the NER task itself to detect entities based on common search engine queries.

How agents see things: On visual representations in an emergent language game One of the central objectives of artificial intelligence (AI) is to enable machines to understand and process visual information in a way similar to humans. This has particularly significant implications for various applications, including computer vision, robotics, natural language processing, and, as this paper focuses, artificial language emergence. In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in the capacity of artificial agents to develop their own "language" when placed in environments where communication and interaction with other agents or humans is necessary. This area of research often involves set-ups where agents are faced with an object segmentation task alongside a language game, in which they must learn to communicate about the visual world. Some of the most notable examples of such setups include the work of Lazaridou et al. (2017), who proposed an "Emergent Communication via Multi-Agent Interaction". In this study, the authors demonstrated that agents could indeed develop a grounded communication protocol purely through multi-agent interaction, without any human intervention, by exploring object configurations within a visual scene and seeking to communicate about them. However, the focus of these and similar works has been primarily on the language itself - the symbols, or "utterances," that agents use or learn to use. Less attention has been given to the question of what these symbols denote, or how these agents "see" the world visually, which is a fundamental requirement if we are to understand the true capacities and limitations of emergent communication systems. Furthermore, understanding the visual representations used by agents in such emergent language games has implications far beyond language itself. It points to the fundamental question of how AI systems might generalize learned knowledge across different tasks or representations in visual or other sensory contexts. If agents develop strong generalizations in terms of language, but these generalizations are not reflected in their understanding of the visual world, it could suggest that the agents' learning mechanisms are focusing more on the linguistic aspects of the game rather than on the conceptual understanding or visual semantics of the world around them. This would be particularly concerning for those interested in developing language-like communication systems that could interact with humans on a symbolic and conceptual level, rather than just producing "strings" that might meet superficial criteria for communication but lack meaningful grounding in the world. This paper thus aims to fill this gap by investigating the visual representations that emerge in these games and whether these representations capture the conceptual properties of objects depicted in the input images used.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a key information extraction task used in a variety of natural language processing applications. Many successful NER systems are trained on large annotated corpora which are costly to obtain and use. These systems often rely on language-specific resources, feature engineering, and knowledge of the training language. This increases the barrier for applying NER systems to new languages, especially in low-resource settings where labeled data is scarce. This paper proposes a novel "phonologically aware" neural model which can adapt quickly to new languages with minimal data. This model uses phonological character representations along with word embeddings extracted from an unlabelled corpus, and applies attention to these features. By leveraging word phonology, the model creates a transferable representation for NER, relying on language-invariant properties of phonological patterns in written words. Previous work has demonstrated that character-based word representations (Wu et al., 2016;Lample et al., 2016) and phonologically-informed approaches can improve performance in various language-processing tasks (Tran et al., 2018;Crego et al., 2019). However, most of these models use orthographic information - that is, the way words are written. Our work explores a different approach by focusing on phonological information - that is, how words are pronounced. This is because phonological structures are more universal and less dependent on the specific script or orthography of the language. For instance, the concept of a "long vowel" can serve as a shared feature across many languages, allowing for cross-lingual inference and transfer even where orthographic representations significantly diverge. Our model is designed to adapt to a new language by analyzing its phonological patterns without the need for large amounts of annotated data in that language. We evaluate our approach on a suite of languages with varying degrees of data availability and inconsistent orthography, which serves as a challenging test bed to highlight the strengths of our design. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in a true low-resource setting where no labeled data is available for the target language. For the more resourceful settings, where a small amount of labeled data or even unlabelled data from the target language is available, the model exhibits fast adaptation and outperforms monolingual baselines. The benefits of our approach can be summarized as follows: -   Cross-lingual generalizability:   By focusing on phonological features, our model can transfer knowledge across languages more robustly than those employing orthographic information alone. -   Low resource adaptation:   Our model efficiently adapts to new languages even with minimal or no supervised data, reducing the dependence on language-specific resources and enabling scalable deployment in multilingual settings.

Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms reliably on limited training data is a fundamental research question. To compensate for this limited data, various approaches have been proposed, such as using noise-regularized models (Goodfellow et al., 2014), leveraging transfer learning (Thoppilan and Rush, 2017; Pan et al., 2019), or constructing artificial data systematically (Abuelma’atti et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2017). A less studied but equally important set of strategies pursues data utilization efficiency through optimal training data selection. A most direct way to improve training data utilization efficiency, especially on limited datasets, is to control the training schedule or learning sequence, often referred to as curricula learning (Schaal, 1992; Jordan and Rumelhart, 1992). The concept of a curriculum here refers to an ordering of training data designed to optimize learning performance. Such exploration is particularly valuable because there is often no a priori knowledge on how challenging instances are for the current model, or how their sequencing should facilitate model adaptation. Offline data ordering often relies on domain knowledge or heuristics, which are not necessarily or even commonly available. A key challenge in learning this ordering is that the downstream task’s performance is a latent ground truth, as is the expected difficulty of any instance in the curriculum. A model may need to explore and learn the entire space of possible curricula to locate an optimal one (Figure 1). Fig. 1: Left: Space of all possible curricula (S) (optimization problem). Observed instances (x1, ..., xn). Expected outputs of all possible curricula (θ) are represented by a latent function (output). Right: Bayesian optimization model learns the likely contour of the latent function, and outputs the next "best" instances. As the fundamental issue here is that curriculum learning is an optimization procedure over a structured (discrete) space, optimization methods should be harnessed for this purpose. Bayesian optimization (BO; Snoek et al., 2012), a probabilistic approach to global optimization over expensive-to-evaluate functions, is well suited to address this problem. The key concepts leveraged here are: 1. We represent the latent function’s likely contour by a probability distribution over possible expected performance values for any curriculum. 2. The optimization is done over the space of curricula, which is discrete but structured. 3. This optimization uses real-valued informative features to guide the search efficiently in the structured space. 4. Exploration and exploitation are balanced based on uncertainty in the expected outcomes of different curricula.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Noise-Robust Morphological Disambiguation for Dialectal Arabic: One of the core challenges in Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks stems from the inherent ambiguity and noise present in unstructured text, particularly when dealing with informal language or dialects. Words in this type of content may have multiple spellings or orthographic variations, and the syntax and semantics may deviate significantly from the standard variety. These characteristics of informal language pose a significant challenge to standard language processing models, as they are typically trained on cleaner, more structured data. The challenges are even more pronounced in the case of dialects. Dialects not only exhibit variability in spelling and phonetics but also in morpho-syntactic structures. This variability renders the problem of processing dialectal text particularly complex. A specific case study of this complexity is Egyptian Arabic. As the most widely used colloquial dialect in the Arabic language, Egyptian Arabic presents a significant challenge due to its rich phonetic and phonological variations, complex morpho-syntactic structures, and a plethora of orthographic inconsistencies. In user-generated content, such as social media posts or text messages, these issues are often exacerbated by irregular spellings and the use of colloquial expressions or words drawn from other languages. For instance, this content may contain unusual or non-standard spellings (e.g., different transliterations of Arabic script into Latin alphabet), colloquial expressions that may not appear in standard dictionaries, or even English and other languages intermixed with Arabic, resulting in orthographic and lexical noise. Traditional Arabic language processing systems, including those for morphological analysis and disambiguation, are often trained on standard or literary Arabic and may fail to perform adequately on dialectal texts due to this noise and structural divergence. This is particularly problematic in a world where user-generated content is increasingly becoming the norm and the colloquial is the preferred mode of expression for much of the Arabic-speaking population. Accurate morphological analysis and disambiguation of dialectal content are crucial for NLP applications ranging from machine translation and sentiment analysis to question answering and text summarization. However, achieving these tasks on dialectal text requires models that can robustly handle the unique challenges presented by dialectal content, including noisy and irregular language use. Our work addresses this gap by developing a noise-robust morphological tagging and disambiguation model specifically designed for Egyptian Arabic. Our proposed model uses neural architectures that are capable of learning from noisy data by leveraging contextual information within the text.

Language is one of the most powerful tools we have for expressing our thoughts and perceptions of the world. To accurately understand and convey these ideas, language relies heavily on sensory and perceptual information. Hence, deep understanding of language inherently involves understanding and interpreting various sensory concepts. In this work, we aim to create a resource that explicitly captures this connection between language and senses, which we refer to as a Sensorial Lexicon. A complete and accurate sensorial lexicon of this kind can greatly aid in a variety of applications, including language comprehension, generation, and machine translation, among others. Our goal is to associate each word in a language (here, English) with a set of senses (sight, hearing, taste, touch, smell). The challenge here is not only in the sheer size of the task, considering the vocabulary is in the hundreds of thousands, but also in accurately capturing relationships among semantic senses. Previous work in the related domains such as Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Word Sense Induction (WSI) has established a foundation for exploring such relationships between words and concepts. However, these existing efforts have not traditionally focused on the sensorial aspects of word meanings. To fill this gap, we propose an approach to automatically construct a sensorial lexicon, which we call Sensicon, using a combination of corpus analysis and machine learning. Our approach includes the following three components: 1.   Bootstrapping Process  : To kick-start the collection of word-sense pairs, we start with a seed set of words and senses derived from specialized lexical resources. This initial set allows us to train a model to recognize patterns and generalize to other words. 2.   Corpus Analysis  : We leverage large datasets of text to identify more word-sense pairs by examining words and their contexts. This step is crucial as it expands the number of word-senses pairs in our lexicon and helps capture nuanced associations that may not be easily found using manual or bootstrapping methods alone. 3.   Evaluation and Correction Mechanism  : To ensure the accuracy of our lexicon, we use a combination of machine learning models to predict word-sense pairs and crowd-sourced human evaluation to validate these predictions. This iterative process allows us to refine our model and lexicon, removing false positives and ensuring high accuracy. Our Sensicon construction is guided by several design principles to maximize its utility for computational applications. These principles include: -   Comprehensive Coverage  : Aiming to cover as much of the English vocabulary as possible.

Training neural models, especially recurrent ones like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, is an efficient way to learn task-specific representations. They have been successfully used for various NLP tasks, including sentence compression (Beau and van Veen, 2016; Lin, 2017; Zhang, 2018), questions answering (Min et al., 2018), and narrative summarization (Eisner, 2016; Allamanis and Sutton, 2013). The LSTM structure is particularly suitable for tasks involving sequential data, due to its ability to learn long range dependencies. However, training an LSTM requires large amounts of labeled examples. When examples come from a single domain, the model may not generalize well to unseen domains. Sentence compression (SC), a task that aims to extract the most important part of a sentence from a set of irrelevant or duplicate content, is well suited to this issue because it involves extracting important points of a document/ summary into its most essential content (Johnides and Ronan,2003; Wu et al., 2009). As it explores this problem, it will encounter the common challenges of domain shift within or even across languages. Current models for this task use context-aware and sequential symbols provided by LSTMs to learn different levels of the textual structures. Their sequential representations often assumed that the model can learn the structure and relationships in the text implicitly. However, even within a single language or domain, training an LSTM requires a large amount of labeled data (e.g., to tag which words should be taken as significant, irrelevant or redundant), posing a practical bottleneck when expanding the model for new domains or languages. Our research addresses this problem by adding domain-independent and language-independent syntactic knowledge into the training process, aiming to improve the model’s ability to compress sentences in new domains. The fundamental question we aim to answer in this work is: can syntactic knowledge improve the domain adaptability of LSTM-based sentence compression models? Our hypothesis is that by explicitly incorporating syntactic information, particularly when modeling the dependency structure of a sentence, we can help the model better understand and adapt to different domain-specific characteristics. Such structure and meaning knowledge may be crucial when a language changing the word order or function significantly (for example, English allows dropping subjects in certain condition while Mandarin requires explicit subjects for most sentences). Our hypothesis is tested by comparing the performance of our model against several baseline models, including a standard LSTM-based model, a non-neural network-based sentential compression model, and BLEU scores.

Classifying Temporal Relations with Rich Linguistic Knowledge Temporal relations are a fundamental component of natural language processing (NLP), essential for tasks such as event extraction and timeline generation. Effective temporal relation classification (TRC) is needed to determine whether two time-stamped events have one of various possible relations, such as the event X precedes Y, event X overlaps with Y, or event X follows Y. A variety of TRC approaches have been proposed, with most of them relying heavily on machine learning and minimal language annotation. In this paper, we present an innovative TRC system that uses a rich set of linguistic knowledge derived from semantic and discourse relations. We differentiate our approach in several key aspects from existing work. First, we classify pairs of events as one of the 14 temporal relations used in the TimeBank corpus 1 , rather than collapsing down to 6 relationships as is commonly done. Second, our system employs a mix of rule-based and learning-based methods, leveraging the strengths of each. Our rule-based system makes use of various linguistic knowledge sources including semantic dependency parse trees and discourse relation annotations2 . While rule-based systems can suffer from overfitting or lack of generality, we modulate their predictions using a statistical model trained on labeled data.We evaluate our system on the TimeBank corpus and obtain significant improvements compared to a state-of-the-art learning-based baseline system. Our system achieves a 15% relative reduction in error, while the system that minimized classification label granularity achieved only 2.6% relative reduction in error over baseline on the TimeBank corpus. Our analysis reveals that using richer linguistic information and a combination of rule-based and learning-based approaches significantly enhances TRC performance. We argue that in fields such as NLP where semantic and pragmatic understanding of language are crucial, incorporating richer linguistic knowledge and hybrid methods can lead to better models. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 briefly reviews related work and our contributions to the field. Section 3 describes the components of our TRC system. Section 4 provides detail on the experiments and evaluation metrics. Section 5 discusses the results. Section 6 concludes with a summary of our findings and recommendations for future work. A wide range of NLP tasks involve temporal relations, but we focus here on event-event relation classification where each event is associated with time. Temporal relation classification aims to determine a temporal order between two events for a given input pair (e1, e2).

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models at a prohibitive cost in terms of time and computational resources remains one of the major obstacles in applying NMT to practical tasks. State-of-the-art deep NMT models, particularly Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) models with attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Luong et al., 2015), are known to require hundreds of thousands of sentences for training and may need several days to a week even on modern GPU-equipped machines. Such models are out of reach for many applications and setups, especially when real-time latency is required. To address this problem, various approaches have been proposed to make NMT models smaller. Knowledge distillation (KD) is one such technique that had been successfully applied to reduce the size of neural networks in image classification (Hinton et al., 2015; Romero et al., 2014). KD works by using the parameters and predictions of a large teacher model as a form of supervised data to train a smaller student model with fewer parameters. However, most existing knowledge distillation work in the NMT domain focus on similar word-level prediction as the teacher model. This paper proposes to extend the knowledge distillation idea to both the word-level and the sequence-level predictions of a teacher NMT model and examines their effectiveness for both size reduction and performance preservation. We introduce two novel sequence-level knowledge distillation (seq2seq KD) methods. The first introduces the entire teacher’s output distribution as a prior for the probabilities over the student model’s outputs, and the second carefully estimates how similar (in a specific statistical way) the student model's distribution should be to the teacher model’s. We experiment on the WMT 2014 English-Romanian translation dataset (Cristian et al., 2014) and demonstrate that sequence-level KD methods lead to further performance improvements over existing word-level KD methods, and even allow complete elimination of beam search, which is one of the main bottlenecks in NMT inference. The measured speed-up in decoding time is substantial: the best of the student models are 10 times faster than the state-of-the-art teacher model. For example, on the WMT 2014 EN-RO test set, the fastest teacher model takes about 8 hours to decode 1000 sentences using 8 GPU’s. Our best student models can decode these 1000 sentences in about 50 minutes on a single GPU. First, we use a set of NER models and use Snorkel's STAGGER (Semi-supervised Learning with Staged Aggregation of Graded Embeddings) algorithm to train a rule-based tagger. Second, we used the same set of NER models and Snorkel's rule-based tagger to generate annotated training data. After we trained and generated enough data via Snorkel, we then used this annotated set for training and testing our classifier. Experimentation: Table 3 in the supplemental material shows the rules generated, and Table 4 in the supplemental material shows the performance of the system before and after adding some domain features. The final 97.2% accuracy is achieved by including among semantic features the question syntax weighted by a rule-based approach. The results are shown in Table 5 of the supplemental material. Comparison to Past Works: We compare our 97.2% accuracy to the previous State of the Art of 91.6% provided by Zhou et al. (2018) who used contextualized word embeddings, while the system described here utilized syntactic markers in combination with semantic rules. Implications: Beyond the immediate improvement on performance, our results have implications for future question classification work. They suggest that focusing on specific syntactic patterns combined with semantic rules learned without labeled data can lead to significant accuracy improvements, and that such rule-based systems could be used in combination with supervised learning techniques to further improve accuracy. These two findings could likely be applicable to other question classification sub-tasks and potentially the main question classification task as well. Future Work: We plan to explore if using structured representations (e.g., graphs or parse trees of questions) can allow capturing more sophisticated syntactic patterns, and if semi-supervised learning can be further utilized to refine the rule-based system. Additionally, we will investigate if deep learning models, after being trained on a large amount of raw data, benefit from the features extracted by our rule-based system. Conclusion: We have advanced the state of the art for rule-based question classification by 6 percentage points and demonstrated the usefulness of combining structure-aware rule-based methods with machine learning for improving accuracy.

Training embeddings directly from unlabelled or anonymized data is of key interest in many applications. To compensate for the limited number of samples or quantity-sensitive data, embedding models can be trained with multiple features of the data. This is well-known for unstructured data, where the ideal choice for such additional features are views (e.g. a sentence and its paraphrases as two views for sentiment analysis; a transcript and video frames for speech recognition; words and part-of-speech tags for language modelling (Chiu and Ng, 2010;Chiu, Golub, and Ng, 2011;Peters, Amodei, and Zaremba, 2017;Saha et al., 2018)). In these setups, we have multiple 'access' points to the same latent structured information. Training dedicated embeddings that align features from different views while ignoring irrelevant or noisy information can lead to significant improvements in downstream tasks. Hence, we hope to achieve a synergistic effect when jointly considering multiple views of data. However, not all datasets are multiview in the rigid sense of having multiple similar views. Some applications inherently involve different information sources or multi-modalty - for example, in medical or biological applications, one might have access to a combination of clinical data and radiography data (visual) or even pathological data (Mangraviti et al., 2019) of the same patients. If the sets of data at hand are conceptually distinct - the core features are different variables or come from different domains or technology platforms - but are still naturally related (e.g., patient's clinical data, physical activity data from wearable sensors, and genomic data), can we leverage this structure to improve the outcome of learning a model on only one 'informative' view? For example, in socio-linguistic applications where the aim is to predict how people communicate, we may have access to textual data (e.g., Tweets or dialogue) but not the underlying characteristics (e.g., measured variables such as age, personality traits, or socioeconomic status matched to each individual). For our purposes, we define a 'multiview' dataset as one that incorporates multiple sources or types of data, but each source provides a distinct view of the same phenomenon or concept (refer to examples mentioned in the above paragraph). Annotations – typically the key for supervised learning - in these multiview setups may only be available for one view (e.g., labels are only on clinical information but not on the genetic information or lifestyle-related data). Yet, by considering the predictive signal from multiple views and aiming to learn a common latent space, the final embedding can capture the relationships across views.

Training natural language processing (NLP) models with maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) has been one of the main approaches for structured prediction tasks, such as machine translation (MT) and text summarization. While MLE is simple to implement and has been shown to work quite well for training sequence-to-sequence models (Sutskever, Vinyals, & Le, 2014; Luong et al., 2015), it has several drawbacks that have been well-documented and discussed in the literature. One of the most critical issues is exposure bias. The training objective keeps changing as new information becomes available in subsequent time-steps. This leads to a discrepancy between training and evaluation objectives. While the model is trained to predict the next best word independently of previously predicted words (i.e., word-level prediction), it is actually evaluated based on semantic completeness and coherence of the generated sequence (sequence-level evaluation). Another issue is the fact that MLE training objectives do not ensure that the most plausible sequences are learned, but rather that each word in the sequence is predicted correctly, given the context. As a result, sequence level evaluation metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU for summarization or translation quality scoring often evaluate trained MLE models worse compared to models trained with other objectives. This is due to the overly greedy nature of the optimization during MLE training, which may not always result in the most coherent sequence given the constraints and requirements in the downstream task at hand. For instance, in the task of machine translation, the model can produce high-quality translations word by word, while the overall structure and meaning might be lost or significantly altered. To address the first issue of exposure bias, as well as to align the training objective more closely with the evaluation criteria, various modifications and extensions of the MLE objective have been proposed. For example, policy gradient methods have been used to train models that directly optimize the final sequence or a fitness-like objective on the target side or structured objective during generation (Shang, Lu, Li, & Li, 2016; Firat et al., 2017). These methods indeed show improvements over MLE on certain tasks, but they are more complex, harder to implement, and suffer from high sample variance and changing objective during optimization that can make training unstable and difficult to converge. In this paper, we propose a new objective for training sequence-to-sequence models. Our proposed CALCS (Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence) objective is designed to address the sequence-level structure similarity aspect that is often overlooked in maximum likelihood estimation.

Training embeddings directly from knowledge graph (KG) is seen as an effective way to represent entities as well as natural language documents. In particular, entities described in articles and documents can be linked to their corresponding entry in a large-scale KB. Most existing works either predict entity candidate from mention (or neighbors) within the KB (e.g., (Min et al., 2014;Bizer & Kobilarov, 2015)), or disambiguate links that have been pre-estimated (e.g., (Bizer et al., 2011)). The former usually employs context information from the surrounding text, while the latter relies on the knowledge network structure to infer accurate link. However, such structures are not always available for external sources like text documents and queries, where only entity mentions in ambiguous forms are provided (as shown in Figure 1). The task of distilling such ambiguous mentions into the precise KB entity representations, and simultaneously discovering the document-level semantic meaning, is known as entity/knowledgebase representation learning (Rlab). It also requires appropriate knowledge representation in the form of embeddings, which can be generalized across various document types and served as a multi-layered bridge between sparse, structured data or even unstructured text and the underlying ontological meanings. Recently, several models have been proposed to produce meaningful representations based on training data from knowledge corpus. A few of them assumed multi-step link prediction and disambiguation processes (Bronner & Bordiu, 2017;Christian et al., 2012;Sethuraman et al., 2017), while others, like TransE (Bordes et al., 2013) and ConvE (Dettmers et al., 2018), are model-specific frameworks designed primarily for knowledge representation but could be adapted for representation learning. Inspired by such work, we propose TextEnt, a simple yet effective neural model that learns the entity and document representations side-by-side, through training on KG descriptions. Our primary objective of the model is to predict the correct entity whenever documents from a KB are provided, and to align the document vector with the target entity vector in an embedding space. While the previous work (Nguyen & Grbovic, 2018; Zeng et al., 2014) predominantly focused on linking local context (mention) to entity IDs, our model goes beyond such local description, covering various information that a document potentially provides such as entity type, attribute, role and even the mentioned KG relationships. Rlab based on KG data has the potential to recover more structured and comprehensive knowledge graph. Previous work (Bizer et al. (2011)) showed that fine-grained entity typing and other compositional knowledge can be inferred when text data is available for training.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) is a class of problems in which systems receive input in the form of two sentences and infer whether the two propositions entail each other (entailment), opposite (contradiction), or have no relation (neutral). While several successful methods have been developed for this task, they have predominantly been based on attention mechanisms – which determine questions such as "What aspects of the subject sentence should be considered while evaluating the relationship between the two sentences?" (Miyato et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017). However, despite their success, these models are often limited in certain ways. Attention mechanisms inherently assume knowledge about what to attend, limiting generalization to unseen relationships. They can also become computationally expensive for large inputs, and their capacity for capturing complex interactions may be limited. Furthermore, their learned weights often reveal relationships among semantic features beyond simple attention weighted sums but do not provide a principled way to model how these features interact. Hence, while attention models achieve strong results, they often do not provide clear interpretability regarding the interactions and paths through which they evaluate entailment. Recent advances have introduced the use of convolution neural networks (CNNs) to predict entailment between sentences (Williams et al., 2018). CNNs provide a means to universally apply filters and view symbols within a sentence through these filters simultaneously, hence capturing the local and compositional structure of sentences. However, the mainstream application of CNNs to NLI has been as a two-layer model (with the sentence features followed by an attention layer). This configuration neither allows direct interaction between the two sentences nor permits the capture of complex sentence-sentence interactions without explicitly learned weighting schemes. In this paper, we propose a new model for NLI called Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), designed to capture the complex interactions between two sentences in a single unified framework without relying on an attention mechanism. The fundamental idea of our model is to encode one sentence with dynamic filters generated based on the other sentence. This allows us to harness the universal applicability of CNNs to explicitly model various interaction patterns between sentences. Instead of learning what parts of the sentences to consider or explicitly weighting them, CIN learns filters that are tailored to the structure and content of both sentences simultaneously. This design offers a natural and elegant solution to interaction modeling, eliminating the need for an additional attention mechanism while potentially reducing the computational complexity for capturing complex interactions.

Extracting opinion targets is a crucial step in opinion mining from online reviews to understand the products's or services' aspects that users like or dislike. Two main categories of methods have been proposed to extract opinion targets: syntax-based methods and alignment-based methods (Lu et al., 2003;Nguyen and Quynh, 2013;Nguyen et al., 2014;Peng and Zhang, 2016;Strube and Ponzetto, 2017). Syntax-based methods typically involve discovering syntactic patterns such as verb-subject-object (VSO) and attributive clauses, which are then mapped to opinion targets (Li et al., 2010;Nguyen et al., 2014). The advantage of this approach is its ability to leverage linguistic knowledge to understand the opinion relationships among semantic entities. However, the robustness of syntax-based methods varies depending on the corpus's linguistic formality. As a result, they may fail to correctly extract opinion targets from informal language such as online user-generated content. For instance, missing proper subject-verb tense agreements, broken sentence structures, or lack of SVO (Subject-Verb-Object) structure can lead to poor parsing and target extraction (Tur et al., 2011). On the other hand, alignment-based methods generally utilize word alignment models to identify opinion targets without relying on syntactic parsing (Mintz et al., 2009;Strube and Ponzetto, 2017). This stems from the observation that opinion expressions (e.g., nice, bad, perfect) often co-occur with entities that are being targeted (e.g., the phone is nice). Thus, word alignment models, which map contexts from query sentences and target sentences through a model like IBM model 4 (Brown et al., 1993), are well-suited for identifying relevant entities that are part of opinions (Tsai and Chang, 2006;Peng and Zhang, 2016). However, the efficacy of word alignment for opinion target extraction is less clear. Limited studies have investigated this explicitly, or compared its performance across different datasets or contexts. Word alignment may also struggle to capture concepts or entities not directly mentioned in the text, especially when the relation between opinion words and targets is abstract or indirect (Tur et al., 2011). For example, a review might express a positive overall sentiment about a hotel by mentioning only its service, but the real target of the positivity could be the hotel's cleanliness. Moreover, while there has been substantial work on improving the performance of specific methods for opinion target extraction, there remains a dearth of research that rigorously compares the general efficacy of these two methods.

Statistical machine transliteration can be broadly classified into two types: rule-based and statistical machine transliteration. Statistical machine transliteration is becoming increasingly popular due to its ability to utilize large amounts of bilingual corpora which are now readily available. While rule-based transliteration can be highly accurate when ideal conditions are met (e.g., the existence of a comprehensive set of transliteration rules), this kind of approach may not always be possible due to various factors such as the complexity and sheer size of the script pair and the lack of linguistic resources of the target language. Statistical machine transliteration, on the other hand, leverages data extracted from existing bilingual resources to learn a representation of transliteration. However, training transliteration models requires large amounts of high-quality data, which is not always available for less resource-rich pairs. Statistical machine transliteration from bilingual corpora employs a matrix factorization approach to model relationships among semantic entities (i.e., words or phrases in one language) and their corresponding transliterations. Core to this approach is the estimation of a bilingual dictionary which maps the known word or phrase transliterations. The challenging part of this task is in accurately identifying the correct transliterations from the noisy raw data. Raw data typically comes from crowdsourced efforts, which suffer from a plethora of issues that include transliteration inaccuracies, incomplete and partial symbols, and non-transliteration symbol parts (e.g., punctuation, foreign terms), all of which can be misunderstood as part of the transliteration. For instance, if a source phrase contains the sentence [highlighted Japanese] (highlighted part is transliteration noise), existing alignment methods may incorrectly align the noise part to some target transliteration. Our model is an extension of Bayesian character level alignment for distinguishing noise from transliterations. It captures the noise inherent in the data by modeling the underlying probability distribution of likely transliterations and uses that to distinguish the transliteration parts from the noise. The fundamental issue we address is to build an alignment model which can separate noise (features not relevant to transliteration) from true transliteration features in the data. We propose a Bayesian framework for modeling the character alignment relationship between source and target words or phrases explicitly accounting for noise. Our model is built on the basis of an augmented Belief Propagation (BP). The architecture of our model (refer to Figure 1 for a high level overview) includes a Noisy Parts Model (NPM), for modeling transliteration and noise in parallel.

Training natural language understanding (NLU) systems at scale over realistic data is key to making breakthroughs in these systems. Wikipedia provides a rich source of text to train and evaluate such systems. In this paper, we introduce the Wikipedia Retrieval task (WIKIREADING) and a new large-scale dataset containing 18 million instances derived from Wikipedia pages. WIKIREADING is designed to test a system's ability to understand and reason over text, with a particular focus on tasks that require inference and minimal language understanding beyond the text at hand. The task requires the system to map text from a Wikipedia article to an object in a structured knowledge representation - Wikidata (Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014). By structuring the task around Wikipedia articles, we obviate the need for preparing a separate and structured dataset, and instead, we leverage the read-write property of Wikipedia for data creation and modification - which we believe makes this setup more representative of future NLU applications. The task is designed to be challenging and requires complex reasoning over text as it comprises several types of sub-tasks, including classification, extraction, and similar reasoning tasks. To facilitate model comparison and development, we share the dataset with the research community and evaluate a range of state-of-the-art models on this task. One key aspect of our task is that it includes many different sub-tasks with varying answer types: some sub-tasks require the system to generate a label from the entire article, while others require the system to extract specific pieces of data from the article (questions with short or long answers, etc.). This variability allows us to evaluate models that can handle different types of summarization and extraction tasks. WIKIREADING is designed to push the frontier of natural language understanding, and we hope that it can serve as a new benchmark task for models that are capable of contextual reasoning over large corpora. We define several fundamental tasks based on textual values in Wikidata and design evaluation metrics to assess performance on these tasks. Our tasks include classification, where the goal is to predict the type of a textual value given a Wikipedia article; extraction, where the goal is to extract a specific type of textual data from an article; and question answering and multi-label question answering, where a question is presented and answers are typically large amounts of text. To accommodate the variety of these tasks, we introduce some general guidelines for designing these tasks.

Linguistic data can be represented using various abstract syntax or semantic structures which often differ from one another. For instance, the Universal Dependency (UD) representation (in which function words are separated from content words by null nodes and many unrealized heads are marked) is topologically quite different from a surface-syntactic representation (which includes all contentinal words and phrase questions) or a linearized tree (which is often used in various NLP tasks due to its simple and compact format). This makes the inference and projection from one representation to another non-trivial, especially in the context of data-driven sentence generation. For example, given a UD representation with a content word (e.g., "book") and an unrealized head (e.g., "nsubj"), the verbal phrase "bought a book" would contain a syntactically incorrect structure (because "bought" was not realized as a function word), but when following a surface-syntactic or linearized form that does indeed separate content words (book) from function words (the unrealized head being marked explicitly with "V"), generating such a verbal phrase seems straightforward. However, when we deal with similar sentences in various syntactic structures (UD and surface-syntactic tree), traditionally their generation has been tackled using distinct models or representations, sometimes avoiding this projection problem altogether. Here, we introduce a novel fully stochastic data-driven generator with the capacity to specifically handle such non-isomorphic projections. This generator can take as input structures represented according to the PropBank formalism (Lin, 2003), an annotated corpus for analyzing predicate-argument structures (e.g., marking who did what to whom), which is topologically different from surface representations in UD or linearized contexts. One of the challenges we face in this task is that PropBank and similar structures can't easily be directly projected to sentences without realizing explicit functional dependencies (e.g., the distinction between a subject and a direct object marked by a particular verb), which means if one starts from PropBank-like structures, generating valid surface sentences requires more than just copying content words and surface syntactic information. Our approach leverages a cascade of SVM-based classifiers to map input argument-verb structures to surface sentences while respecting the syntactic and semantic constraints and handling projected dependencies between non-isomorphic structures. This is particularly useful for applications such as machine translation, dialogue systems, and question answering systems where generating sentences from abstract linguistic representations is necessary but not straightforward. The architecture of our generator can be roughly divided into several main components.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have increasingly become essential sources of data for social and political analysis. In particular, the task of sentiment analysis, where the overall attitude of a piece of text, in this case a tweet, is determined as positive, negative or neutral, offers a indispensable lens through which to understand the political opinions, attitudes and sentiments of large segments of the population. The present work seeks to expand the scope and applicability of this type of analysis by offering a framework that allows the inference and modeling of political sentiment between nation-states. The approach described here is specifically concerned with assessing how citizens of one country respond to and discuss another. This not only provides insights into the general mood of the citizenry with respect to foreign relations but also has the potential to identify dynamic shifts and changes in these sentiments over time. The study employs Twitter as a primary data source, due to its global reach and the volume of political discussion it hosts. Twitter’s facility for open and real-time discourse provides a unique forum for citizens to express their opinions about other nations and international affairs. This data is challenging, however, given the short, informal nature of tweets and the nuances of sentiment within them. Processing this data therefore requires sophisticated natural language processing techniques to accurately and robustly capture underlying political sentiments. For this task, this paper explores various approaches to sentiment analysis, both at the token and document levels. We compare shallow machine learning techniques, such as support vector machines (SVMs) and logistic regression, with deeper models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), including the long short-term memory (LSTM) variant. The latter show particular promise in capturing the context-dependent nature of political sentiment, where the sentiment towards one nation is often strongly influenced by the contexts in which that nation is mentioned (e.g., in discussions about foreign policy, economic ties, or international conflicts). A critical aspect of our approach is the use of an attention mechanism in our models. By using attention, we aim to identify within each tweet which specific words, phrases or concepts are most salient in determining the sentiment towards a given nation. This provides valuable interpretability to the models' predictions, revealing which factors (e.g., name of the nation, adjectives, references to historical events or treaties) are most influential in shaping political sentiment.

Social media platforms, especially Twitter, have become essential in political discourse analysis due to the high-volume online political discussions (Lasko, 2014). To better understand political polarization, deep analysis of these discussions is crucial and has various applications, including voter modeling (Das and Chen, 2011; Zhang, 2013), questions on political representation (Rosenberg & Abowd, 2015), and media influence (Martens & Roy, 2015). In light of this, political ideology detection (PID) for news articles has recently gained increasing attention as it can provide fine-grained insights into public opinion and polarization (Wasabi, 2017). Previous research on PID for news articles typically focuses on leveraging features from textual content. Sentiment analysis (Hutto and Gilbert, 2014; Hopkins and King, 2010) and content-based linguistic features (Bhatia and Smith, 2013) have been used to build models for this task. However, such approaches are limited in that they might miss subtle information and bias nuances that are revealed through a hierarchical or top-down interpretation of information structure (Giles, 2003). For instance, a news article can be about a specific topic (e.g., "affordable healthcare") with political bias coming from the presentation of the topic rather than direct sentiment about it. This implies that the ideology detection can be benefited from leveraging not just the content but also other contextual features such as title, author (e.g., media organization), hyperlink network structure, and media citations. Considering the network structure can in itself be insightful for understanding dissemination patterns (Guilbeault and Greenwald, 2018), and how content from different sources might be connected (e.g., echo chambers and the spread of misinformation). A potential limitation of previous work on PID is overlooking or underutilizing such contextual features or combining them in a naive way without proper structure recognition. We argue, as popularly used in other domains such as NLP and computer vision, multi-view learning can integrate these diverse cues effectively. Specifically, in our approach, we consider each cue provided by different views (text content, title, and hyperlink structure) as a separate input channel that can independently contribute to the decision of the political ideology for a given news article. This approach can potentially leverage the unique strengths of each view: textual content for capturing opinion and stance, title for capturing the author's leading perspective, and network structure for capturing relationships and potential biases in how this content is disseminated. However, combining these different views in a naive way, without leveraging their interplay and hierarchy, may not fully exploit their potential.

Training embeddings using all the fine-grained semantics and syntax from unstructured text is an increasingly popular method to improve many NLP applications, from language understanding to machine translation and question-answering (QA). While word embeddings are well-suited to represent generic semantic properties, we argue that for specialized tasks and domains, embeddings capturing more specific – instance-of questions , which are common in conversations (e.g., What kind of narrative structure offers the possibility for "multiple viewpoints" that makes Heart of darkness useful for academic discourse? — fractals?), require word representations that can distinguish among related concepts. For example, an entailment prediction task requires representation of not only synonymy knowledge but also semantic entailment, which may involve complex relations such as hyponymy or causality. Moreover, recent studies have shown that embedding similarity corresponds with human judgements (Mitchell et al., 2018). As shown below, following recent work that demonstrated the effectiveness of modeling fine-grained semantics through explicit supervision (e.g., interclass, morpho-semantics, and relation-specific embeddings) (Ruder2017,Smith2017,Nishida2017), this paper introduces a novel approach to model domain-specific linguistic relations within or even across languages. By taking a minimal supervision view, it uses cause-effect symbols provided by domainspecific knowledge sources (e.g., the English shallow semantic network WordNet), assumed to be error-prone. Instead of relying on sets of hand-labeled examples for each relation (as is plausible for general-purpose datasets such as WordNet or Wiktionary for synonyms or hypernyms), we take advantage of sparsity, learned patterns, and transfer learning to bootstrap and improve the embeddings. One could similarly bootstrap general-purpose lexical resources (e.g., and WordNet ) to model lexical semantics such as synonymity or hyponymy, see also the recent work of Conneau2017 on modeling cross-lingual morpho-semantics through bilingual embedding transfer or Ruder2017 for modeling semantic relations using weakly labeled data. This work focuses on modeling casual relations because causal relations are common in conversational or explicitly structured language and have been argued to be a fundamental concept in human cognition (Sloman, 2005). Accurate representation of causality is also important in many other NLP applications such as event extraction (e.g., Rodrigues2010), multi-choice and analogy qestion answering (e.g., Goyal2016,Rupesh2017), and reasoning over the web (e.g., Yatskar2010). Recent work has also started to explore the use of causal language in QA and entailment, including examples that aim to model whether a statement causes another one (Bolukbasi2016,Narasimhan2015,Mossel2017,See2017), however these prior works typically require training on a gold data that either labels whether a pair of arguments is causally related or relies on the ontology of specific applications.

Social media platforms have become the preferred mode of communication for people worldwide. Each demographic, from teenagers to grandparents, uses social media; these platforms have become an integral part of everyday life. Hence, social media data provides a rich source for understanding various sociographical aspects of language use, including expressions of sentiment. However, the language variations among different demographics in social media are not yet fully explored. This is a vital gap in improving multilingual sentiment analysis (MSA) models. While the field of MSA has seen considerable advancements, most research focuses on generic (and often American-centric) data extracted from online sources that can be less representative of global societal nuances, particularly those dependent on demographic factors, such as gender and age. The vocabulary, linguistic structure, emoticons, and even the use of hashtags can differ significantly between demographics, even within the same language. For instance, younger speakers may use slang or more acronyms, while older generations might be more formal or use less common expressions of sentiment such as the greater use of positive words with negative sentiment. Gender also plays a role in language use, with studies showing significant differences in the frequency of certain emotive or sensational terms between male and female English speakers (Pennebaker, 2011). We hypothesize that there are similar gender-based language variations across languages, such as different emoticon preferences or use of positive/negative polarizing words. The exploration of such demographic language variations in social media data can significantly enrich and improve sentiment analysis models across languages. This paper focuses on exploiting gender differences in sentiment language for three languages: English, Spanish, and Russian. Additionally, we explore cross-cultural differences in emoticon and hashtag use as these elements are often underutilized by existing MSA models. We extract large-scale Twitter datasets in these languages and apply unsupervised techniques to identify gender-specific language patterns. We then train models to leverage these differences for polarity and subjectivity classification. Our hypothesis is that by incorporating these demographic nuances, MSA models can better capture sentiments, particularly in previously understudied languages, cultures, or subgroups within a language. Our experiments show statistically significant relative F-measure improvements for both polarity and subjectivity classification by considering gender in MSA. For example, English sees a 2.5% and 5% relative improvement for polarity and subjectivity respectively, while Russian improves by 1.5% and 1% for polarity and subjectivity, and Spanish improves by 2% and 0.5% for the same tasks.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on "Machine Learning for Metrical Analysis of English Poetry": Poetry, an art form that has flourished for centuries, often employs rhythmic patterns to structure its lines, and meter is one of the key tools used to create this structure. A particular meter, such as iambic pentameter or trochaic octameter, defines the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line, thereby creating a rhythm that makes the poetry more enjoyable and understandable. In English poetry, there are a few dozen commonly used traditional meters, each with its own character and expressive potential. However, few poems strictly adhere to these standard meters, introducing meter variations, contractions, and other deviations to suit the poet's intent. The problem of automatically identifying these patterns—known in poetics as "scansion"—has recently drawn attention among natural language processing researchers, in part because of its similarity to earlier challenges such as sentence segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition. In this paper, we present an exploration into the metrical analysis of English poetry using machine learning. We introduce a task and build models that aim to automatically identify the underlying rhythmical patterns in poetry, drawing on recent developments in both natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. Despite the existence of established poems that fit well into these traditional meters, we find the task to be difficult due to the assumed departures from 'ideal' forms. Variations in meter—which could be substantial across even within a single poem—challenge us to learn more flexible models or carefully design our features to capture meaningful patterns. The task is perhaps most simply understood as predicting stressed and unstressed syllables in line of poetry, but doing so in a way that generalizes well and avoids overly simplistic or 'informative' patterns is non-trivial. Our approach begins with a thorough review of the existing annotated corpus that we utilize for this task and the textual preprocessing we undertake. This corpus has been specifically curated for studies on poetic meter and includes a wide range of English poetry, both canonical and less widely studied. The variety within this corpus allows us to stress test our models against different styles, time periods, and poets, which are all important factors in the complexity of English metre. Following a detailed description of the data and preprocessing, we discuss several NLP techniques that we use to extract features from the poetry.
