The earliest automated systems incorporated semantic considerations using thesauri, and the various forms of entity extraction, including named-entity recognition, continue to be important components of advanced IR systems (Voorhees, 2013). However, until very recently, most research in the area focused on "shallow" semantics that could be computed without constructing language models or using external sources of knowledge. Two significant recent developments have set the stage for this study: the growth of large-scale collaborative knowledge bases (such as Wikipedia and Wiktionary) that are easily accessible for computational use, and recent advances in natural language processing and machine learning that allow more sophisticated analysis of semantic relationships. Despite their potential to improve IR, among semantic resources, Wikipedia and Wiktionary have advantages over WordNet - the most commonly used lexical database in IR - because of their larger size, ease of access, and greater coverage of contemporary language (Rogers et al., 2008; Kampas et al., 2008). However, their possible use in IR is less understood compared to WordNet or even other resources such as Forth (Mihalcea & Tarau, 2004). The different properties of the knowledge structures within Wikipedia and Wiktionary, while adding to their benefits in some respects, also pose challenges for their use in IR (Auer et al., 2007; Wellner et al., 2010). Because query terms are significantly limited in summarizing the user's information need, incorporating more semantic contexts from both user session history and the document collection itself has been explored to improve system effectiveness through semantic expansion (Xing et al., 2002; Yilmaz & Turksen, 2006). One particular approach that leverages lexical semantic knowledge to do this is to compute the semantic relatedness of terms - in this case, query terms, document terms, and terms from the knowledge base - and then to use those relatedness scores to inform IR decisions such as candidate term expansion, document selection and ranking, and topic analysis (Magdy, 2010; Feng & Huang, 2011). Computing semantic relatedness between terms in this way has several proposed methods, but it can be broadly categorized into two main approaches: those employing external knowledge bases like WordNet (Hirst & Edwin, 2001; Evert, 2005), and those that rely on the distributional co-occurrence of terms in text. The latter, often inherently topic-dependent but robust with large volumes of text (Turney & Pantel, 2010), can be seen as more grounded in corpus data than knowledge bases like WordNet or those that use semantic triples but any deeper semantic analysis might already conflate the term itself with its context (Guthrie et al., 2006

Anaphora resolution is the task of resolving pronominal (e.g. pronouns or coordinating conjunctions) or nominal (e.g. definite noun phrases) references to their antecedents in natural language text. It is particularly challenging because of various linguistic phenomena such as bridging (where mention–antecedent pairs are separated by another mention), ellipsis, and paraphrasing. One promising strategy for improving the performance of anaphora resolution systems ( Gunther and his students (2006)) (Chieu and Ng (2002)) (Carreras and Marquez (2005)) is to identify and prune non-anaphoric (i.e., non-referential) mentions before performing coreference resolution. Determining anaphors and non-anaphors accurately improves performance in part because coreference systems have been shown to perform poorly when among the candidates for resolution there are many non-anaphoric mentions (Ponzetto and Strube (2006)). However, this leads to a problem known as identifying anaphoricity. The challenging nature of this task is highlighted in the following examples. Example 1: "The Beatles were great. They were also called The Fab Four." In this example both mentions of 'The Beatles' are coreferential, but it would be quite challenging to identify both mentions accurately. Example 2: "President Bush spoke to reporters at the White House while the Vice President watched. President Bush gave a detailed statement at the conference." Here it is also plausible that the second mention of 'President Bush' could refer to 'the Vice President'. Sample (2) is an example of bridging where 'President Bush' can in principle be either an anaphor pointing to 'President Bush' or a non-anaphor and "the Vice President" is the likely antecedent. Identifying candidates as anaphoric or non-anaphoric requires detailed and often subtle modeling of context and discourse structure (Erk et al. (2009)). Traditional approaches to this problem have used a variety of techniques. 1.   Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging  : For example, Cooke et al. (2007) proposed using part-of-speech features to discriminatively classify entities according to their dependency structure. This is an attempt to determine the likelihood of a mention being an anaphor based on its syntactic structure. 2.   Machine Learning  : Huang, et al. (2006) trained a machine learning classifier on a large corpus of English to identify anaphors and non-anaphors. The classifier uses features like the type of word, the syntactic position, and co-occurrence with certain words and phrases. 3.   Rule-based systems  : Scheffler et al. (2006) and other early work on coreference focused on manually coding rules to classify entities based on their referring properties or discourse environments.

Social interactions on digital platforms have evolved significantly over the years, becoming an integral part of our social fabric. Online discussions today span nearly every topic imaginable, from casual conversations about hobbies to deep, informed debates on the most pressing current events. These discussions are often characterized by their indispensable role in the development and dissemination of knowledge, as well as their capacity to foster a wide spectrum of social behaviors, both positive and negative. One of the most significant challenges facing these platforms is the prevalence of harmful and undesirable behavior, such as harassment, personal attacks, and other forms of antisocial conduct. These behaviors not only disrupt individual user experience but can also undermine the societal value of knowledge-sharing and community building that online platforms aim to facilitate. Previous research has primarily focused on detecting these undesirable behaviors after they have occurred, often relying on post-mortem analysis to identify patterns or signals that could have flagged the issue earlier. While this retrospective approach can inform design and policy changes that might mitigate future instances of antisocial behavior, it is ultimately a reactive strategy. This paper proposes an alternative, proactive approach: detecting early signs of conversational failure—what we call "Conversations Gone Awry"—from the very beginning of a discussion. The term "early" here is used intuitively but tightly defined as this research operates on the premise that problematic behavior often reveals early indicators that could have been identified with the appropriate models and data analysis. Our focus on 'early' signs is driven by the observation that at the start of a conversation, the dynamics are more predictable and the stakes are lower, offering an opportunity for intervention that might prevent or mitigate harmful outcomes. To explore this concept, we introduce a novel task: Predicting whether a conversation initiated by a question or another type of starter, will eventually result in antipathic discourse that might need moderation. This doesn't imply determining the content of the conversation from the start but rather identifies factors indicative of a higher likelihood of the conversation veering into problematic territory. Our framework for addressing this task is grounded in pragmatics—a branch of linguistics that studies meaning in communication—and leverages insights from sociolinguistics to understand conversational comportment. Specifically, we focus on capturing certain pragmatic devices or strategies that individuals use to start a conversation, as these can set the tone for how the discussion unfolds.

Training machine translation (MT) systems using minimum error rate training (MERT) requires an evaluation metric that accurately reflects human perception; however, collecting human judgment data for each candidate generated during MERT is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. To address this, we developed a novel metric that reuses human input into a database without the need for further manual judgment at tuning time. Referred to as Reused-Yielded Predictor (RYPT), this metric adapts the Reused-Yielded Score (RYS) of Schwenk et al. (2012) by incorporating human judgment data extracted from an initial human evaluation. This allows MERT to search for MT parameter settings that maximize the human-based metric efficiently. Our investigation into the feasibility of MERT using RYPT reveals several intriguing implications. 1. Diversity and Redundancy in MERT Candidates: During MERT, the system converges on a particular set of parameter settings that yield the best automatic scores on the tuning set. However, exploration of this parameter space can be highly redundant—candidates are sometimes extremely similar, differing only in minor ways. This redundancy can be strategically used in various applications such as greedy ranking, MERT for greedy decoding, or even in data or system adaptation. Our analysis provides a quantitative overview of the diversity within the candidate set generated during MERT, highlighting that different training data or heuristic initializations can lead to varying levels of redundancy. 2. Predictive Power of RYPT: We evaluate the predictive power of RYPT by comparing it with the standard metric used in MERT, BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). Extensive experiments on different language pairs and MT systems show that RYPT is consistently a stronger predictor of translation quality as assessed by human evaluators. These results suggest that by leveraging real human evaluation, it is possible to develop better MT systems through more informed tuning. 3. Adapting Human Judgments for Machine Learning: The foundation of RYPT is the reuse of human input in the form of confidence scores, which are matched against candidate translations. This approach requires a human to allocate uncertainty or confidence explicitly for translation pairs presented during the candidate set creation phase. Our study sheds light on the collection process of human judgments and their effectiveness in large-scale MT tuning. 4. Scalability Considerations: Key to making RYPT feasible is the efficient use of human input. By reusing judgments over and over, we reduce the need for zero-shot human annotations at the tuning step.

Training neural networks with large amounts of labeled data has clearly seen successful applications in many domains, including natural language processing (NLP; Cooijmans et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2018), computer vision (CV; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015), and speech processing (Deng and Yu, 2014). However, training large neural networks typically requires a large amount of labeled data and significant computational resources. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), in particular, have been shown to be very powerful in NLP tasks (Sutskever, 2011; Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017), but even for moderately-sized problems, training RNNs can be computationally expensive. For such reasons, making the process of training RNNs more efficient has been a topic of active research (Jozefowicz et al., 2016; Pascanu et al., 2013; Whitney et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2016). Different approaches have been proposed that try to reduce this overhead, including model pruning (LeCun et al., 1989), projected gradient descent (Martens, 2010; Raiko et al., 2012), low-rank approximations (Le Roux and Bengio, 2008; Le et al., 2013), A  sparsity optimization (Bach et al., 2017), and more recently, reformulating the optimization problem and directly training sparse models with early stopping and scheduled pruning (Xue et al., 2019). On top of improving computational efficiency, pruning models also has the additional benefit of improving the generalization of the models (Han et al., 2015; Li et al., 2017; Bhojanapalli et al., 2018). In this paper, we focus on the next step in model compression and efficient training for Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems. With large-scale parallel datasets becoming available, NMT models can now be trained on more data than before. Due to the complex non-linear relationships between the input and output sequences in NMT, training large models is thought to be beneficial (Sennrich et al., 2015; Bapna et al., 2018). However, as mentioned in the previous paragraph, training such large models can be computationally expensive, and translating inherently requires a certain latency. Model sparsification is one key technique to trade off model size and latency. Ideally, however, such a compressed model should not only be small but also perform as well as a full model. In the practical setting where large neural network models are trained, many optimization techniques have been proposed that use intermediate outputs of the model, such as gradients (Zoph and Le, 2016), activations (Lillicrap et al., 2016), and trust regions (Hestness et al., 2016).

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental medium of contemporary communication, reflecting social contexts, personal attitudes, and relationships (Boyd and Ellison, 2007). Consequently, social media data has also become a popular choice for linguistic research, including the study of vulgar language (Beretta, 2014; Shapiro et al., 2017). This trend is motivated by the accessibility and the vastness of social media data (Mislove et al., 2012), as well as by the opportunity to investigate language use in a “natural”, relatively context-free setting that can still provide fine-grained insights due to the knowledge of users’ socio-demographic traits. However, while recent research has reported analyses of the distributions and diachronic features of vulgar words in social media (Beretta, 2014; Gillespie, 2018; Lewandowski et al., 2019), the multifunctionality of vulgar expressions remains relatively ill-understood. This multifunctionality is an appealing and also a challenging aspect of vulgar language study: the same words can be used in various ways and in different contexts, transmitting contradictory or complementary messages. For example, a vulgar expression might be used to express aggression or to signal group identity or intimacy. It may be intended to offend or to create a certain mood. In certain situations, using vulgar words may be an act of transgression, while in others, its function might be to emphasize or to underline a statement. This extent of variability in meaning is distinct from formal language, where the significance is determined by the syntactic structure, semantics, phonology, or pragmatics, as well as by the syntagmatic context (Hymes, 1964). While vulgar words certainly inherit some socio-linguistic characteristics from the colloquial and the informal language they belong to, they also have a unique nature because of their restricted and loaded nature (Enright, 1992). More specifically, together with slang and swearing, they form a base for casual language that is used to ease informal communication or to explicitly convey certain attitudes (Agha, 1998; Fromkin et al., 2000). These expressions are especially prominent on social media, where informal communication is dominant and where vulnerabilities that often lead to offensive or vulgar language use are also often present (Király et al., 2016; Wallace et al., 2017). Identifying the context and the role of vulgar language could have practical implications for Natural Language Understanding (NLU) in the social media domain. For example, applications such as chatbots or content moderation tools (which aim to detect hate speech, profanity, or other forms of harmful language) would benefit from algorithms that can infer the intentions of vulgar expressions, rather than simply detecting them as forbidden or inappropriate content.

Training neural networks with large amounts of data has been shown to produce state-of-the-art performance on many natural language processing tasks. However, training neural networks that learn to perform tasks such as machine translation, which require processing very large natural language inputs (e.g. long sentences), is challenging due to severe computational and computational memory constraints. Current research efforts exploit strategies of phrase-based translation which uses sub-word length translation units and manage to make use of the increased training data access by means of a shortlist of pre-computed phrase translation equivalents. In this paper, we present an alternative approach based on continuous space representation of words and phrases, and jointly learn their probabilistic representation in a latent space with knowledge of translatable word units, using a multilayer neural network architecture. After training, we derive a dynamic programming alignment algorithm to compute translations based on these learned continuous representations of source and target language translations, as described by the latent space model. We present experimental results on both English-French and English-German translation benchmarks using standard phrase-based and NIST test sets which show significant improvements in translation quality compared with state-of-the-art phrase-based translation models. We also study extensions of our basic approach including the use of n-grams in the proposed model and the application of decoding strategies beyond greedy search or beam search. Finally, we demonstrate that our model is able to train with large amounts of data and is applicable even for training data significantly larger than has previously been possible for neural network based approaches to machine translation. Continuous Space Translation Models with Neural Networks The main goal of the paper is to show that the use of continuous space for representing translation units (e.g., phrases or sentences) allows for more effective generalization, especially in situations where the large amount of available training data can be exploited to ensure high quality generalizations, and to propose neural network architectures and learning methods that can learn such models. The motivation for continuous space models comes from the inconsistent nature of discrete representations for contextualized and semantically relevant linguistic units. This inconsistency can be understood in two ways: first, recurring phrases or idiomatic expressions may vary in their surface form (e.g., matched "to be able to" versus "can"); second, translations may couple different surface forms in complementary ways that are not captured by simple co-occurrence statistics (e.g., "policy decision" translating to "décision politique").

Relation Extraction (RE), which involves identifying semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text (such as "inventor discovered device"), is a fundamental task in Knowledge Graph (KG) construction. Distantly-Supervised Relation Extraction (DS-RE), an approach that relies on distant supervision from corpora such as Wikipedia and Freebase, has been a compelling method for tackling the scarcity of labeled data. This approach has shown promising results and has been applied to numerous tasks, including the extraction of spatial and temporal relations (Fader et al., 2011), and influential relations (Asri et al., 2015). However, the major challenge in DS-RE is noise, primarily arising from incorrect inference of relationships. Previous research has tackled this problem by designing various models that utilize attention mechanisms in order to selectively focus on those parts of the text most relevant for the task at hand. Conventional attention mechanisms, however, are generally 1-dimensional, that is, they project individual components of the input into a vector space, and compute attention weights between them based on how well their projections align. While such models have been effective in many sequence modeling tasks, such as Natural Language Inference (Conneau et al., 2017), Machine Translation (Luong et al., 2015), and Question Answering (Yao et al., 2014), the sequential nature of 1-D attention may limit their capability in capturing the multi-level hierarchical and structured nature of linguistic context, particularly in relation extraction tasks. In recent years, there has been a surge in the studies focusing on multi-level attention models, where, for example, an attention model can attend over the outputs of another attention model (Vaswani et al., 2017). However, these models often still operate in a sequential manner, adhering to the 1-D nature that may not fully exploit the benefits offered by structured attention. Furthermore, these studies primarily focus on tasks such as machine translation or sentiment analysis, where the input structure is essentially a single sequence, and the question of attending across multiple layers or selecting among different instances (in multi-instance learning) is not presented as a significant challenge. In this paper, we present a novel approach to leveraging structured 2D self-attention for DS-RE. Specifically, we propose a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework that extends beyond standard 1D self-attention models, by introducing structured 2D attention at both the word-level and sentence-level. Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Bridging Languages through Images with Deep Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis. 1 Learning cross-lingual embedding spaces has been a centerpiece activity in natural language processing research aimed at various tasks, including machine translation (MT) (Artetxe et al., 2017), cross-lingual questions answering (Xie and Sun, 2017), and multilingual text classification (Pagliardini et al., 2015). In recent years, there has been significant progress toward learning joint embedding spaces using data extracted from parallel corpora (Chen et al., 2017; Artetxe et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017), dictionaries (Cellsabasi et al., 2017), and even unsupervised semantic lexicons derived from weighted graph kernels (Gillick et al., 2014). These approaches have shown stellar results and serve as the foundation for a plethora of cross-lingual tasks. However, parallel corpora are rare in lesser-resourced languages and are not readily available for many potential language pairs. As a result, achieving robust cross-lingual representation or even mapping has proven challenging For languages that are under-resourced and do not have extensive parallel corpora. Recent studies have explored the use of extra-linguistic information to bridge the gap between sparse parallel data and large scale learning of cross-lingual embeddings (Guo et al., 2018; Artetxe et al., 2018). In (Artetxe et al., 2018), the authors propose to use image captions to learn cross-lingual representation, and they achieve state-of-the-art results over a wide range of languages. However, their approach uses only a small subset of image captions that have been manually translated or extracted from textual descriptions (e.g., Flickr’s photo tags). As a result, scalability of their approach may be limited by a dependence on the availability of matched image descriptions across the languages of interest. This paper proposes another approach to couple cross-lingual embedding spaces while being less dependent on explicitly available parallel corpora or image descriptions. Our idea is to use shared images to condition the learning of bilingual embeddings by leveraging advanced techniques from canonical correlation analysis (CCA) in a deep learning context. Canonical correlation analysis aims at finding linear projections of two variables that are maximally correlated, conditioned on a potentially informative third variable. However, as most NLP-related tasks are inherently non-linear, we turn to deep non-linear extensions of CCA and propose a scalable and effective model dubbed Deep Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (DPCCA). At the heart of our DPCCA model lies a composition of two autoencoders that learn to map tokens from two typologically or resource-rich languages into a shared latent space.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on "Building Chinese Discourse Corpus with Connective-driven Dependency Tree Structure": The analysis of discourse is an important aspect of Natural Language Processing (NLP), with comprehensive understanding of discourse structure leading various downstream NLP tasks, including discourse parsing, summarization, question answering, and text simplification. For many languages, corpora annotated with discourse structures have significantly advanced the development and evaluation of various NLP models. For example, the Penn Discourse Treebank (Mi and Palmer, 2004) and the Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) extracted from it (Pitler, 2003;Pitler, 2013) represent the foundations of much current research in discourse analysis, especially for English. However, similar developments in other languages, including Chinese, have been limited. This paper aims to contribute to the development of a comprehensive corpus for Chinese discourse analysis. We present a novel representation scheme called the Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT), which takes into account both syntactic dependency and rhetorical structure. This scheme, partly inspired by the RST framework, uses connectives to represent the discourse structure and hierarchical relations among elementary discourse units. Drawing on the dependency theory (Weinreich, 1966;Mann and Thompson, 1987;Huddleston and Pullum, 2002), we assumed that the nucleus of each discourse unit can be determined with reference to dependency relations. This mixture allows us to align syntactic analysis with discourse theory, making our proposed tree structure easily interpretable and useful for both discourse and syntactic tasks. We manually annotated a Chinese Discourse Treebank (CDTB) of 500 documents under the proposed CDT representation, and conducted preliminary evaluation. Results from this evaluation highlight the feasibility and potential usefulness of our corpus in supporting research on various aspects of Chinese discourse analysis. We provide detailed description of the annotation scheme, highlight some insights obtained from the corpus, and discuss the issues discovered or recurring in the process of manual annotation. As discourse research relies heavily on corpus development, particularly for a language like Chinese where research is still in its early stage, this corpus can serve as a useful resource for confronting various challenges in Chinese discourse understanding. The first section of the paper introduces the concept of Discourse Tree Annotation and its importance for NLP. We then review existing annotated discourse corpora, in particular for English and Chinese, pointing out the gaps and requirements for a more robust Chinese discourse corpus. In the next section, we thoroughly describe our proposed Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT) scheme.

Training embeddings using neural language models (LMs) or unsupervised methods such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) has become a standard way to represent words or other textual elements as vectors, leading to many downstream applications in questions such as semantic role labeling (Socher et al., 2013), machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014), text classification (Kim, 2014), and many others. For these applications to be successful, it is important that the embeddings learned have certain properties, such as capturing semantic similarity and word analogy relationships. Embeddings have traditionally been evaluated through a combination of intrinsic tests (which measure their quality by their ability to capture linguistic relationships among semantic entities, without relying on labeled data from a specific task) and extrinsic tests (which measure their usefulness through their performance on specific NLP tasks such as word analogy, sentiment analysis, or language modeling). Intrinsic evaluations evaluate whether embeddings capture the underlying structure of natural language, which is necessary for useful general-purpose representations. They usually fall into two categories: point-based or subspace-based. Point-based tests, such as cosine similarity, evaluate the similarity between points (words) in their representation. These tests are often shallow measures of linguistic relationships and assumed properties of the embedding space. Subspace-based tests, on the other hand, evaluate properties of the embedding space itself, often by identifying certain subspaces or their interactions. However, existing subspace-based evaluations for word embeddings are lacking in several aspects: - There is no unified framework in which various intrinsic tests for word embeddings can coexist. - The choice of tests and their relative importance is usually heuristic. - Most subspace-based tests are designed to capture a specific relationship or structure that may not be fundamental or generalizable across NLP tasks. This work aims to address these issues by introducing a new methodology for intrinsic evaluation of word representations that emphasizes the identification, evaluation, and unification of fundamental foundations or criteria that word embedding representations should satisfy. We explicitly define four fundamental criteria derived from the characteristics of natural language that pose significant challenges to NLP systems: 1.   Analogy  : Words with related meanings should be nearby in the embedding space. 2.   Synonymy  : Words with the same meaning should map to overlapping or nearby locations in the embedding space. 3.   Antonymy  : Words with opposite meanings should be far apart in the embedding space. 4.   Contextual Mutual Exclusivity  : Words which almost never co-occur should have non-overlapping or orthogonal representations in the embedding space.

Regular Expression Guided Entity Mention Mining from Noisy Web Data Entity detection is an essential step in various natural language processing (NLP) and information extraction (IE) tasks. It involves finding mentions of named entities within unstructured text. Named entities can be broadly categorized into several types, such as persons, locations, organizations, dates, times, numbers, email addresses, percentages, and so on. The diversity of these entity types and the ways they are represented in web documents make entity detection a challenging task. Regular expressions (REs) are powerful tools for pattern matching and can be used for identifying specific entity types based on their string representation. For example, an RE for dates could be used to identify patterns like '2021-09-20', MM/DD/YYYY' or 'Monday, 14 September 2021'. However, due to the noisiness of web data and the complexity of capturing all possible valid patterns, it is impossible to have REs that achieve perfect precision and recall for entity identification. This paper proposes an integrated framework that combines the expressive power of REs, the capacity of deep learning to learn from large data, and the judgment of human experts to guide the entity identification process from noisy web data. Our framework utilizes a two-stage process. The first stage is based on regular expressions. Candidate entity mentions are first identified using predefined REs. These REs are designed to capture common patterns associated with particular types of entities. For instance, a set of REs might be used to identify dates, times, email addresses, or course numbers within web documents. These REs are applied over a large corpus, allowing us to collect weak labels for potential entity mentions—a process often called 'dataset bootstrapping'. The second stage leverages deep learning and fine-tuning. First, a neural network model is trained on the weakly labeled data from the first stage. The model learns contextual features and patterns that help identify mentions that are likely to be true entities. However, the accuracy of this initial model may be limited due to the noise and variety in the training data. The third and final stage employs a human-in-the-loop approach to refine the outputs. A small set of web documents is presented to a human expert for manual annotation. This fine-grained labeled data serves as a guide for fine-tuning the pre-trained model. This fine-tuning step is crucial for improving the model's accuracy on specific and challenging cases, particularly those where REs alone might struggle.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems are known for their successful applications to real-world translation tasks. To translate from a source language (SL) to a target language (TL), they typically rely on a set of statistical models, and a decoding algorithm that combines these models to generate a TL translation. A particular and important aspect of this process is the decoding strategy, questions such as "What is the order of constructing the hypotheses?" and "How do we take advantage of the SL and TL sentences jointly?" (Charniak, 1997). The word order (or direction of hypotheses construction) has been mainly an object of theoretical and experimental interest in the task of language modeling (Brown et al, 1992;Tillmann, 2000). Recently, we observed that similar questions arise in the context of machine translation (Sundermeyer et al., 2010), but from a different perspective: the "direction" of translation. For instance, translating English to French can be achieved by either constructing hypotheses from left to right, following the order of the English source sentence, or from right to left, following the resulting French sentence. In fact, the possible combinations of direction between the decoding steps and the actual or hypothesized translation string are more complex, so a more general question would be: what is the optimal strategy for constructing the hypothesis in order to maximize the final translation quality? The focus on this problem benefits from previous work in the directions of language modeling and even within machine translation, where papers on training and decoding techniques have covered some related issues (e.g., (Collins, 2004;Bangalore and Joshi, 2006)). However, these studies typically did not consider the direct benefits and drawbacks of left-to-right and right-to-left decoding strategies when applied to full machine translation tasks. Our work is the first large-scale investigation that systematically evaluates the influence of the direction of decoding (left-to-right, right-to-left, or bidirectional) in phrase-based SMT systems measured by BLEU scores. We also conduct an analysis to identify factors that may favor one decoding direction over another for different language pairs, and we introduce a novel bidirectional decoding strategy that combines the strengths and compensates for the weaknesses of previous methods. This strategy improves translation quality consistently on a diverse set of language pairs originating from 272 unique language directions. Specifically, we show that for most language pairs and across multiple benchmarks, the bidirectional decoding strategy outperforms both the left-to-right and right-to-left decoding strategies.

To improve event extraction, we need systems that can tolerate the absence of clearly identifiable event keywords, and which can intelligently "zoom in" on relevant context. In this work, we present a hierarchical or layered event extraction system that aims to fill this gap. We questions how this kind of hierarchical processing could be possible and what kind of evidence would support this type of "peeling back" strategy. Consider this example of a very generic event with no noteworthy event keywords (e.g., "pass", "attend", "have"). While verbs like "pass" and "attend" do not carry any inherent action properties in isolation, they frequently denote events in appropriate verbal contexts. As we peel off the layers from generic verbs, we find that their role filling is often determined by semantic features beyond the verb itself. For example, in the sentence "The doctor passed the patient to a specialist", the doctor is filling the agent role, and the patient is filling the theme/patient role. The event here, "pass", in the context of a "medical scenario" (secondary context layer), suggests a possible interpretation of "refer" or "transfer", both or which infer additional implicit event roles. Our main idea is that such contextual inference can be automated through a layered architecture that progressively accumulates relevant knowledge. We propose a multilayered approach, while the system initially benefits from evidence of the entire document’s genre and its general topical structure to provide plausible scenarios for event role filling, gradually "zooming in" on specific syntactic and semantic features for more specific role filling decisions. Our system architecture is presented in Figure XX. The architecture comprises of four key components that operate in parallel and are represented as a sequence here for clarity: 1.   Document Genre Classifier  : This component aims to recognize the document type or domain (e.g., medicine, law, finance). It's crucial for understanding the types of events one may expect within the document. For instance, a legal document is more likely to contain a "hearing" event, whereas a medical document would be more likely to contain a "consultation". 2.   Sentence Event Classifier  : This layer examines individual sentences to determine if they contain an event. It relies on both generic (e.g., action verbs like "give", "receive") and domain-specific features for detecting event-like sentences. 3.   Event Role Filler Detector  : At this layer, we focus specifically on detecting zero or one role filler (e.g., agent, theme, patient, location) per event.

Language acquisition is traditionally understood as the process of learning a system of symbols to convey meaning, where these symbols include both words (the lexicon) and sounds (phonetics). Understanding this process is crucial for both theoretical linguistics and for designing various tools that can assist language learning, including pedagogical materials or artificial language interfaces (e.g., language learning apps or voice questions). Generally speaking, the process of language acquisition has been approached as two separate tasks: "lexical acquisition" and "phonetic acquisition". Lexical acquisition refers to the process of learning word meanings (and their set of possible pronunciations), while phonetic acquisition refers to understanding how words vary in pronunciation (e.g., due to phonological rules or phonetic lazy speech effects) and perhaps even learning the underlying representation of sounds used by the language. However, infants face a more complex task than is often modeled in the computational linguistics literature. They need to develop a coherent view of language where words are well-defined entities that can have varying pronunciation depending on certain linguistic or non-linguistic contexts (e.g., "the" [Di], "the" [D@] when spoken in isolation or in connected speech, respectively). This suggests that acquiring a lexicon and acquiring a phonetic model or system are interrelated processes that infants perform simultaneously. The problem is further complicated by the lack of ground truth: infants do not have access to the "true" lexicon or the "true" phonetic system in the way that a machine learning model might (with, say, annotated training data where orthography maps precisely to phoneme sequences). Instead, infants have to infer both sets of knowledge from the complex, variable speech signals they are exposed to, much of which is child-directed and designed to be simplified, but still reflecting real spoken language variability. While previous work has been conducted on models of language acquisition (e.g., "minimalist" language learners that infer grammars from sentences (Niyogi, 2006; Voorhees and Tieu, 2009)), a focus on the blurred boundaries between lexical and phonetic learning is relatively novel. Such a view is comported with recent evidence from developmental psychology that infants are sensitive to phonetic cues in word learning very early on (e.g., Mani and Plunkett, 2010) and that understanding of phonetic variability is crucial for vocab acquisition (M. B. Smith, 2016). However, formal models of this integrated process are scarce. This work aims to bridge this gap by presenting a computational model and algorithm that could potentially replicate some aspects of early language acquisition, particularly the joint learning of lexical items and a phonetic model from speech input, without explicit word boundaries or phoneme transcriptions.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on unsupervised Chinese word segmentation using Adaptor Grammars: Chinese word segmentation, also known as lexicalization, refers to the process of segmenting Chinese text into word-like units from a string of characters. It is a critical step indispensable for almost all NLP tasks such as information retrieval, machine translation, and questions answering. However, this task isn't straightforward due to the various and complex rules governing words and idioms in Chinese. While character bigram and trigram models can predict word boundaries with impressive accuracy, they struggle with very short segments or complex words that appear infrequently in training data, and would benefit from incorporating deeper knowledge of language rules and phonetics. This is especially true for Mandarin, where word boundaries often span multiple syllables and tone can drastically alter the meaning of a word. Furthermore, traditional supervised approaches to word segmentation, while effective, require annotated training data, which can be both labor-intensive and expensive to obtain, and might not be readily available for less common words or domain-specific texts. The problem of unsupervised word segmentation is challenging, as we aspire to accurately segment words into meaningful units without prior knowledge or labeled training data. This problem is analogous to the task of English word segmentation from child or baby-directed speech. While Forbs and Weinshall (1998) noted that word boundary location in different languages is highly systematic, most models specifically designed for unsupervised word segmentation rely primarily on syntactic markers in the text, often over relying on simple bigram probabilities (Antolak and Dagan, 2005; Cai and Jin, 2013) or character-based measures, such as phonetic density or similarity in visual character cluster (He, 1988; Lin and Sun, 2007). Other approaches model word segmentation using rational approximations or finite state automata (Oflazer, 1992; Zhang and Shuki, 2002), or incorporate heuristic features (Shang, 2004; Krapivsky et al., 2005), yielding promising performance on standard word segmentation benchmarks. However, these approaches have their limitations. Simple models often fail in highly ambiguous scenarios, such as discriminating between changing the tone of a vowel within a word (key words in Mandarin often use tone to indicate different meanings) and identifying word boundaries. More complex models, while often providing better accuracy, can struggle with overfitting when dealing with varied linguistic structures within the Chinese language. Recently, Adaptor Grammars (AG) have emerged as a robust framework for representing and learning non-parametric models of linguistic structure.

Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms reliably on large unstructured text corpora often requires hand-labeled data (Lasko and Rudnicky, 2002). However, deep features such as those learned by neural networks (Collobert et al., 2011;Krizhevsky et al., 2012) are easily affected by brittle features (Cui et al., 2017). Furthermore, while a deep learning model may achieve state-of-the-art performance on the target task with thousands of labeled instances (e.g., for sentiment classification (Kim, 2014)), temporal relation (TR) classification remains error-prone, particularly on more intricate types such as TimeBefore and TimeWithin (Bamman et al., 2014). Sentiment classification has been successful with even dozens of annotated examples (Kim, 2014); in contrast, the best state-of-the-art performance on TR classification still requires thousands of labeled examples (e.g., the TimeBank corpus (Pustejovsky et al., 2003) contains over 12,000 manually annotated sentences). As collecting labeled data for such sophisticated linguistic tasks is expensive and time-consuming, we investigate how to effectively leverage a more limited amount of annotated data to train a TR classifier. Our work focuses on two main contributions: First, we propose a simple, dependency parse based method for classification. Second, we explore the acquisition and use of selective crowdsourced annotations to improve training performance while significantly reducing the annotation burden. 2.1 Deep Temporal Relation Classification (DTRC) While previous work has demonstrated deep learning can in principle be effective for TR classification (Bamman et al., 2014; Smirnova et al., 2014), most existing methods require extensive hand-crafted features that exploit different aspects of linguistic and semantic structures, e.g., dependency parses or structured representations (e.g., events (Bansal et al., 2014)). Instead, we question whether base syntactic foundations can be directly utilized. Dependency parses are abstract representations of sentence structures, but they are straightforward to generate using standard NLP tools and can easily represent a variety of semantic roles and dependency relations. Our new model, DTRC, uses only dependency parses as input. The input to each model is a pair of dependency trees, representing the event and time expressions. Given the complexity of classifying semantic TRs from raw dependency outputs, we use an approach inspired by convolutional networks and attention models. DTRC creates a kernelized representation of the two dependency trees and classifies the relationship based on these representations. Previous work has applied similar techniques successfully in other NLP tasks (Kumar et al., 2015; Dyer et al., 2016). Specifically, for each word in both trees, we compute a matrix representation of any word to word dependents.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models reliably on low-resource languages (i.e. languages with limited parallel data) remains a major challenge. The gap between high-resource NMT models and their low-resource counterparts is widening, as high-performance NMT models typically rely on large training datasets (Koehn and Knowles, 2017). In practical settings, collecting and processing large-scale bilingual texts for hundreds of languages can be prohibitively expensive, prohibiting the widespread use of machine translation technology (Smoilitskiy et al., 2019;Mogadham et al., 2020). Overcoming this challenge is not only an objective in its own right, but also a necessary step in realizing the dream of creating a universal translation system (Tiedemann, 2012). One promising approach is to share linguistic insights among many languages via multilingual pre-training (Zoph et al., 2016;Vaswani et al., 2017;Wieting et al., 2019). However, current multilingual training strategies struggle to capitalize on the limited amount of data available for a particular low-resource language, as their primary goal is global learning rather than adaptation to specific languages. We propose to apply meta-learning to this problem, learning how to adapt quickly to new languages given little initial data. Meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017;Andrychowicz et al., 2016;Hochreiter et al., 2001) is a formalism for learning to learn (optimize) across tasks, implicitly summarizing the commonalities and differences inherent across the tasks. Here, our key insight is that adapting an NMT model to a new language can be framed as a meta-learning task. Given a meta-learner that has "learned to learn how to learn NMT," we should be able to adapt to any new language (task) with a very small initial training set, effectively "memorizing" a few key parameters for that language and leveraging the learning from other languages. If we think of NMT as a task that we are trying to optimize across many languages (tasks), we should leverage a meta-learning framework to compensate for the lack of data on each individual language. We use a model-agnostic meta-learning algorithm for this purpose. The MAML algorithm proposed by Finn et al. (2017) is conceptually simple: for each task, initialize the network with arbitrary parameters, and then for each training sample, take a few gradient steps to update those parameters. This update procedure is carried out frequently (e.g., 5 steps), and across many tasks (different languages). The intuition behind this is that fine-tuning should yield a good starting point across different tasks.

Opinion mining, which extracts fine-grained opinions and sentiment from unstructured text (Pang et al., 2002;Liu, 2012), has been drawing increasing attention due to its wide range of potential applications including product review analytics (Liu et al., 2010), political discourse analysis (Kovacs et al., 2011), and behavioral science and economics research (Das and Choudhury, 2011). Most commercial applications and academic studies of opinion mining are still confined to English, despite the growing demand for systems that can operate in multiple languages (Chen et al., 2013;Pang and Lee, 2004). Cross-lingual opinion mining can be viewed as a task of cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) and has been attempted recently with methods such as machine translation followed by domain-specific post-processing or by exploiting the "universal" properties of opinion terms using purely corpus-based techniques (Trivedi et al., 2014;Rashad et al., 2015). This work presents a cross-lingual framework for fine-grained opinion mining using bitext projection between the English and Brazilian Portuguese languages or any other language for which a running system and aligned resources are available. We exploit parallel data to produce opinion frames in different languages while significantly limiting the need for annotated data for the target language. We show how a novel dependency-based model trained on a substantial corpus of English sentiment-labeled sentences aligns opinion frames in the target language (Portuguese) by exploiting syntactic dependencies and features extracted from parallel English-Brazilian Portuguese translations. The crux of the method is the creation of dependency contexts aligned across languages (Fig. 1). We assume that opinions are expressed through a fixed set of opinion frames: a phrase head connected to an opinion word (e.g., "book  is  recommendable"). We use dependency parse trees to construct these contexts and align them across English and Portuguese. For each side of the aligned pairs in the bitext, we create an opinion extraction model. For the source language (English), we use a standalone system trained on a rich annotated corpus. For the target language (Portuguese), we create a probabilistic model based on the automatically aligned dependency contexts. This is done using a Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) approach that learns from the aligned contexts in the bitext. The strength of our approach lies in its adaptability and potential for extension to any language for which a running system and sufficiently large parallel data are available. Our method requires minimal target-language resources and can be easily adapted to different domains or sub-domains (e.g., product review or movie discussion).

Learning to Link Entities with Knowledge Base Introduction Entity linking (EL) is an important problem in Information Extraction; it is to identify entities in unstructured text and link them to their corresponding entry in a knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia. For instance, in the sentence "Obama attended the meeting", after identifying the token Obama as an entity mention, EL would link it to the entity entry for Barack Obama in the KB. EL can be viewed as a sequence labeling problem where the sequence is the mentions in the text, and each mention is to be labeled with an entity from the KB. However, due to the fact that there are many candidates (usually hundreds or even thousands) for each mention to be linked, EL can also be reasonably regarded as a ranking problem - ranking candidates for each mention from most likely to least likely to match the mention. In semantic search, we can treat the tokens of a mention as a query and send it to the KB. Ideally, the KB should return the most relevant entry which corresponds to this mention. In practice, however, sometimes no such entry exists in the KB, or the correct entry might not be ranked at the top among the returned top k entries. Therefore, the problem of linking an entity or a mention to the KB is tightly connected with this ranking problem. Previous works on learning-based EL typically adopt different classification frameworks for each mention. A mention is labeled with the true link in the KB. The system learns a model which predicts the link based on features derived from the mention itself and other contextual information. This method, however, does not utilize the relationship information among candidates (other possible links for this mention) effectively. It is a known fact that the relevance of candidates to a mention can depend not only on the features of the candidate and mention alone but also on the relationships between different candidates and their contexts (e.g., the surrounding text). Therefore, treating EL as a ranking problem seems more natural and flexible. This paper aims to utilize the relationship information among candidates when linking the measured entity mentions in the test phase to the KB. More specifically, we are interested in learning ranking algorithms for EL. Different from previous works, we do not treat EL as a classification problem but instead treat it as a learning to rank problem.

Training natural language dialog systems to conduct bargaining negotiations is a challenging task. Not only must an agent be able to understand human language; it also needs to be able to compete for the best outcome, while using natural language to communicate its intentions. Most current approaches to negotiation modeling train a single end-to-end model that decides on the system’s response based on its current state and the status of the dialogue. This end-to-end approach has two main disadvantages. First, it makes it difficult to design a negotiation strategy (such as “always propose 20% above the last offer” or “propose 75% of the current midpoint”), because this strategy would need to be learned purely from data, along with the rest of the dialogue. Second, end-to-end training often leads to degenerate solutions, such as repeating the same numerical value over and over (as seen in negotiation models like Li et al., 2016), or “Ping-Pong” behavior where agents take turns proposing the same price indefinitely (as observed in human human negotiations, see Ramchurn et al., 2013). In this paper, we propose a modular approach that decouples strategy from generation in negotiation dialogues. Our approach allows the negotiation strategy to be designed or learned independently of the generation component, so that this strategy can be based on symbols provided by a domain expert, learned using reinforcement learning or heuristic shallow rules. We use a coarse, abstract representation of actions in the form of dialogue acts: e.g., propose(price=50, item=bike). Our dialogue acts can capture high-level strategic decisions such as “propose a higher price,” while avoiding the problems of degeneracy that can arise with unrestricted natural language generation. Our approach consists of three key components: An action selector (Strategy), which chooses the system's next move based on the current state and a predefined strategy; a contextualized generator (Generation), which given an action description produces appropriate natural language to carry out that action; and a dialogue tracker (Dialogue State) that keeps track of ongoing variables such as the current price and goods, as well as the history of the dialogue. The Dialogue State component acts as a buffer between strategy and generation, ensuring that the generator has access to the necessary context but does not need to decide on the strategy. We demonstrate our approach on a challenging setting based on DEALORNODEAL (Fortnow et al., 2019), a negotiation game that requires agents to bargain over single items.

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Comparing Objective and Subjective Measures of Usability in a Human-Robot Dialogue System: Human-robot interaction (HRI) is an emerging field of research that has various applications, including assistive robotics and everyday household tasks. One of the key challenges in HRI is designing a user interface that is intuitive and easy to use for humans. However, measuring and understanding the usability of a system can be inherently subjective and may not always be aligned with users' actual experiences. To better understand how to measure usability and how different aspects of interaction design contribute to it, we need a comprehensive approach that incorporates both subjective and objective measures. In this paper, we present such an approach through the lens of human-robot dialogue systems. We designed a human-robot dialogue system that enables a robot to work collaboratively with a human user to build wooden construction toys. The Dialogue System is based on a state-of-the-art Natural Language Understanding (NLU) and Dialogue Management (DM) architecture, and it allows users to communicate with the robot through natural language commands. After the initial deployment of our system, we conducted a user study involving naïve participants to gather both subjective and objective measures of usability. Subjective measures, such as users' self-reported satisfaction and perceived ease of interaction, are valuable indicators of how users feel about the system. However, they often lack the precision and quantifiable nature of objective measures, such as task completion time, dialogue duration, and error rates. Our approach, based on the PARADISE framework (Walker et al., 1997), aims to combine both types of measures to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of system usability in practice. We conducted extensive user testing under various conditions, including varying levels of system instructions and different interaction speeds. We also analyzed the human-robot dialogue transcripts in detail, capturing various objective metrics such as dialogue length, request for repetition, and users' compliance with system instructions. The design of the study allows us to control for various factors that could influence the interaction quality, including the users' prior experience with the task or the robot. The user-satisfaction questionnaire, filled in by participants following their interaction with the system, provided us with rich and detailed subjective feedback. While subjective measures can be heavily influenced by individual user preferences and expectations, they offer valuable insights into aspects of usability that are more qualitative and holistic.

Understanding and Quantifying Creativity in Lexical Composition Abstract Why do certain combinations of words such as "disadvantageous peace" or "metal to the petal" appeal to our minds as interesting expressions with a sense of creativity, while other phrases such as "quiet teenager" or "geometrical base" not as much? We present statistical explorations to understand the characteristics of lexical compositions that give rise to the perception of being original, interesting, and at times even artistic. We first examine various correlates of perceived creativity based on information theoretic measures and the connotation of words. We then present experiments based on supervised learning that give us further insights on how different aspects of lexical composition collectively contribute to the perceived creativity. Introduction Lexical creativity, often considered the realm of poets, writers, and avid word-players, is a fascinating subject among semanticists, cognitive psychologists, and language professionals. The ability to form novel, impactful, and meaningful word combinations is not only a measure of language mastery but also an indication of cognitive flexibility and artistic literacy. However, the creative potential of lexical combinations, specifically the aspects that make a pair of words or a phrase stand out as creatively novel or simply commonplace, is not well understood or quantified. For instance, consider this pair of words: "metal to the petal". The combination might evoke the sense of a sharp contrast, a metaphorical journey from rigidity to fragility, or even a poetic juxtaposition. Such combinations might be perceived as creative or inventive. On the other hand, phrases like "quiet teenager" are more commonplace and do not perhaps evoke the same intellectual, emotional, or aesthetic response. Our quest begins with questions central to understanding creativity in word pairing, and lexical composition: 1. What linguistic and cognitive factors make certain word combinations stand out as creative or original? 2. Can these factors be quantitatively analyzed or modeled using computational methods? 3. How can we design or enhance systems that generate or recognize creative word combinations? Literature Review The study of creativity in language, including the formation of novel word combinations, is a rich field. However, most research focuses on factors such as figurative language, metaphor, and rhyme, but these elements alone do not fully capture the breadth of creative potential in lexical composition. For example, research on figurative language (Gibbs, 1994) or metaphor (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980) explains how word combinations can have meanings beyond literal interpretation, contributing to creativity.

Training neural networks with large amounts of data has been a fundamental approach achieving state-of-the-art performance in various domains such as natural language processing (NLP). While phrase-based translation (Sproat et al., 2001) has been a dominant technology for machine translation in the past decade, it suffers from the limited reordering capability of lexicalized models. Reordering is necessary due to the non-concatenative nature of languages (Koehn et al., 2003) and it can have a significant impact on translation quality. To address this issue, previous work has proposed context-sensitive reordering models with hand-crafted features (Gilbert et al., 2002; Soroa and Nakov, 2012) to guide the reordering process. However, hand-crafted features may not capture semantic context beyond adjacency in the source sentence and thus fail to capture the deeper semantic relationships between different source phrases. Moreover, these hand-crafted features are known to be sparse and limited, as they rely on human intuition and engineering effort. Recent advances in deep learning have shown that neural models can learn useful features automatically from raw text data and can achieve state-of-the-art or even human parity performance in various NLP tasks (Devlin et al., 2019; Radford et al., 2018). The potential of using neural approaches for reordering has been recognized previously; e.g., the popular model proposed by Klementiev et al. (2012) builds a language model over a fixed-length context window (current phrase pair and one preceding phrase pair). However, the previous model still suffers from insufficient contexts to capture deep semantic understanding of the entire sentence. In this paper, we explore a novel neural approach to reordering in phrase-based translation. Our model is the first that conditions reordering probabilities based on complete sentences (including both the source and previous translation) rather than the current or previous phrase pairs. More specifically, in addition to a single word, each of the current and previous source phrases is represented as a dense vector, allowing the model to integrate rich context for making reordering decisions. This representation naturally incorporates semantic understanding of the entire sentence, overcoming the limitation of context sensitivity in previous models. To accommodate large amounts of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, we propose a variant of a character-level language model, which maps each source word to a dense vector representation regardless of whether it is in the vocabulary or not. To alleviate the data sparsity problem, we use continuous vectors to represent source phrases, making our model applicable to all phrase pairs in the source sentences.

Commonsense Knowledge Base Completion Commonsense knowledge bases present a powerful way to capture the everyday knowledge possessed by humans; these are often manually curated and are useful for various NLP tasks. However, comprehensive and complete commonsense knowledge bases are limited in their range and breadth of knowledge. A particular challenge comes from the need to represent relations between concepts or questions and answers that involve combinations of everyday concepts and attributes. For example, knowing that "Eating at a fine dining restaurant" makes someone “satisfied” requires the ability to combine various independent facts and observed regularities. While commonsense extracted from existing knowledge is indeed a form of knowledge base completion (KBC), most current KBC work focuses on a fixed set of entities with attributes (e.g., Freebase), whereas commonsense knowledge is expressed as unbounded relations (e.g., ConceptNet relationships among semantic concepts). This paper proposes an approach to directly tackle the problem of commonsense knowledge base completion using modern neural network techniques. The central idea is to treat known ConceptNet relationships as a corpus for training a model to score how appropriate or likely a new proposed relation between concepts or sentences is. By leveraging this framework, we aim to extend the range of existing commonsense knowledge, capturing implicit regularities and rules of this domain. One key challenge here is how to effectively represent and score different relationships when the set of concepts involved is unbounded—a significant challenge for traditional KBC techniques. The architecture developed for commonsense KBC leverages neural network models capable of processing arbitrary phrase forms (e.g., entities, questions, and answers). We introduce a bilinear model augmented with learned summarizations of phrases using a simple additive neural network. This architecture is designed to capture the interactions between different elements of the query and the target relations through a model that learns effective representations and their interactions. By evaluating the performance of this model on held-out relations from ConceptNet and tracking its ability to score novel, unseen relations or questions, we aim to gauge how well our method captures measured commonsense patterns and rules. The core contribution of this work is a neural network-based approach to automatically predict or score the "truth" or appropriateness of new relations in a commonsense knowledge base. We present methods for training and evaluating these models on large amounts of commonsense knowledge. To train and evaluate our model for commonsense knowledge base completion, we start with the manually curated ConceptNet 5.5 (Speer and Havasi, 2012).

Relation Extraction with Matrix Factorization and Universal Schemas Many successful applications of natural language processing (NLP) rely on the ability to extract information from text sources. This includes information about people, places, events, and the many-faceted actions they take. For instance, one might wish to build a database of the relationships between scientists and their academic institutions, questions and answers asked on forums, reviews of products and vendors, and so on. In machine learning, this often takes the form of relation extraction, which seeks to determine the relations between two entities expressed in text (e.g. "FERGUSON is a professor at HARVARD"). This information can be used in downstream applications, such as question answering and knowledge graph population. Relation extraction has historically been framed as a problem of assigning a known set of relations to text (or to entity pairs therein). For example, we might be asked to estimate whether a particular sentence tells us that entity [X] has the relation [employed-by] with entity [Y]. This known set of relations is often called the schema, and most existing work in relation extraction presupposes a fixed and predefined schema of these relations. For instance, the popular MUC schemas and the newer NELL (Weischedel, Harris, Patel, & Etzioni, 2004) provided a well-defined set of binary relations (e.g. born-in, employeeof), assumed complete while the system was designed. However, in practice this is often unsatisfactory, as it forces the system to operate on a limited set of relations (e.g., for a population of scientific studies, you'd perhaps also want to extract has-coauthored-with, or has-supervised, etc.). To handle an unlimited set of relations, and automate construction of schemas, the "Open Information Extraction" (OpenIE) paradigm has gained prominence (Etzioni et al., 2008). OpenIE systems aim to extract any statement that expresses a relation or fact (e.g., FERGUSON is a historian at Harvard) using a single surface predicate. This work proposes an extension to OpenIE that addresses several key limitations of existing systems: 1. Improved Precision and Recall: We present WOE, an open IE system that uses a novel self-supervised learning method to significantly improve precision and recall over existing systems like TextRunner. WOE uses heuristic matches between Wikipedia infobox attribute values and corresponding sentences to construct training data, enabling it to perform better than TextRunner. 2. Leveraging Universal Schemas: While OpenIE allows for capturing relation types not pre-specified by the schema, it usually cannot generalize beyond this.

Training and Evaluating Pragmatic Sentiment Classifiers on Microblog Texts: A Comprehensive Analysis Abstract The successful development of sentiment analysis systems relies heavily on the quality of the annotated data used for their training and testing. Microblog texts pose many challenges for sentiment analysis including the prevalence of informal language, the brevity of messages, and the presence of non-standard questions and statements. To analyze the adequacy of annotated data and the impact of the complexity of microblog texts on sentiment classifiers, we propose a comprehensive evaluation framework. We use two strategies for creating annotated datasets: Active Learning for Human Annotation (ALPHA) and Sentiment Annotation with Twitter API (SATA). We then evaluate the performance of a state-of-the-art sentiment analysis system on both the annotated datasets. We also examine the features of the annotated data regarding their quality, coverage, and distribution. This work aims to provide insights into the needs of comprehensive sentiment datasets for microblog texts and to lay the groundwork for improving future sentiment analysis systems. It advances the understanding of the challenges and potential solutions for creating high-quality annotated data, which is crucial for developing practical sentiment analysis systems. 1 Introduction Sentiment analysis deals with automatically determining the emotional or evaluative content of text. A landmark in the field was the creation of the widely used Subjectivity Annotation Schemes (SU) provided by Pang and Lee (2004) with initial annotations coming from The Corpus of Linguistic Analysis of Sentiment (CLAS). In more recent years, the availability of sentiment-labeled data has increased significantly, driven by the extent to which Web technology companies rely on user feedback and sentiment for product evaluation, service enhancement, and targeted advertising. Sentiment analysis is often in practice at the sentence level. One reason for this is the availability and ease of generating annotations at this level over the more daunting task of annotating sentiment toward explicit entities (e.g., "The movie [title] is [adjective]."). Another reason is that many applications can operate at this level (e.g., general product review systems, political polling, etc.). However, the blurred boundaries between sentiment toward a product or service versus a review's author can lead to ambiguity. Sentiment expressed towards an explicit entity or target (e.g., "I found the [product] [adjective].") offers more clarity, but such annotations are less common, though becoming more common (e.g., (Deng et al., 2013;Hu and Liu, 2004;Turney, 2007;Stoyanov et al., 2005;Titov and McDonald, 2008)).

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a vibrant space for expressing and disseminating dialects. However, natural language processing (NLP) tools that can process and understand dialect varieties are scarce. One of the less studied but richly varied dialects is African-American English (AAE). This paper delves into the particular case of AAE on Twitter, aiming to fill this gap in resources and tools for dialectal NLP. Our case study starts with the observation that links between dialectal features and demographic language can be leveraged to identify dialectal language in online text. Given the abundance of data extracted from Twitter, we can approach this problem with a large-scale analysis. By analyzing geographical locations, we assume that a user's location can serve as a proxy for their dialect, and we are specifically interested in language varieties associated with locations that have a predominantly African-American population. This assumption bridges our understanding of in-person language use and language use observed online. To achieve this, we propose a distantly supervised model to identify AAE-like language by its geographical and demographic associations. This approach builds on the existing literature which often implicitly or explicitly uses demographic and geo-located data for language identification (Ghawi et al., 2014;Wei et al., 2015). Distantly supervised models have shown promise in identifying domains or dialects based on different training data distributions (You et al., 2019). We fine-tune existing large language models on the identified AAE-like data to predict the likelihood that given text exhibits AAE characteristics. We evaluate our model by quantifying its performance against human annotation of AAE features, such as phonological, syntactic, and lexico-semantic features. One of the strengths of our approach is the verification that the identified AAE-like language does indeed exhibit well-known characteristics of AAE (Green 2002; Rickford 1999). These linguistic features range from phonetic realizations (e.g., "brotha" for "brother") to syntactic preferences (e.g., the repetition of a question word in a question as in "What it do? What it do?" for "What is it doing?") and lexical items unique or more prevalent in AAE (e.g., "finna" for "fixing to"). However, our investigation does not stop there. We also scrutinize the quality of existing NLP tools when applied to AAE-like text. We find that such tools, originally trained on standard English datasets, perform poorly on AAE-like text, demonstrating the need for dialect-aware models.

Dependency parsing is traditionally composed of two stages: parsing model estimation (e.g. first or higher-order CFG) and parsing; these are two separate problems and are often analyzed and solved separately. Instead, this paper connects the two stages of dependency parsing into one problem, namely the one of maximum-likelihood inference, and show, both analytically and empirically, that a simple randomized greedy algorithm can lead to a very good solution even for complex models. The idea of greedily selecting the best inference sequence (path of choices or decisions) is at the heart of dynamic programming and it is also a key component of more sophisticated optimization techniques like dual decomposition (DE) and Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC) sampling. However, while these techniques optimize an objective function, they are often used for problems that do not naturally lend themselves to just that. While the objective function can be chosen to capture certain weighted sums of dependency structures, the global optimization objective we are interested in is usually complex and includes sums over all possible dependency structures, which quickly makes it intractable. Our work demonstrates that, for very large inference problems, even when higher-order dependencies are taken into consideration, it may often suffice to use a randomized greedy inference algorithm to arrive at a good approximation of the optimal solution. This is a surprising result, especially given the theoretical result from Zhou et al. (2017) who showed that for certain classes of decoding problems the greedy method can actually be exponentially worse than other techniques. Furthermore, we perform the first cross-lingual comparison of first, second, and third-order (and global) features for dependency parsing, which is an important, yet still rather unexplored area. Our contribution can be summarized in three key ideas: 1. Analytical quantification of the "local optima" problem for greedy inference algorithms in the context of first-order parsing (and the implications that this might have on higher-order parsing). 2. Demonstration of the performance of a greedy algorithm in second-order parsing against the state-of-the-art DE algorithm. 3. Evaluation of a greedy algorithm on a wide range of first, second, third-order, and even global feature models across 14 languages. The paper’s contribution should appeal to both theoretical and empirical researchers in natural language processing and machine learning. From a theoretical perspective, our work provides new insights into the role of greed in complex optimization.

Training neural networks with adaptive softmax and incremental softmax for large scale learning Adaptive learning's effectiveness in various classification scenarios is largely accelerated by its ability to learn from less informative instances early in the learning process. Adaptiveness particularly proves beneficial when various subsets of instances need to be considered at different time points or when only a small number of instances need to be considered for questions or decisions.
