Another way of constructing adaptive models is to group the instances based on complexity, frequency or some other criterion and train the respective class models of each group as fractals or independent models. This structure can be seen as a hierarchical softmax, and is indeed a form of adaptive learning in which each class model adapts to the data points in its group. In many NLP tasks involving text classification, having a very large number of classes is not uncommon, making traditional softmax methods impractical due to computational and memory constraints. This paper proposed two strategies to tackle this issue: adaptive softmax and incremental softmax. Adaptive softmax is achieved by assigning different parameter sets to different groups of classes. This allows the model to focus on the most relevant classes during the early stages of training. As it explores fewer parameters initially, it requires less computation and memory, making it more efficient for large scale learning. Incremental softmax on the other hand gradually introduces new classes into the training process as needed, with initial bias towards easier-to-learn classes while the system initially benefits from simpler decisions in learning more complex classes over time. Both methods significantly speed up training by reducing the extent to which the model must rely on large numbers of features for every possible class during the early stages, especially in scenarios where not all classes in the large-scale dataset need to be considered equally from the start, and they are particularly useful when the classes are ranked in terms of ease of learning or real-world importance. To compare the performance and the nature of these different strategies, several tasks were considered including sentiment analysis on IMDB and movie reviews datasets, question type classification on the TREC question set, together with subjectivity detection in the Movie Reviews dataset and Twitter. The performance on each task was compared against traditional softmax models and other adaptive models like structured softmax for comparison. Results generally show that both adaptive softmax methods outperform traditional softmax significantly on large scale datasets, while also demonstrating better training speed and model size.

Learning to recognize quantities from visual scenes is a fundamental ability that underlies many aspects of our perceptual and cognitive capabilities. On the one hand, humans and other animals are capable of estimating numerosity, or the total number of items in a set (e.g. Cantlon et al 2009) and, on the other hand, we are able to engage in comparative judgments such as determining whether the number of items in one group is greater than, less than, or equal to that in another (Cheng and Holyoak 1992). Furthermore, we can set up scales or proportions that allow us to estimate quantities relative to a given reference point (Saenz 2003, Agrillo 2012). A moment’s reflection on the nature of these three tasks - numerical estimation, ordinal comparison, and proportional estimation - shows that among them, numerical estimation can be considered a more 'primitive' or "lower-level" form of quantity processing. After all, if we can estimate exact numbers, we can use that ability to inform our comparative and proportional judgments. However, numerical estimation in itself does not directly allow for proportional reasoning or even straightforward ordinal comparisons (which may require an understanding of what constitutes "same," "more than," or "less than" in a given context). Nonetheless, it is clear from both cognitive and behavioral research that these tasks interact. For instance, humans can typically provide more accurate estimates of quantities when they can compare the quantities against a standard (psychophysical research; [e.g. Stevens 1957; 1975]). Similarly, judgments about proportions often imply judgments about cardinality (how many) or can in practice be informed by them (e.g., understanding the ratio of a large set compared to a small set may help estimate proportions). These insights raise a question that is central to this paper: how are these different aspects of quantity processing related, and can understanding and computing one aspect enhance or improve performance in the others? In particular, the question is whether together these different aspects can be fruitfully modeled as a single, integrated learning process that can generalize across tasks. Human cognition provides evidence for such integration. For example, infants and children (e.g., Mix 1999, 2008) exhibit surprising abilities in proportion estimation that seem advanced over what would be predicted from their abilities in numerical comparison alone. Similarly, research in comparative psychology has demonstrated that animals can perform above chance in ordinal comparisons tasks (Pfungst 1907; Gallistel and Gelman 1996) and more recently in ratio tasks (e.g., Agrillo 2012).

Paraphrases play a crucial role in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. They have been used for various applications, such as text summarization, question answering, machine translation, and natural language understanding (Ragan and Rose, 2010;Das and McCarthy, 2010;Nguyen and Le, 2014;Ruder et al., 2017). A paraphrase lexicon can represent a set of words or phrases that are inter-convertible under paraphrase relations, i.e., presenting very similar meanings despite differing in surface form. Traditionally, paraphrases are manually created by crowd-sourcing, or, more recently, automatically acquired through heuristics based on lexical variations (e.g., inflections or stems). For example, Sentence Compression by Deletion (SCD, Xiao and Lin, 2010) expanded a pre-existing lexicon using an automated method. However, purely heuristic methods limit the range of words they can cover, and do not explicitly enforce semantic equivalence. Thus, creative yet proper paraphrases might be overlooked. In this paper, we propose a data-driven method to expand paraphrase lexicons by exploiting their linguistic generalities or patterns. A key observation that motivates our approach is that paraphrasing symbols (i.e., words or phrases) often exhibit "lexical variation" across their occurrences. Lexical variations include inflectional forms (e.g., "looks", "looking", "look"), derived forms (e.g., "INFLECTS: (inflect, inflected, (but also: 'inflecting') )), hyponyms and hypernyms (e.g., "car" vs. "vehicle"), and even entirely different forms that can't be perceived as likely synonyms without context (e.g., colloquial "kick the bucket" for "to die"). The general idea of our method is to first learn these patterns from the given or initial paraphrase set, and then use these patterns to discover new paraphrases matched by the patterns but not necessarily sharing word identity with the initially given ones. To learn patterns from paraphrases, we use an unsupervised learning approach inspired by distributional semantic methods. These methods are based on the observation that words or phrases that co-occur frequently in the same contexts are likely to be related (Firth, 1957;Harris, 1968;Deerwester et al., 1990;Bengio and Le, 2003;Ruder and Plank, 2018). We generalize this idea to paraphrases, observing that if a certain word/phrase pair appears in paraphrase relations in multiple sentences, then this pattern can be generalized to other word/phrase pairs that similarly co-occur often in the same environments. However, instead of simply counting any co-occurrence, we focus purely on paraphrase relations, examining the patterns of word substitutions that happen across these sentences. Once a paraphrase pattern has been learned, it can be used to make new predictions about paraphrase relations that were not seen in the training data.

Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated training data. However, while such data is available for some languages today, for many languages there is scarcity of annotated data. Probabilistic natural language parsers can be trained with unrealistically low amounts of annotated data, leveraging the indispensable proportion of unannotated, monolingual data available for essentially all languages. A key idea driving this success is the exploitation of cross-lingual generalization, the insight that part-of-speech tags, parse-trees and dependency structures of various languages share fractal patterns independent of linguistic (and scriptal) particularities. This idea keeps coming up in the form of synchronous grammars (Kaplan and Kay, 1994;König, 2006;Kuribayashi et al., 2010;Lin et al., 2011;Bakker et al., 2011;Mosbach et al., 2012;Wiesemann et al., 2013;Kuribayashi et al., 2014;Hajič et al., 2015;Clark et al., 2016), where cross-lingual or even fully unsupervised models are trained to account for common structural and syntactic trends. In this work, we propose to significantly simplify the most basic form of phrasal, synchronous grammar induction, one based on the classic n-gram models over strings and trees (Kaplan and Kay, 1994;König, 2006), to tackle unsupervised parser training as an optimization task. We model translate-able syntactic forms across languages using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) in a probabilistic framework, and leverage the "universal grammar" approximation leading to a novel phrasal synchronous grammar (PSG) parser for which we propose an efficient Gibbs Sampler for parameter inference. Our approach design avoids structured model training typically imposed in previous phrasal synchronous grammar models, where training involves resolving a dependence between the alignment of matched words and syntactic structures. We directly induce hierarchical structure over interlingual couplets or phrase pairs derived from parallel texts, implicitly assuming globally and locally consistent generation of sentences across source and target languages. We motivate our choice of Gibbs sampling as a method of inference for a sparse, approximated probabilistic grammar for efficiency reasons. The compact nature of proposed phrasal models compared to full structure grammars combined with efficient SG algorithms provides an attractive prospect of large-scale, cross-lingual unsupervised parser training and strengthening the predictive capabilities of PSG parsers almost as an afterthought in the form of recoverable hidden representations. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 discusses the generative model and reasoning behind our PSG model, which will be trained using continuous MLE to sum for phrase pairs taken from the parallel data.

Training natural language parsers to fine-tune and specialize for achieving strict evaluation targets can yield improvements. In particular, parsers trained exclusively for supertagging (or for the NER task, which closely relates to the ST task) have achieved marked improvement in accuracy over the usual indispensable training. A particular and important case of this is the SuperSequence part-of-speech (POS) and annotation (ST and NER) corpora compiled by the SuperARV initiative (Strubell et al., 2017). The SuperARV corpora contain detailed annotation and set strict targets. For example, keeps changing as new guidelines emerge. A further example is the POS tags in the SuperARV corpus. Rather than the 38 POS tags in the Penn Treebank (Marcus et al., 1993), the SuperARV uses 113 semantic categories. These tags allow the parser to better model the observed distribution of tags in the training data. Hence, while POS and NER tags can capture semantic distinctions between word meanings (such as "cats" and "fish" both being common nouns, but distinguishing "fish" as food from "fish" as an animal), they do not generally provide structure about how the words or phrases relate to one another For instance, a parser trained on POS and NER tags may well produce S+NP+VP structure for "John has eaten", but it is still the job of the parser to label the head of each syntactic constituent correctly. This is where fine-grained syntactic annotations can serve as an additional source of high-quality labeled data for training syntactic parsers. The most obvious candidate for such fine-grain structure is dependency parsing (Goldberg, 1995;Nivre (1999);Nivre and Hall 2011), which parses the dependencies between head and dependent candidates (e.g., "John" [nsubj] "has eaten" [root]). While dependency parsing has been done in various studies (Kudo and Matsumoto, 2008; McDonald, 2006;Weiss et al., 2015), explicitly using dependency structures for joint language modeling is less explored. This paper contributes to filling this gap by leveraging dependency structures for fine-grained syntactic information in a joint language model. A challenge in using fine-grained syntactic tags for training a language model is scalability. Standard language models usually deal with word/token-level features, such as POS, word embeddings or even word sub-sequences. However, as we introduce more structural information about those words (e.g., dependency labels), the feature space exponentially grows. For example, in parsing 8.5 million words of the English Treebank (Penn Treebank v3.0), there are 1,997 different head-dependency relations specified by PTB's typestring notation (Marcus et al., 1993).

Social media platforms, online marketplaces, and consumer review websites have given rise to an unprecedented amount of user-generated content. These reviews and feedbacks, while valuable for understanding consumer sentiment towards products, pose a significant challenge for the natural language processing (NLP) community due to the complex nature of human language. Sentiment analysis specifically, aims to determine the emotional attitude corresponding to the speaker or writer's affective state and aesthetic evaluation. This affective state may be directed towards "entities" such as a product, service, event, person or organization as fractals or independent word-embeddings and set theoretic notions of extracted context keeps changing as new information streams. Existing works in sentiment analysis on product reviews, however, suffer from two key limitations: Firstly, they often fail to fully capitalize on the hierarchical relationships among product attributes in order to provide a more nuanced understanding of consumer sentiment. Unstructured review corpora in many places do not respect the pre-defined schema making the process of disambiguation and labeling of attribute-related sentiment complex. Secondly, they struggle when dealing with sentences that address multiple attributes or attribute classes simultaneously. For instance, consider the following product review: "This product has a great battery life, but it is also heavy. I love the look or design, but the feel is a bit disappointing". Such a sentence is quite common in product reviews but is not straightforward to handle in the sense that multiple positive and negative sentiments are expressed while the attributes being referenced need to be properly labeled. In this paper, we address the aforementioned limitations by proposing a novel hierarchical learning (HL) sentiment ontology tree (SOT) approach for sentiment analysis on product reviews. Instead of treating each word or sentence as a separate unit, as is often done in conventional sentiment analysis techniques, our proposed approach hierarchically categorizes and learns over product attributes and their associated sentiments in a structured manner that respects the inherent hierarchical and relationship-based nature of attributes. The fundamental idea is to learn a sentiment ontology over product attributes based on structured hierarchical relationships inferred from a predefined generalizable taxonomy of commerce domains and subsequently learn sentiment annotations for reviews by taking advantage of this learned ontology. The proposed hierarchical learning (HL) process explicitly models the complex relationships between product attributes by means of a hierarchical and compositional semantic structure. This permits dealing with the complex and varied expressions of sentiment that are common in product reviews by ensuring that every sentiment evaluation on an attribute is understood within the framework of its hierarchical context.

Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is a fundamental task of Natural Language Processing (NLP) that has been approached using a variety of methods. Two leading state-of-the-art approaches to GEC are machine learning classification and machine translation. The first method relies on machine learning algorithms to identify and correct grammatical errors, typically by training a classifier on annotated data. The second approach uses machine translation technology to translate a sentence with grammatical errors into a corrected form. Both methods have been successful in different contexts and for different types of errors. In this paper, we present a comparative analysis of these two approaches, identifying key strengths and weaknesses and discussing their relative performance. We further propose and evaluate an algorithmic approach that leverages the strengths of both methods, demonstrating significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art. ### Machine Learning Classification in GEC Machine learning (ML) classification is a straightforward method for GEC. At its core, this approach consists of training a classifier on a set of annotated sentences to recognize and correct grammatical errors. Classification-based GEC systems typically predict correction labels (such as "subject-verb agreement" or "missing article") for each word in the input sentence or for the sentence as a whole. These systems have several advantages, including their ability to generalize or even infer corrections not explicitly seen during training. However, there are challenges: -   Data Requirements  : Building effective classifiers usually requires large amounts of annotated data. Where this data is scarce or expensive to obtain, classification-based GEC can be less effective. -   Limited to Training Patterns  : The accuracy and correctness of these systems are directly tied to the patterns and examples they have been trained on. A sentence featuring an error not covered by the training data can go uncorrected. -   Adaptation to Semantic Context  : While some classifiers are trained and fine-tuned to consider contextual cues, they might struggle with complex errors where the correct correction is heavily dependent on the surrounding semantics or discourse. ### Machine Translation in GEC The machine translation (MT) approach to GEC involves translating the input sentence into a corrected version using a language translation model. At first glance, this seems counterintuitive—how can translating into one’s own language help correct grammatical errors? The effectiveness of this method lies in the systematic nature of translation models and their tendency to compensate for grammatical errors in the input. -   Automatic Learning from Parallel Data  : Unlike classification-based methods, MT-based GEC does not require explicit annotation of error types, as it learns robust error correction patterns implicitly through parallel texts.

Social Search is an important area in web search and user profiling. A key challenge in this area is how to build effective profiles for users who have limited interaction with the search system. On one hand, using only user's past interaction with the system (e.g., search history, clicks) to build the profile may limit the system’s ability to personalize search for questions or topics that the user had never handled before (Ehret and Heckerman, 2010;Strand and Croft, 2006). On the other hand, incorporating other sources of information about a user can potentially provide a more comprehensive user profile and address this shortfall (Song et al., 2007). For example, Sushc’s research (Sushc, 2010) uses Web of Trust (WOT) ratings as a measure of trust among web users to perform personalized weighted search but without explicit language modeling techniques or incorporating user's usage history. In recent years, social media has provided an alternative data source for user profiling (Cheng et al., 2020;Hui et al., 2016;Sun et al., 2014). For instance, user-generated data like likes, comments, and shares on a social media platform can provide rich and diverse information about a user's interests and preferences (Holleis and Javadang, 2019;Lu et al., 2017). However, relying only on social annotations also has its limitations. For example, people may create or follow posts for reasons other than their personal interests (e.g., to participate in social conversation or to show support for a cause). Therefore, it is crucial to ensure that we’re accurately interpreting and incorporating social annotations into user profiles. To tackle these problems, we develop models that combine user’s usage data (e.g., searches, clicks) with social annotations (e.g., likes on posts, comments) and external knowledge bases (KBs) into one comprehensive profile, which together better represent a user’s interests. We present two probabilistic latent topic models that learn user profiles from: (i) explicitly user-supplied data (e.g., likes, shares) augmented with implicit KB-based concepts, and (ii) user's search history (if available) along with user's explicitly stated interests (e.g., user bookmarked pages or tagged concepts/persons) and broadly available concepts from KBs. Our first model, SG-LDA (Social + Gaussian Latent Dirichlet Allocation), builds on LDA and incorporates the user’s explicitly marked items (e.g., likes, tagged concepts) and implicitly observed socially relevant concepts inferred from KBs (e.g., co-occurrence with user activity). The second model, KB-LDA, builds from the user’s past search patterns and explicit annotations and supplements these with knowledge concepts often associated with this activity.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models with a large amount of monolingual data has led to significant progress. These models have also been shown to learn phrase and sentence structure through the attention mechanism, demonstrating that they can simulate some of the translation process. However, despite the success of NMT on many languages, the system still exhibits a number of limitations. First, the recurrent neural networks (RNN) used in the encoder and decoder may have trouble retaining "distant" information that may not contribute significantly to the current time step prediction, a known problem with RNN structure (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). Second, NMT models often disregard the word order, word relationships, and structures in the source sentence when creating the representation, although these relationships are crucial for accurate translation in many cases. Third, and related to the second point, semantic ambiguities in source language can be resolved by considering the source language's syntactic structure. However, this requires explicit syntactic analysis which is not always feasible, especially for languages with little or no explicit syntactic parse data. Thus, handling these issues is highly challenging for NMT. To tackle these limitations, various approaches have been proposed. Some studies have attempted to incorporate syntactic knowledge into NMT or even pre-process the source text with tools like dependency parsers (Zhou et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016), though these methods require explicit structures. Others have explored the use of attention models over the source to learn to focus on different parts of the source sentence during decoding (Bahdanau et al., 2015). Although attention models have significantly improved NMT's ability to model long-range dependencies, the distillation of source information is still based on the encoder’s fixed-size hidden state. Another line of research has focused on how to learn better source representations. Some works have used the output of the encoder to influence the next timestep prediction in the decoder, such as through attention over the encoder hidden states (Luong et al., 2015; Gehring et al., 2017). However, these methods do not explicitly couple the source words before they are fed into the decoder. This limitation may be problematic as it does not help address the issue of losing information about long-range dependencies or word relationships. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for improving the source representations in NMT by explicitly capturing word relationships using relation networks, inspired by the work of Rocktäschel et al. (2017) in relation reasoning tasks.

Automatically Constructing a Normalisation Dictionary for Microblogs Microblogging platforms, such as Twitter, have become essential parts of modern social media communication. The texts in such platforms are character-limited, abbreviated, and contain many informal expressions. For instance, in Twitter, the character limit for a single post (tweet) was originally 140 characters, although this was increased to 280 characters in 2017. To compress their messages, users frequently use abbreviations (e.g., "btw" instead of "by the way"), shorten words (e.g., "tomorrow" is often replaced with "tmr"), and apply other types of lexical variations. These varying forms of expression pose significant challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including text analysis, sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and named entity recognition (NER). For instance, NLP systems might struggle when dealing with abbreviations or colloquialisms, as they might not be familiar with these forms. Moreover, some NLP tasks are particularly sensitive to textual variations, as small changes in form can significantly alter the meaning of a word. One common approach to these problems is normalisation: the process of transforming text into a standardized form, which can then be used as an input for various NLP systems. In the context of microblogging data, this includes expanding abbreviations to their full forms, converting slang and colloquial expressions to standard language, and resolving other types of lexical variations. However, existing normalisation approaches, based on complex models like language models and taggers, often struggle to distinguish between correctly spelled unknown words and lexical variants of known words. This can lead to incorrect normalisations and in turn, affect the performance of downstream NLP tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a novel method that can automatically construct a normalisation dictionary for microblogs. Unlike existing methods that are typically inconsistent in handling lexical variations due to their complex architectures, our proposed approach is simple, efficient, and handles variations in a structured manner. This method leverages context information together with string similarity to generate, rank, and select candidate normalisation pairs that populate our dictionary. The core idea of our method is as follows: 1.   Generating Candidate Pairs  : From large microblog corpora, we generate possible variant and normalisation (V-N) candidate pairs. These pairs could be inferred based on typical contractions, abbreviations, colloquialisms, or other forms of lexical variations. For instance, "tmr" could be inferred as a variant of "tomorrow". 2.   Contextual Weighting  : We use context information to generate and weight these candidate pairs. This allows the method to focus on variants that occur in semantically or formally similar contexts.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models is a prohibitive task due to the high computational cost during inference. Beam search is a widely used technique that reduces this cost while aiming to improve the translation quality compared to greedy search. In beam search, a fixed-sized beam (typically 5-10) is used to track, at each decoding step, the most promising translation hypotheses. The final translation is given by the hypothesis with the highest (or average) score among the top-k generated hypotheses. While effective, it has been observed that increasing the beam size does not always lead to better translation quality. For example, increasing the beam size beyond a certain point (typically 10) leads to a drop, rather than a rise, in translation quality. This counterintuitive phenomenon is often referred to as the 'beam search curse'. It presents a paradox to researchers and practitioners, as ensuring the best translation quality needs a faster and more scalable inference - which larger beams are expected to provide. Hence, understanding and addressing the beam search curse is crucial to improving NMT models' inference efficiency while maintaining their translation quality. The key intuition behind the beam search curse can be traced back to the hierarchical greedy nature of beam search. At each decoding step, the current or 'best' hypothesis is determined based on a uniform scoring function on the partial symbols generated so far. However, if different parts of the hypothesis have varying lengths, this uniform scoring can lead to 'divergence' of the beam: the hypothesis with the longest length (i.e., the one with the most symbols) receives high scores at later decoding steps, while the hypothesis with shorter (but potentially more accurate) translations falls behind. Evolutionarily, longer hypotheses tend to include more frequent substrings, which are more likely to be scored higher, but may not necessarily contribute to a better overall translation. The ideal goal is to find the set of the top-k most viable translation candidates, based on complete translations (the end-to-end objective), rather than partial ones evaluated at each step. One of the most straightforward ways to address this problem is to relax the static beam size. Instead of evaluating N hypotheses each time (N is the beam size), we can allow the number of candidates to vary dynamically and adaptively across the search space. This changing beam strategy can potentially help to balance between diverse hypotheses and can avoid the divergence of beam that occurs in the static beam size case.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental source of real-time information and have revolutionized the way today's society communicates and consumes news. The sheer volume of information produced daily presents significant opportunities for comprehensive information analysis, but also various challenges, including information organization, analysis and tracking. A subset of these challenges is related to the need to extract insights from questions and answers asked and provided over these platforms and across different languages and domains. A particular type of question that has garnered significant interest in the past few years, due to the volume at which they are asked and the criticality of their answers, is that of how to identify misinformation on Twitter. Many societal and demographic factors have contributed to a large-scale proliferation of misinformation online, including political propaganda, scams, and hoax stories, that have been shown in some cases to have real-world consequences, such as panics, violent reactions, and even influencing elections. The need to tackle misinformation has led to many new research efforts on the topic. One important aspect of the problem is the identification and tracking of questions with missing or wrong answers, known as knowledge gaps. Questions might be answered over time, similar or identical ones are continuously asked by different individuals. As for the answers, their quality and completeness or even correctness depend on many factors, such as the context, available information, relevance to the domains being discussed, and different levels of "authority" of those who provide them. A key research problem in the area of online question-answering over social media platforms is to algorithmically identify knowledge gaps in the form of questions or their answers. This necessitates a deep understanding and formalization of the concepts of questions, answers, knowledge gaps, and quality in the context of social media. One aspect of understanding the questions, and their contexts, is to identify "problems" that the questions likely reveal. A problem is a sub-topic or domain-specific topical area that contains different questions, or even different textual expressions (e.g., "How can I improve my memory?" and "What methods should I use to try and remember?" could be relating to the same question "How to improve memory?"). Our first contribution in this paper is a method to discover such problems from questions by means of clustering. While there is rich literature on clustering questions and changing the set of questions over time (Mulder et al., 2017; Jatkowski et al., 2016), these methods typically do not consider real-time changes and so do not perform well on dynamic data such as social media messages.

Training embeddings using all the available data can optimize the word meanings achieving overall better generalization performance. However, domain adaptation is still challenging due to domain shift. While several works (Dhingra et al., 2018;Kumar et al., 2017) provide methods to improve domain adaptation through adversarial learning, these methods do not questions if the representation of words should be the same across domains. This paper instead offers an alternative: "What if, instead of trying to share word meanings across domains, we preserve the domain-specific properties of words? Our key hypothesis is that this will provide better results in tasks involving domain-adaptation." Consequently, we propose an unsupervised word representation learning solution to capture domain-specific word semantics without using any external resource/domain-aware annotation beyond a domain-partition. The approach is based on two novel constraints derived directly from domain-specific semantic properties. The first one addresses a word in a particular domain - "Two words in the same document should be semantically similar if they co-occur." This constraint ensures that the representation of a word is closely tied to its semantics within its own domain. The second constraint addresses the similar meanings across domains - "Words with the same meaning in different domains should have similar representations."We propose a method to intuitively capture domain-specific word meanings using common words and enforce their representations to be similar across distinct domains. These two constraints are jointly optimized through an objective function that we derive for word representation learning. The proposed method sets itself apart as unsupervised, yet it also aligns with the widely accepted theory of "semantic meaning is relative" Aharoni (2012)Hualing, 2014). Our hypothesis is demonstrated through sentiment classification tasks involving domain adaptation. We adopt a standard baseline embedding model and fine-tune it on target-domain data, followed by domain adaptation. This approach is contrasted against models that do not enforce domain differences or use external domain-aware resources. We demonstrate that preserving domain-specific properties of words (instead of forcing representations to be the same across domains) leads to improved sentiment classification accuracy for a variety of domain adaption tasks, even surpassing state-of-the-art domain-agnostic embeddings in certain cases. The approach is systematic, easily implementable and computationally efficient. It also aligns with the recent trend of domain adaptation by ensuring that domain-specific information is preserved and not overlooked. Moreover, this method of preserving domain specific information in word representations provides a basis for further research such as better semantic interpretation for domain-adaptation tasks, and has significant potential in other NLP tasks like document summarization, question answering, and almost all tasks that

Training embeddings using large unlabelled text corpora has proven an effective means of capturing lexical-level semantic relationships (Mikolov et al., 2013;Pennington et al., 2014;Levy & Goldberg, 2014). Further work improving these embeddings by incorporating semantics beyond the size of corpora has shown positive results for machine translation (Socher et al., 2013;Zhou et al., 2016). This work extends those efforts by combining neural word embeddings with structured knowledge for machine translation. Our Knowledge-Based Semantic Embedding (KBSE) model incorporates a knowledge base into the word embedding, using the graph representation of the knowledge base to jointly train the embeddings. This work builds on our previous work in knowledge-based semantic embedding (Hosanagar, 1999;Xiong et al., 2017). In this model each word is mapped to a latent vector that is a function of its context within the sentence and its relationships within a knowledge base. This latent vector captures how semantically similar the word is to other words similar in meaning within the document (as captured by standard embedding methods such as Word2Vec or GloVe) as well as its relationship to other words which it might be connected to conceptually within a knowledge base. This allows our model to use extra contextual information from structured knowledge bases while still leveraging the advantages of large scale learning on unannotated text corpora. Our algorithm aligns the knowledge base with a word embedding model through an inference over a joint joint probability distribution over the knowledge base edges and the word embeddings. This is akin to previous work suggesting that neural networks trained on semantic tasks can capture general cognitive abilities and automate many cognitive processes that were previously solved through manual efforts (Sloman, 2001). The proposed model consists of two main parts: 1) a word embedding model that maps each word or phrase in the source and target languages to a fixed-dimensional semantic vector; 2) a knowledge base, which serves as a base for understanding the world and assisting translation. The embeddings are explicitly tied to concepts in the knowledge base by making each word in the embeddings generation function depend on a likelihood term based on the shared concept within the knowledge base. The knowledge base is treated as a graph where each node represents a concept in the knowledge base and edges capture relationships between concepts. The structure of this graph is such that each semantic concept within the knowledge base has some informative association to a word or phrase in the text.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models with a prohibitive number of training instances can yield better generalization capabilities (Dzmitry and Schuster, 2012;Sennrich et al., 2015;Hulth and Nivre, 2016;Wolf and Ney, 2016;Arivazhagan et al., 2017;Peng and Zhang, 2017;Strubell et al., 2017). However, building large parallel corpora (and thus large scale training datasets) is very challenging due to practical limitations, such as time and cost (Firat et al., 2016). SMT (SMT) models, relying on statistical alignment and phrase tables, do not face this issue. In fact, SMT is known to be very effective in extracting large weighted phrase translation dictionaries (Vogel et al., 2003;Koehn and Hoang, 2007;Junczys-Dowmunt and Pouliquen, 2017) over big parallel corpuses. Offline phrase extraction can be done without major computational resources, opening the possibility to integrate or even pre-process the extracted phrase translations before NMT training. Integrating these SMT pre-processed phrases into the training data is the focus of most previous works on phrase-informed NMT (Rizzo et al., 2017;Liu and Zhang, 2017;Liu et al., 2018;Ronen et al., 2017). A significant drawback, however, is that the additional information is added as a handcrafted auxiliary file, which is read and considered at test time. This "offline" model lacks the ability to adapt real-time to the specific contextual information from the source sentence that is necessary to contextualize and choose the relevant phrase translations. This means that one may end up falling back to the less general side of phrase-based methods: hard-coded and inflexible. This work proposes a novel neural easy-first NMT model to automatically leverage pre-extracted phrase translation knowledge during training.   Motivation  : There is a rich array of concepts in language that can be best captured by identifiable units larger than words. These units include phrases, idioms, and multi-word expressions but also larger constructions like named entities or fixed expressions. These concepts can be abundant in parallel training data but also in general language usage. For example, the term "unpaid holiday" may be manifested as distinct words across languages. Neural machine translation almost universally uses word-based models which struggle to identify such regularities and sufficiently capture their translation dynamics, particularly when they span a certain length. A skilled human translator could match "unpaid holiday" to "vacances non payées" in French, by considering the phrase as a whole, while this might not be obvious when looking at the words individually. In contrast, phrase-based SMT literature has successfully used a range of techniques to extract such phrases and their translations and then apply these in translation prediction.

Training natural language parsers without manual annotation is a major challenge. A key difficulty is the inherent cost of annotation itself. Even for welldefined tasks, such as dependency parsing, the annotation of a corpus larger than a few million words is prohibitively expensive (Edmonds & Cotton, 2010;Nivre et al., 2013). A related challenge is cross-task performance; a parser trained on one corpus often fails when applied to another (Xu et al., 2015). This can occur even when two corpora are similar (e.g. for English, both extracted from online sources), due to changes in content or linguistic structure (Nakatani, 2013). Even for fully supervised learning, where training data is expensive, domain adaptation techniques have been developed (Blitzer et al., 2006;Blitzer et al., 2005), though recent work shows that fully unsupervised approaches can also benefit from adaptation-like strategies (Henelius et al., 2014;Blunsom et al., 2014). In fully unsupervised parsing, these problems are exacerbated. Without any annotated data, training relies on structure inherent in the data or derivation from other phenomena (e.g. bracketing from coreference and anaphora; Johnson, 1973;Steedman, 2000). A key approach for unsupervised parsing in the past 20 years has been unsupervised grammar induction followed by treebank reconstruction. This method, though successful for dependency parsing (Collins, 1999;Toma et al., 2015;Seginer, 2007), has faced challenges in contexts where treebank annotations may not be available or when the underlying language model diverges significantly from the training data (Matusov et al., 2016). Many fully unsupervised parsers (Xia et al., 2009;Seginer, 2007;Alshawi et al., 2010) initially perform either explicitly or implicitly by clustering similar sentences or by making assumptions about sentence structure (e.g. sentences are often assumed to be tree-branching structures (Sect. 3)). Though appealing, such approaches sometimes make simplified assumptions about linguistic structure or fail to capture cross-domain boundaries and task variations. In this paper, we explore an alternate strategy for improving unsupervised parsing performance across domains or tasks. Our key idea is to adaptively choose a training subset from the data during the training process itself. Informally, this could be achieved by looking for out-of-sample subset pairs that improve a certain performance metric when used for training. We term this “zoomed learning”. The idea of zoomed learning generalizes previous notions of sample selection or subset evaluation. In domain adaptation and transfer learning (Blumer et al., 1998;Blumer et al., 2001), the aim is to learn a model that performs well across multiple domains by selecting a subset of data from across domains to train on (Kim, 2014;Fraiman et al., 2015).

Training natural language parsers across languages requires large amounts of annotated training data to capture the linguistic variability across languages. However, many languages have few or no available annotated resources and therefore automated annotation methods are crucial for these languages. In this paper, we consider the problem of dependency grammar induction from bitext. A particular challenge in this setup, as opposed to monolingual questions, is that word-aligned bitext itself does not contain enough evidence to fully determine the target language's grammar, thus our proposed methods must balance minimal language-specific assumptions with effective use of available bitext resources. Our key contributions are twofold: First, we devise a novel approach to grammar induction from bitext, using constraints based on word alignments, which allow partial and lazy transfer of grammatical structures across languages. Second, we evaluate our approach on three languages from different language families (Bulgarian, Spanish, and Persian), comparing against several alternative methods in the scope of grammar induction from bitext. These evaluations reveal that our methods consistently perform well and even achieve state-of-the-art results on the CoNLL shared task 2008 Spanish corpus. The problem of grammar induction from bitext can be viewed within the context of general language induction. The main assumption in our approach is that both the source and target languages are generated according to a uniform grammar, allowing the partial alignment provided by bitext to ground the different surface forms in the languages. This alignment may come from word aligners of varying accuracy. The challenge in this setting is that the bitext itself does not provide enough syntactic information to fully learn the target language's grammar without additional language-specific assumptions (e.g., universal grammar principles or treebank resources, see van Noord et al. 2006; Silva and John 2011, and Yamada and Matsumoto 2003). Previous approaches to grammar induction from bitext (e.g., De Gispert 2002; Zhang and Resnik 2012) or zero-shot parsing (e.g., De Smedt 2008; Lopez 2008; Johnson 2008) were based on fully projected or abstracted trees or had strong assumptions about the type of grammar or structure of the target language. While these methods could benefit from the bytext information, our new approach takes a step back by avoiding these advanced assumptions – it instead learns a general dependency grammar in the target language by defining and using informative constraints on partial structure over words. More specifically, our method computes a global alignment of a bitext segment between the source and target languages.

Creating a learner corpus that is both manually error-tagged and shallow-parsed is a first step toward making research more replicable and inter-comparable. By making such data and tools available to the public, we also hope to facilitate research and education on various aspects of language learning. As we describe in Sect. 3, the process of creating a manual errortagged corpus is labor-intensive and time-consuming because a human annotator has to carefully read the text and identify the errors and judgments that they perceive (Chodorow, 2010). Table 2 (and Appendix A for more details) provide a detailed description of our approach, including a discussion of our categorizations and annotations, along with explanations of why we chose our approach over others. By creating such a corpus, we hope to stimulate similar efforts from others. Sentences that have been manually errortagged are not only useful for error detection research but can also be used for grammatical error correction and even automated grading. As a recent review (Biber and Gray, 2010) suggests, learner corpus studies have made significant contributions to how we conceptualize English grammar, particularly in relation to second-language acquisition. In fact, the study of grammatical errors and the development of error detection tools or even grammar checkers are often tightly interwoven. In addition, we see that some domains have already begun using different levels of automata to interact with foreign language learners, including the error correction tools. For instance, in ITS development, research has focused on several tasks such as sentence segmentation, part-of-speech tagging (POS), named entity recognition, and basic error tagging (see Akaichi et al., 2012; De Witte, 2006; Granger, 2011). However, progress in these efforts has been somewhat slow due to the restricted availability of learner data and lack of progress in developing more advanced error tagging or textual analysis techniques that could be applied directly or indirectly to learner texts (Ling and Reinhard, 2010). Our corpus can also be used for the development of automated essay scoring systems since error tagging can potentially help in judging the linguistic complexity and accuracy of candidate texts. Recent approaches in automated essay scoring have incorporated elements of error detection (Nenkova and Vanderwende, 2005; Roth, 2011; Tetreault et al., 2014). However, these systems often rely on training data such as student essays graded by human instructors or rubric-based scores (Page, 2006; ETS, 2002). The availability of error-tagged data like ours may potentially enrich these approaches by introducing direct linguistic errors as an additional feature.

Training neural sequence-to-sequence models often involves assuming that the input is perfectly recognized first, by an upstream system such as a word segmenter or part-of-speech (POS) tagger. However, this assumption may not always hold, as many practical problems exhibit imperfect input quality. For instance, the up-stream system may produce incorrect hypotheses, miss important details, or predict multiple possible predictions for the same piece of input. To address this issue, this paper proposes "Lattice-to-Sequence Models" (LSTMs), which explicitly incorporate the uncertainty of the input into the neural network. LSTMs operate on "lattices" alongside with their corresponding posterior probabilities. Unlike standard error measures like word error rate (WER), lattices can represent all possible input sequences and their likelihoods, offering a richer representation of uncertainty. This allows neural networks to learn directly from this uncertainty, ensuring that the model can derive a comprehensive understanding of the input - which we hypothesize will improve robustness and performance on imperfect data. We extend the TreeLSTM architecture (Tai et al., 2015) to handle lattices, resulting in a LatticeLSTM. The TreeLSTM generalizes regular LSTMs by running over nested, hierarchical data structures, such as parse trees. For lattices, it would thus view symbols as branches or leaves of a binary tree (or "candidate set" if extending beyond binary), while the 'pointer' in the TreeLSTM architecture allows for selecting the active path (i.e., the correct sequence). To incorporate posterior probabilities (i.e., the likelihoods of the lattice paths), we modify the TreeLSTM's child-sum and forget gates to dynamically allocate importance based on these scores. Additionally, we adapt the attention mechanism to directly incorporate the lattice's posterior confidence scores through a model-specific bias term, aiming to steer the attention towards the most likely hypotheses the lattices imply. We focus our experiments on the speech translation task, which naturally accommodates noisy inputs due to speech recognition. This task allows for evaluation under scenarios where up-stream speech recognition, as a primary uncertainty source, may introduce significant variability. We specifically consider lattice inputs produced by state-of-the-art Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems and investigate the comparative performance of Lattice-to-Sequence models versus conventional sequence-to-sequence models trained on either 1-best hypotheses or raw lattice symbols without posterior scores. The main hypotheses guiding our work are: (i) incorporating uncertainty represented in lattices will improve robustness to up-stream errors, and (ii) informative integration of posterior scores through LSTMs and attention will enhance performance.

Variability within documents of the same topic can significantly hinder topic classification achieving performance. In this paper, we propose an innovative variabilitiy normalization algorithm based on linear projection for topic classification. The algorithm primarily includes three key steps: (i) construction of an optimization problem to minimize intra-topic variability; (ii) solving the optimization problem using a kernel principle component analysis (KPCA); and (iii) constructing a new feature space and applying linear projection for feature transformation. The essential idea is to reduce the intra-topic variability of documents, as fracturing out this variability can lead to improved performance for classifiers. The extracted low-dimensional representation is then passed on to a support vector machine (SVM) or a k-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm for training and classification. The method is evaluated on a corpus of free-style conversations. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm leads to significant improvement in performance, particularly in micro-F 1 measure by 3.8% compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in improving topic classification by normalizing intra-topic variability. The paper also discusses the potential implications of this work in various domains such as sentiment analysis, document clustering, and information retrieval, where achieving robust performance under varied data conditions or noisy inputs is often a challenge. We discuss the impact on model interpretability provided by our approach, as well as potential applications in multimodal text analysis and cross-lingual topic modeling. This research can contribute to the broader development of more flexible and adaptable natural language processing (NLP) systems capable of handling data variability and complexities. The concept of variability in document analysis has garnered attention as an obstacle for various document-related tasks such as in text categorization, clustering, and information retrieval. Algorithms that handle this variability achieve better performance and generalization over unseen data. For example, in sentiment analysis, documents within a topic may vary due to differences in opinions, tones, or writing styles, while maintaining similarities on the topic itself. In text categorization, different documents under the same topic category can exhibit diverse patterns, making it difficult for models to generalize effectively. The proposed method aims to address this issue by normalizing this variability through linear projection before classification. Traditional approaches often address variability in topic classification through methods such as changing the representation of text documents, such as using TF-IDF or word embeddings, or by modifying the classification algorithm itself, including ensemble methods for improving robustness.

Language models are fundamental components of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and text generation. These statistical models learn to predict the likelihood of a sentence or a sequence of words given prior experience. Most current language models fall into one of two categories: count-based n-gram models or neural language models (NLM). Both have distinct advantages: count-based models are scalable and efficient in terms of computation, while neural models are known to achieve superior performance but often at a computational and resource cost. The fracturing of language models into two categories has set up a debate about which type is more suitable for a particular application. However, both categories can be seen as different, limiting representations of a rich underlying space of possible models. This work attempts to bridge this gap, by unifying the count-based and neural language models into a single, flexible framework. Unifying the two paradigms in a single framework offers several benefits: 1. Scalability and Efficiency: Count-based models are widely used due to their ability to quickly compute probabilities, even on large vocabularies. However, these models suffer from the problem of sparse data, often resulting in zero probabilities for unseen word sequences. Neural models, on the other hand, avoid this issue but are computationally expensive. Our framework utilizes a mixture of uniform distributions, allowing the models to learn a shared probability distribution for common vocabulary items while still being able to handle unseen data by relying on the count-based component. This can offer the best of both worlds - efficiency and scalability for common words, while being able to generalize to unseen or rare words using the neural component. 2. Improved Modeling Performance: A mixed-model framework allows for hybrid benefits. By learning a shared representation across all models, each model can benefit from the information represented by the others. For instance, while neural models are generally better at capturing long-range dependencies and complex patterns, the count-based models can contribute by focusing on more fundamental statistical patterns or vocabulary-specific patterns that do not require complex architectures. 3. Dynamic Resource Allocation: In our formulation, the mixture weights are parameters that can be learned jointly with the language model. This means that the model can adaptively decide when to rely more or less on the neural versus count-based components based on the characteristics of the input sequence.

Word segmentation is an important preprocessing step for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including statistical machine translation (SMT; Koehn, 2005). In languages with explicit word delimiters, the word segmentation problem is trivial, as words can be directly obtained from the input representation. However, this is not the case for languages like Chinese, Japanese, and Arabic where no explicit word delimiters exist. Without proper word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging and dependency parsing of a sentence would be incorrect. Table 1 (Koehn, 2005) shows that word alignment performance deteriorates when word segmentation errors occur. This implies word segmentation is crucial for MT. SMT models rely heavily on word-level alignments, so accurate word segmentation is critical. Automated Sentence Split (ASS) is a commonly used word segmentation method for Chinese in the context of SMT (Wang et al., 2009). An ASS module segments a sentence into words relying on the known language model (LM) of the target language, handling overlaps and providing a raw segmentation for further refinement. However, automatic approaches suffer from potential errors in their proposed segmentation, mainly because these techniques are designed to achieve general word segmentation, not specifically optimized for SMT application. The available annotated corpora for word alignment (WA) can be a valuable resource to correct automatic segmentation techniques. For example, the OpenMT corpus (Black et al., 2001) and several Chinese-English aligned corpora (Sun et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015) could provide an opportunity to align word boundaries with the manually annotated word alignments, thereby refining the initial automatic segmentation. In this paper, we propose an approach that refines word segmentation using a manually aligned corpus, aiming to better align the segmentation boundaries with those used for constructing word alignments. The fundamental idea is to use the word alignemnt as a "gold standard" for the expected segmentation. This differs from prior approaches where alignments are used as just one of several features to be learned for improving segmentation quality (Sun et al., 2014). Our method starts with an automated word segmentation using an available segmenter, such as the ASS module. Then, we align this raw segmentation with the gold word alignment to identify anomalies or segmentation errors, that is, word boundaries proposed in the raw segmentation do not match those in the aligned word structure. Our refinement step involves adjusting the word boundaries iteratively based on these identified conflicts. We show that most automated segmentation outputs indeed contain a significant number of mismatches compared to the manually aligned word boundaries (Section 3).

Modelling Sequential Text with an Adaptive Topic Model Topic models offer a powerful framework for capturing the underlying thematic structure of unstructured data such as text. While several works have tackled the problem of using topic models for sequential data, current approaches are not well equipped to model the transient nature of topics or the structure within the text, such as clauses or sentences. In this paper, we present an adaptive topic model (ATM) and an associated inference algorithm that are equipped to model short-term and long-term structural dependencies in sequential text. We extend a hierarchical topic model to include local and global adaptation for each data point, based on its previous and parent document context. This leads to a model capable of revealing, for example, a change in topic over the course of an individual sentence, while also being sensitive to the overall thematic structure of a document. Our ATM is derived by generalizing among semantic models, including topic models, LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation), and mixtures over topic models. We use a Gibbs sampler to efficiently compute posterior inference for parameter distributions in our ATM, as well as efficiently handling missing data. We conduct experiments on a range of datasets including sentences from various texts and hierarchical text documents. The results show that the ATM significantly outperforms existing approaches, especially in terms of perplexity and revealing fine-grained sequential structure and changes within the text. In this introduction, we first give a brief overview of the traditional topic model assumed in the context of static text. We then discuss the inadequacies of such models and other proposed approaches, leading to the motivation for the adaptive topic model proposed in this paper. Firstly, the traditional topic model (such as LDA) has been incredibly successful in capturing large-scale thematic structure in static text. The key idea is to assume that each piece of text is generated from a mixture over latent topics, each of which doesn't change over the course of the text. The topical structure that emerges from this generative model captures themes, but it doesn't capture dynamic or structured changes within the text. The dynamic nature of text - in terms of a single document, a paragraph, a sentence, or even a clause - means that the thematic content or focus can change quite rapidly. For example, within a long narrative or report, themes can shift over entire paragraphs changing the topics included in the text.

Multi-Target Machine Translation (MT) is a special type of machine translation (MT) where one uses a single source language to translate into two or more target languages at the same time. This type of translation may benefit the low resource target languages due to the information shared from the strong resource target language or other languages, as well as from the source language itself. In some multilingual and cross-lingual applications, multi-target MT can be more convenient and efficient than using separate MT systems for each target language (Smoilitskiy et al., 2014;Mogadham et al., 2015). In most existing NMT systems (Sutskever, 2014;Cho et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015;Vaswani et al., 2017), the translation from a source language to a target language is modelled as a single sequence transduction task. One example is the popular Hierarchically Character-Level Sentence Representation (HCL) NMT model (Dai et al., 2018). However, directly extending hierarchical NMT to support multi-target translation can be challenging, because both the encoder and decoder need to handle multiple target languages simultaneously. The formalism of Synchronous Context-Free Grammars (SCFGs) with shallow structures has been widely applied to multi-lingual and cross-lingual language learning tasks, such as MT and cross-lingual coreference resolution (Zhou et al., 2012;Peñas et al., 2014;Tjong Kim Sang et al., 2013;Das and Smith, 1993). We propose expanding this formalism to handle multi-target translation. Essentially, in our proposed framework, the SCFG for multi-target MT describes the contextual dependencies and the mappings between the source and all target language sentences. The main idea is to leverage the information contained in multiple target language structures to help disambiguate the source to target language mappings. The SCFG rules can be automatically extracted from parallel corpora or can be derived from deep models if available. For example, in MT, each SCFG rule describes a possible byte-pair encoding (BPE) or character-level tokenization of source words to multiple target words simultaneously. Due to the complex nature of multi-target translation, we need efficient methods for rule extraction, rule scoring, rule pruning, and efficient search using the SCFG. Rule Extraction: To extract rules for multi-target MT, we can adopt the standard rule induction algorithms, adapted for the specific task. These algorithms typically consider dependencies among source words, target words, and rules. The extracted rules can be induced from training data or further filtered and refined using statistical language models or neural language models (NLMs).

Social media platforms, such as Facebook, Twitter and blogs, have become an integral part of contemporary online communication. They provide unparalleled access to vast amounts of user-generated content, which represents a valuable resource for understanding the dynamics and trends of society, individual behavior, and the voice of various groups or communities. Words and language, as a product of human expression, are particularly revealing. Hence, the development and use of demographic lexica – sets of words or idioms that are used more frequently by members of specific demographic groups – have potential for widespread use in social science, economic and business applications. Traditionally extracted from existing demographic segmentation approaches, these lexica are commonly based on knowledge from marketing, sociology, and psychology. However, with the dawn of big data analytics, computational approaches have been introduced to automatically derive such lexica. This method allows for online analysis and is flexible enough to incorporate the dynamic nature of language usage across various platforms, genres, demographics and even time [1] [2] [3]. Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach, identifying lexica with high predictive performance [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] for gender, age, and other demographic or psychological traits. For instance, a significant body of work exists in predicting age from written text, with applications ranging from cybersecurity to marketing. [6] [7] while another research direction focuses on deriving predictive lexica for gender. However, several key limitations remain in the current state-of-the-art. First, many existing lexica are generated using specific datasets (e.g., AGEIST.com, crowdsourced surveys) or text genres (e.g., social media platforms, books, blogs) that may not generalize well across other domains. Second, while model performance on the dataset used for training is often reported, the analysis is inconsistent in evaluating generalization across different platforms or message types (e.g., short vs. long posts). Third, studies rarely consider or report the sensitivity of measured variables (e.g., a single word, a set of words, a vector space model) to demographic prediction. Different lexical measures will likely yield different results and may be more or less suited to specific prediction tasks. Lastly, the provided lexica are generally not shared publicly, limiting transparency, reproducibility, and the potential for future advanced research – a critical challenge for the field [12]. In this work, we aim to address these limitations by developing and publicly sharing age and gender predictive lexica based on comprehensive and diverse social media data.

Response-based Learning for Machine Translation of Open-domain Database Queries Summary: Developing an open-domain online database query translation system is challenging due to its open language and domain and the inherent noise from natural language use. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn a machine translation (MT) system by leveraging response signals retrieved from a database querying process. In particular, we adapt an MT system using a response-based learning algorithm, aided by the execution and feedback from a semantic parser that checks the feasibility and accuracy of the translated queries against the database. The approach demonstrates promising results and outlines a potential direction for improving open-domain query translation systems. 1. Introduction Machine translation (MT) systems, while remarkably powerful, are typically trained on large parallel datasets. These datasets often span specialized domains and require significant domain-specific resources and expertise. This is a significant limitation for open-domain systems, which are expected to perform well in a broad range of language and domain contexts. Open-domain database query translation systems face additional challenges due to the inherent noise and openness of user language and the absence of direct parallel data. Typically, translation output evaluations in such systems are focused on fluency metrics or entity translation accuracy. However, these metrics alone do not directly reflect the system's ability to generate queries that successfully retrieve the correct information from a database. The lack of direct feedback from a database query execution is a significant limitation in the training and evaluation of open-domain query translation systems. Database query success depends on syntactic correctness in the database’s query language and semantic correctness in the database’s schema and content. A successful query must both meet the formal language requirements of the database (e.g., SQL) and express an appropriate request within the database’s semantic framework (e.g., correct use of entities and relationships). To address this gap, we propose an approach that learns a model using feedback signals generated from real-world query execution against the database. We elicit supervision signals from responses to queries — whether the query successfully retrieved results and, if so, whether these results match the expected or desired information. The measured variables may include the execution time, the validity of the matched results against a reference set, and the types of errors encountered during or after query translation and execution. 2. Response-based Learning Response-based learning is a paradigm where feedback from task outcomes (e.g., query success on a database) is used to adapt a model.

Compositional Semantic Parsing on Semi-Structured Tables One of the central objectives of natural language understanding today is the development of systems that can interpret and utilize knowledge from broad-domain, deeply structured resources, particularly for question answering (QA) tasks. This is challenging for several reasons. First and most fundamentally, language exhibits a kind of "compositionality" which allows complex meanings to be built up from simpler statements (Ara, 2019; Barros et al., 2015; Gildea et al., 2015). However, this property of language scales with its expressive power, creating a combinatorial explosion in the knowledge space it describes, making it hard to capture in a machine-readable format. Second, such verbalized knowledge today often resides in heterogeneous formats - in structured databases, semi-structured online resources, or unstructured natural text - each of which presents unique challenges for interpretation. For example, while structured databases are well-documented and consistent, they are generally limited in scope, and semantic ambiguity can still exist at the interface between data and query (Ren et al., 2017). On the other hand, while semi-structured (and unstructured) sources like Wikipedia can provide broader, more diverse or even dynamic knowledge, they often lack the formality needed for direct and precise interpretation (Dremel et al., 2010; Shneiderman and Plaisant, 2005). These challenges make the acquisition and representation of meaning from such diverse sources a complex and multi-faceted problem (Li et al., 2018). To address this, systems must be able to cope with the compositionality inherent in language, as well as the semantic structure (and potential ambiguities) of the knowledge sources themselves. In this context, semantic parsing has been a central technique in NLP (Informatics and Language Instruction, 2012; Wong and Mooney, 2007). The goal of semantic parsing is generally to translate natural language queries or statements into formal, machine-processable, meaning-representations such as logical forms or programs (Allen et al., 2007; Berant et al., 2013; Belz et al., 2010). These meaning representations aim to capture not just the vocabulary choices of a sentence, but also the logical relationships and roles of entities within it. For example, a query like "Who directed the movie that won Best Picture in 2017?" might be semantically parsed into a relation between entities (a director, a movie, and an award) and an assertion of the movie's relation to the award (it won). However, current semantic parsing systems are typically narrow in scope, focused either on limited domains or on shallow, rather than deep, compositionality.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) systems have been shown to produce highly effective translations using large corpora. A central component in nearly every SMT system is the language model which estimates the probability of a source sentence. While the original and well-known N-gram language modeling technique is ideal for training language models because of its simplicity and efficiency, a compelling argument can be made for using more advanced and context-sensitive models given that the state-of-the-art SMT systems are very effective and seem to have already accounted for most useful language model statistics. We argue that there are still significant gains to be had for SMT systems that use more sophisticated language models alongside the standard N-grams. In particular, while we know that part-of-speech tagging (but not POS vocabulary) improves translation, we claim that a more significant performance gain in SMT systems can still be made by directly incorporating more lexical semantic context beyond simple part-of-speech tags into language models. Our contribution in this work is to develop an extension of the traditional N-gram language model which is designed to account for more lexical context, as well as to demonstrate its effectiveness in statistical machine translation. To incorporate more lexical context, we build separate local language models for each word and part-of-speech pair. This approach allows each word to be estimated using a probability distribution more context-sensitive to the specific word's lexical properties and surrounding syntactic properties. These local language models are built during a pre-training phase while the system is still trained on large in-vocabulary corpora. During decoding (i.e., translation), we use the local models to create a more refined language model probability estimation for each word based on its local context as provided by the partial translation hypothesis being considered. The intuition behind this approach is that words should be estimated by the probabilities of all contexts they appear in and that such context should be lexicalized. For example, in English, it is known that "strong" has different interpretations depending on whether it is used to describe wine, human strength, or emotion (e.g., strong sun or strong love). More specifically, in SMT a word like "strong" matched with a translation unit in Chinese that may also be ambiguous, should be associated with a probability distribution that reflects its potential to appear in various and appropriate contexts in English.

Training embeddings using large unlabelled data sets has seen exciting developments in recent years, achieving state-of-the-art performance in nearly every NLP task. While these embedding spaces are normally assumed to be single-purpose (e.g. for a visual task, a language modeling task, etc.), training embeddings that are robust and general, able to exploit similarities across different questions or modalities, could have profound practical applications and could be seen as a generalization of the "zero-shot" generalization idea. For example, pre-trained visual language models can predict labels for images never seen before, but only if those labels were seen during training (for instance, due to a large text corpus in which those labels appeared) (Kiros et al., 2014;Xiong et al., 2016). The idea is then naturally extended to "cross-lingual zero-shot" among semantic languages (Xian et al., 2017;Lan et al., 2017), but less is known about how such semantic mappings extend to cross-modal settings (image-to-text) or even cross-task (e.g. using a cross-validation set similar to Wang et al. (2017)). However, these techniques all require at least some training data in the target domain, so a more ambitious goal would be to exploit the semantic similarity obtained from unsupervised training across multiple spaces, without any target data (i.e. the "true" labels). If the similarity space is at all related to the task at hand (and can serve as a form of "semantic transfer"), it should be feasible to scale current supervised task performance to domains where no labeled data is available. This in itself remains as an open question in cross-space mapping for "zero-shot" contexts, but there are some encouraging results (Wang and Gupta, 2016; 2017; Tan et al., 2016). One particular approach that receives attention is using structured representations (e.g. graphs or parse trees of measured variables) together with GNNs (Pai et al., 2018) or hierarchical attention (Nonchev et al., 2018) to align distributions across domains and embeddings spaces. While these methods are changing the landscape of learning-to-learn and meta-learning methods, they also require careful tuning over sparse cross-modal data.
